    5. The stated concrete smooth model. The graph embedding in (D.T32) represents three
times the generator. Its oriented real rank-four normal bundle is trivial: the ambient manifold
is spin and w2 (T S 2 ) = 0, and w2 classifies such bundles on S 2 . The framing is unique up to
homotopy because π2 SO(4) = 0. The framed surgery preserves simple connectivity and spin.
Its integral sequence and duality give H2 = H3 = Z/3, with b3 = 0. The mod-three class from
the first S 2 extends across the surgery trace, since it evaluates to zero on the attaching sphere.
The original pair (S 2 × S 4 , u) spin-bounds S 2 × D5 over K(Z/3, 2). Thus the resulting model
has zero spin-bordism class over this Eilenberg–Mac Lane space. Zhubr’s Theorem 3 (Zhubr,
1975, p.795) identifies it, orientation-preservingly, with every manifold in (D.T31), since both
classifying maps induce isomorphisms on H2 and both have b3 = 0.

    Let A : H2 (V ) → Z be evaluation by the pullback of the marked weight-one class used in

     Every literal fixed-loop peripheral torus is anti-invariant, since inversion reverses its fibre

     Every nonfinite fibre kernel and its marked normal. All the unchanged caps in this construction
have torsion-free H2 . For the rank-two cusp this is the explicit normalization calculation. For a
rank-one gamma cover the normalized components are S 2 bundles of degree zero over a covered

is free. The nonzero-Chern originals have the primitive Gysin presentations of 4.41–33, also free.
     The covering square on regular fibres multiplies bivectors by Λ2 Sd . The needed ranks come
from the actual caps, as follows. At the rank-two zero the short-period map has Smith factors

particular the regular-fibre coinvariant of rank four injects into the cap. This proves that the
rational fibre kernel is precisely the monodromy image, without a local invariant-cycle assumption.
     For the rank-one cap, the explicit cycle of ρ spheres times T 2 has four independent nearby-fibre
classes: the sum of the component spheres, the surviving nodal-circle class times each transverse
circle, and the transverse T 2 area. This is the full four-dimensional fibre coinvariant, so again its
kernel is exactly the monodromy image over Q. For an original zero-degree additive cap, the
permutation mapping torus of the Kodaira tree gives the two independent images: the nonzero
multiplicity-weighted whole-fibre class in the component-orbit space, and the transverse δγ area.
These are the full two-dimensional fibre coinvariant, also for the original odd-star fibres. The
zero-degree multiplicative original has the same four explicit classes as the nodal-cycle model.
     Thus in every zero-degree case the rational fibre kernel is exactly the inverse image of the old
one. For a nonzero-Chern original the actual area and principal-bundle formulas give the same
statement directly. Since the target H2 is torsion free, the integral kernel is the saturation of

     For clarity we also fix the sphere convention. The homomorphism π3 SO(3) → π3 SO(6) has
image 2Z. Consequently changing the normal framing of an embedded S 3 does not change the
parity of its induced stable framed class. For the standard sphere bounding a ball, the induced
stable framed class is zero and its tangent three-frame represents the nonzero class in π3 V6,3 = Z/2
relative to a constant ambient three-frame. Equivalently, the tangent Lie framing on S 3 has
class ν, and a change of ambient frame by degree d changes that class by dν, while the relative
three-frame class changes by d mod 2. Thus Zhubr’s required nontrivial relative three-frame is
equivalent to even induced stable framed class on the sphere. These conventions agree with the
quaternionic calculation in (Zhubr, 2013, Section 5).
     Since λ(X) = 0, T X is stably trivial: the only obstruction for a spin bundle on a six-
dimensional complex is its class in H 4 (−; π3 Spin), namely λ. Moreover T X is actually trivial
on X ◦ = X \ {p}. For example its complex bundle has c1 = c2 = 0 and its last obstruction lies
in H 6 (X ◦ ; Z) = 0. Any framing there extends stably across p, since π5 SO = 0. All such full
framings have the same relative three-frame parity on an embedded torsion S 3 : their difference
lifts to Spin(6) and its degree-three class is a class of H 3 (X ◦ ; Z), which evaluates to zero on a
torsion three-cycle. An embedded sphere in the integral class of the regular torus T = he1 , e2 , γi
used below can also be constructed explicitly, so its existence is not an additional representability
assumption. Apply Kaplan’s construction to the spin structure induced on the normally framed
T : it gives a four-dimensional filling with one zero-handle and only two-handles, preserving that
almost framing (Kaplan, 1979, Definition 1.7, Remark 1.8, Theorem 3.1). Delete the zero-handle
and reverse the cobordism. Realize the resulting two-handle attachments as ambient surgeries
in X ◦ . Their attaching circles bound embedded disks with interiors disjoint from T and from
one another, since π1 (X ◦ ) = 0, 2 + 3 < 6 and 2 + 2 < 6. Prescribe a boundary collar along the
first normal vector. The two tangent framing directions of each attachment and the other two
normal directions give a four-frame around the boundary of its disk. Its extension obstruction
in π1 SO(4) = Z/2 is exactly the spin obstruction of that two-handle, and vanishes. Thickening
these disks therefore performs the prescribed surgeries inside X ◦ . The resulting embedded S 3
has the same integral homology class as T . Brown’s identity already supplies its parity; this
construction additionally verifies its geometric realization without changing the prescribed spin
structure. Zhubr’s Theorem 1 now implies

       P (X) = 0     ⇐⇒     a full ambient framing is admissible on the torsion S 3 .          (D44.4)

Indeed the forward implication is not an assumption about arbitrary three-frames. Take the
admissible three-frame supplied by that theorem. If P = 0, its spin rank-three complement
has vanishing primary obstruction c2 ; the only possible further obstruction on the punctured
six-manifold is in H 5 (X ◦ ; Z/2) = 0. The complement is therefore trivial, and the three-frame
extends to a full framing. Conversely an admissible full framing has trivial complement and hence
refined class zero. Independence of the full framing proves (D44.4) for the particular framing
used below.
    The reference frame and the actual critical-cycle defect. Write f : X → P1 for the torus
fibration and V = ker(df ) for its holomorphic differential kernel. This is a locally free rank-two
sheaf, including at the critical curves. In the nodal chart f = xy it has basis x∂x − y∂y , ∂z ; in the

triangular cusp chart f = xyz it has basis x∂x − y∂y , y∂y − z∂z . The scalar δ-action defines a
nowhere-zero section of this abstract vector bundle, although its image as a vector field vanishes

lattice vector, so they cannot both vanish. This description is unchanged by the translation clutch.
As H 2 (X; Z) = 0, the quotient line V/Oδ is topologically trivial; hence V has a global smooth
frame whose first vector is δ. The line L = f ∗ T P1 is also topologically trivial.

in these spin six-manifolds is trivial, and its framing is unique since π2 SO(4) = 0. The stated
surgeries have H2 = H3 = Z/c and zero free third Betti number. The classifying map to K(Z/c, 2)
extends across each surgery trace. The model Zc,0 has refined class and fundamental-class

    Here is a proof that includes the missing parity. Remove a point away from all chains. Write
b = 2a q with q odd. Join q parallel copies of N by normally framed tubes. Kaplan’s prescribed-spin
construction, followed by deletion of its zero-handle and reversal, gives a cobordism to a sphere
using only two-handles (Kaplan, 1979, Definition 1.7, Remark 1.8 and Theorem 3.1). As in 4.53,
its attaching disks and normal four-frames can be realized in the punctured simply connected
six-manifold: general position gives disjoint disks and the spin condition is exactly their π1 SO(4)
extension obstruction. Thus the outgoing sphere is actually embedded and represents q[N ], the
two-primary generator. Now choose Zhubr’s admissible three-frame v for this particular embedded
sphere, as permitted by his Theorem 1 Zhubr (2013), and put ξ = v ⊥ . Its spin framing obstruction
is o4 (ξ) = P , and λ(ξ) = 2o4 (ξ) with his normalization. Choose a spin frame τ of ξ|N . It extends
over the tube and two-handle trace: the relative obstruction groups are π0 Spin(3) and π1 Spin(3),
both zero. Hence the framings induced by v + τ on the incoming and outgoing manifolds are
stably bordant. On the outgoing sphere, admissibility means even framed parity, as normalized in
4.53 and (Zhubr, 2013, Section 5). Since q is odd, [N ]v+τ is even as well.
    The complement of the real codimension-four curve strata is simply connected, by general
position applied to disks. Both ρ|N and v + τ therefore induce the same spin structure. Their
difference lifts to Spin(6). Let a be its normalized degree-three integral class and k = ha, [N ]i.
The stable J image of the π3 Spin(6) generator is ν, so the two even framed parities imply k is
even. The integral transgression of λ gives, with consistent transition-map direction, the identity
of relative classes

                       λ(T X, ρ|N ) = 2o4 (ξ, τ ) + δa   in H 4 (X \ {p}, N ; Z).         (D45.10)

     The complete fundamental-class invariant and recognition. The global auxiliary-line
comparison and localization of 4.53 apply over Z/4 and Z/8, respectively. All actual original-II
coefficients are zero and all finite-II normal coefficients are bn and −br; hence the same mod-b
class extends for every parameter in (D45.2). For b = 20 apply that calculation separately over
Z/4 and Z/5. The C4 action has only the rational fixed curve and the I4 elliptic fixed curve, with
characters 2, 0. The C5 action similarly has the rational and I5 curves, with characters 0, 0; all
remaining stabilizers are prime to the relevant coefficient order. The actual Tate normal weights
have square one modulo four, and weight two modulo five. The cube formula is zero in each
coefficient ring: on the rational curve it is −3 times the square of its point character, and on the
elliptic curve the possible mixed degree-one term has square zero. Thus the full fundamental-class
invariant is zero, since H6 (K(Z/b, 2); Z) = Z/b is detected by the cube for b = 4, 8, 20 (Zhubr,
1975, Sections 3.11–3.14).
     The finite data therefore agree with the first two surgery models of 4.53. For b = 20, the
two primary parts of P = 14 are 2 ∈ Z/4 and a nonzero element of Z/5. The inclusion
K(Z/4, 2) ∨ K(Z/5, 2) → K(Z/4, 2) × K(Z/5, 2) is a homology equivalence: all cross tensor
and Tor terms vanish because their positive-degree homology has coprime primary orders. Both
spaces are simply connected, so it is a homotopy equivalence. The reduced spin-bordism invariant
consequently splits into these two summands, as in 4.47. The complete invariants agree with
Z4,1 #Z5,1 , and the free third Betti numbers also agree. Zhubr’s Theorems 3 and 5 Zhubr (1975)
give all the oriented diffeomorphisms in (D45.3).

Proof. The initial data are actual section-line data. Let M = O(P − O) and J = M ⊗ (TQ∗ M )−1 .
On a smooth elliptic fibre, translation acts trivially on Pic0 , so J is a vertical line bundle. At a
singular fibre its component multidegree is the difference of that of M and its Q-translate. It is
zero if P is narrow, and also if Q is narrow. Thus (D.GI1) makes every local multidegree zero.
The intersection matrix of each Kodaira fibre has kernel generated by its full multiplicity vector;
hence J is pulled back from the base. The height calculation in 4.28, equivalently the height
pairing with all local mixed corrections zero (Schütt and Shioda, 2010, Section 11.8), gives

                                           J ≃ f ∗ O(ab/d0 ).

This proves integrality of ab/d0 in the compatible sector. A base section with precisely the
chosen nonnegative divisor gives the required linearization. This does not introduce a component-
supported vertical correction to M .
    For completeness, the monodromy formula is also an integral geometric formula. The
rigidified Poincare bundle has elliptic section cocycles pi , qi ; its commutator pairing gives the
row ri = ((pi )2 , −(pi )1 )Bi . A local logarithm of Q gives the central entry ri zi , and a zero of the
linearization adds wi δγ ∗ . This is the same marked local calculation used in 4.28 and 4.46, now
before restricting either section coefficient. Changing zi by a fixed vector changes no entry: ri
annihilates ker(Bi − I).

    Why these detectors are complete. We include the low-degree integral target calculation to
exclude an undetected finite subgroup. For a cyclic group,
                                     H2 (K(Z/d, 2); Z) = Z/d,
                                     H4 (K(Z/d, 2); Z) = Z/D2 ,                              (D.WI22)
                                     H6 (K(Z/d, 2); Z) = Z/D3 .

The degree-four assertion follows from Whitehead’s exact sequence: on K(A, 2) its two adjacent
homotopy groups vanish, so H4 = Γ(A) (Whitehead, 1950, Theorem 1 and Section 2). For
A = Z/d, the universal quadratic generator q(1) has relations d2 q(1) = 2dq(1) = 0. Conversely
q(j) = j 2 modulo gcd(d2 , 2d) = D2 is well defined and quadratic. Thus these are its complete
relations and the image of CP2 generates. The ordinary or Pontryagin square evaluates on that
image as one modulo D2 , so it detects the entire group.
    For degree six, Zhubr’s epimorphism in Section 3.11 and his two free bordism generators
in Section 3.12 show that the spin-realizable part for a cyclic coefficient group is generated in
homology by the image of [CP3 ]: his other generator has zero fundamental-class image. For
odd-primary cyclic groups this is all of H6 , since the only obstruction in his Lemma 3.7 has
mod-two target. For a two-power cyclic group Section 3.12 explicitly gives ker α = H6 = Z/2a
(Zhubr, 1975, Lemmas 3.7 and 3.11, and Section 3.12, pp.805–807). The decomposition of Z/d
into its relatively prime primary factors gives the corresponding product of Eilenberg–MacLane
spaces. All cross tensor and Tor terms vanish, since their positive homology has relatively prime
orders. Hence H6 is cyclic and is generated by the image z of [CP3 ] for every d.
    The order of z divides both d3 and 3d. Indeed the class dh on CP3 becomes zero modulo d,
while its integral cube is d3 . On CP1 × CP2 the class dx + y reduces to a class factoring through
CP2 , whose degree-six image is zero, while its integral cube evaluates to 3d. Thus the order
divides gcd(d3 , 3d) = d gcd(d, 3) = D3 . The opposite bound is detected by the ordinary cube
when 3 - d, or by Thomas’s operation when 3 | d: on the reduced hyperplane class of CP3 the
full target value is one (Thomas, 1956, equation (2.8), p.267). This proves the last assertion of
(D.WI22) with its stated perfect detector.
    Finally K(Zr ⊕ Z/d, 2) = (CP∞ )r × K(Z/d, 2). The first factor has torsion-free homology
in even degrees and zero homology in odd degrees. The integral Kunneth formula has no Tor

                                                 194
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                       Paper III


term and gives exactly (D.WI14). Integral cubic monomials, uxi xj , Q2 (u)xi , and Q3 (u) are the
respective perfect coordinate detectors. Therefore (D.WI15) computes all of µ, including the
extra factors two and three.
    Application of smooth classification. The manifold is simply connected and spin, has H2 =
Zd−1 ⊕ Z/d and middle Betti number zero by 4.43, refined class zero by the first proof, and the
complete fundamental-class invariant (D.WI15). These are exactly the four invariants in Zhubr’s
Theorem 1, with the definitions on pp.794–795 (Zhubr, 1975, Theorem 1). Their values are
independent of every marked parameter in (D.WI1). Existence is supplied by the constructed
manifolds, and the injective classification gives one oriented diffeomorphism type for each d. This
proves (D.WI16) by an applied complete classification, rather than by ordinary cohomology or
an asserted connected-sum model.

     The normalization and conductor at every order. The cap retracts equivariantly to its central
rank-one toric fibre. The quotient of its q-gon dual graph by the reflection is an interval. There
are ρ vertex orbits and  edge orbits, with ρ +  = q + 1; the number of fixed vertices plus fixed
edges is two. The normalization and double-curve incidence graph is the barycentric subdivision

     A paired vertex has stabilizer generated by the square of the deck map. Its open C∗ bundle
has an abelian period lattice. The angular circle is primitive because gcd(N, k) = 1. Thus its
normalization is a ruled surface over a torus with zero Chern class, and its two pole sections have
the same class σ. A fixed vertex instead has a pole-interchanging clutch. Around the transverse
λ circle the relation Aλ = λ − α gives the projective loop z 7→ e−2πiu /z. Its determinant winding
is odd. Passing to the primitive quotient gamma loop uses an odd power of this map, since

bundle over a torus. Choose a section σ with σ 2 = 1 and denote its complex sphere fibre by F .
Its connected conductor bisection has class 2σ − F ; its self-intersection is zero because the pole
normal line becomes trivial on the cover.

Theorem 4.59 (all vertical corrections and new simply connected fillings). Let f : S → P1 be
one of the twenty-one recorded rational elliptic surfaces with Mordell–Weil group ZG, zero section

                                                                       −1

section-translation automorphism. Some such D makes JD the pullback of a base line bundle if
and only if d0 | ab. For every such correction the exact identity is

                                         JD ≃ f ∗ OP1 (ab/d0 ).                               (D.VC1)

Thus the compatible initial line bundles are not exhausted by requiring P or Q narrow at every
fibre. All corrections are determined by the integral local equations below, with precisely the
invariant component orbit sums as ambiguity. For a, b > 0 and any nonnegative whole-fibre
weights of total ab/d0 , the corrected punctured family has exactly the marked monodromies
(D.GI2). This does not identify its newly permitted original caps.

Proof. The actual original cap and the circle bundle. The reduced additive fibre is simply
connected and is homotopy equivalent to a wedge of its v rational component spheres. The
tangency in type III and the triple point in type IV do not add a graph loop; the same
assertion follows directly by taking the union of the rational components and their actual
connected intersections. The other listed fibres have a tree of rational components. The elliptic
neighbourhood retracts onto this fibre. The unit original linearization makes its compact cap the
mapping torus of the principal scalar-circle bundle Pc → K, with the lift of Q. This is the same
actual original filling used in 4.40–32, now retaining the full degree vector.
    A principal circle bundle over this wedge is determined by its v Chern evaluations. Its cellular
complex has one zero-cell, the scalar one-cell, v two-cells with boundary degrees ci , and v three-cells
with zero boundary. The lift of Q acts by the component permutation on the two- and three-cells.

                                                    204
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                       Paper III


There is no additional homotopy class of a gauge transformation: [K, S 1 ] = H 1 (K; Z) = 0. More
explicitly, after choosing a fixed point of the induced component-tree map and a fibre point there,
the component maps are homotopic to their orientation-preserving permutations. The invariant
vector c lifts this homotopy to the circle bundle. A comparison unit has a continuous logarithm
on K, so its lift is homotopic through bundle maps to the identity. A constant scalar at the
chosen point is removed by a scalar isotopy. This fixes the scalar circle and its product with the
mapping-torus direction throughout the comparison. The signs in (D.IC3) use the literal product
orientation t = δ ∧ γ: the boundary of a two-cell crossed with the long interval contributes +ci t.
This is the usual mapping cone after changing the signs of its shifted summands. Thus (D.IC3)
is an actual model, not merely a rational model with the same permutation.
    The circle-bundle homotopy sequence gives π1 (Pc ) = Z/g for c 6= 0. The return fixes the
scalar generator; the mapping-torus extension by the infinite cyclic group therefore splits. This
proves the fundamental-group statement and H1 .
    The integral extension. In C2 / im d3 , successive cells in an orbit have the relations

                                         ei+1 − ei + cj t = 0.                                (D.IC9)

Eliminating them leaves one free ej for each orbit, and the remaining relations are lj cj t = 0.
Hence this quotient is Zρ ⊕ Z/h. Its remaining boundary sends ej to cj δ and sends t to zero. Its
kernel is therefore Zρ−1 ⊕ Z/h. This proves the full nonsplit extension in H2 . For example, two
interchanged components of degree 2 contribute a relation 4t = 0, not two unrelated order-two
summands. The fibre product torus δ ∧ γ is the cone generator t itself.
    The degree-three cone has the direct sum of the coinvariants of the component three-cells, of
rank ρ, and the invariant component two-cycles with Chern evaluation zero, of rank ρ − 1. Both
groups are free. Degree four is the invariant component three-cell group of rank ρ. The same
calculation with c = 0 gives (D.IC5).
    There is also an intrinsic check of the extension. Let Y be the mapping torus of K and
Q. The cap is the principal Sδ1 bundle over Y . The Euler class evaluates as cj on the orbit
representatives in H2 (Y ), and as lj cj on invariant orbit sums in H3 (Y ) paired with the positive
γ. The integral Gysin sequence therefore injects Z/h into H2 (U ) by γ 7→ δ ∧ γ. The quotient is
the free kernel of the first Chern functional on H2 (Y ). This verifies both the extension and the
actual generator without a choice of an abstract splitting.
     The regular area and the full boundary image. In the single circle bundle Pc → K the map
H2 (Pc ) → H2 (K) is injective, with image ker(ct ). The regular elliptic area projects to µ, the
multiplicity cycle of the central fibre, and hence has its unique lift (µ, 0). The elliptic loops
crossed with the scalar circle vanish because H1 (K) = 0. After passing to Y , this area projects
to the orbit vector (lj µj ). Its content is qQ . The equality with the order of the component of Q
follows directly from the marked component permutations and multiplicities for the seven listed
types; the retained exact certificate checks every component class. The actual section-cocycle
model has the same order in coker(B − I), so the logarithm z has exactly this denominator.
    To identify the rational mixed area coefficients, pass to the qQ -fold long-circle cover. The
section qQ Q is narrow; its marked local logarithm straightens the translation through the original
elliptic neighbourhood, as in 4.25 and 4.40. Its corrected long direction is qQ (γ − z). An elliptic
loop crossed with this direction is zero in the base mapping torus because the elliptic loop bounds
in the Kodaira neighbourhood. Thus the two mixed free coefficients are z2 and −z1 times the
elliptic-area coefficient. The integers qQ , qQ z1 , qQ z2 have gcd one. Consequently these actual
fibre tori generate the primitive free orbit vector (lj µj )/qQ . The torus δ ∧ γ already generates all
cap torsion. This proves the claimed fibre image and its free cokernel.
     Finally H2 (U, ∂U ) = H 4 (U ) = Zρ , since H3 (U ) is free. The boundary first Betti number is
three, while that of U is one for c 6= 0 and two for c = 0. The boundary maps onto H1 (U ): it
contains the scalar and long generators. The relative sequence therefore makes the full boundary

degree-two image have rational rank one or two, respectively. Those are already the ranks of the

possible. The images are equal integrally. The Wang projection of the full kernel is therefore all

    For completeness, the scalar fixed-normal torus bounds the scalar-circle bundle over the

Theorem 4.61 (all height-integral initial pairs with corrected original additive caps). For any
of the twenty-one recorded Mordell–Weil rank-one profiles, take P = aG, Q = bG with a, b > 0
and d0 | ab. Choose any nonnegative whole-fibre linearization weights of total ab/d0 , supported
at multiplicative or additional regular fibres. Use the actual corrected line bundle of 4.59. The
following filling choices have an exact all-order fundamental-group presentation and complete
integral homology algorithm:

  (i) every marked same-fan rank-one or triangular Mumford cap at a multiplicative or regular
      site;

 (ii) every free finite-good additive logarithmic cap, with all its affine powers and all five integral
      Thom columns retained;

(iii) every original additive cap whose corrected multidegree has h = 1 in (D.IC2), and every
      unchanged zero-degree original additive cap;

 (iv) every original multiplicative cap with its uncorrected degree vector, as in 4.55;

  (v) arbitrarily many regular logarithmic caps and any ordinary integral clutch.

The odd-star fibres are filled originally in this algorithm. In particular, the recorded Smith
corrections from 4.59 admit every positive pair with integral height: all newly non-narrow additive
positions are the component pair (2, 2) at an odd star, and their corrected degrees are (D.IC8).
Newly non-narrow multiplicative positions may all use the marked Mumford filling. Thus this
theorem removes the narrowness-OR restriction on the initial sections in 4.55. It does not identify
original multiplicative caps with their nonzero vertical corrections, nor the unresolved marked
h > 1 additive caps.
    The exact implementation is code/manifolds_corrected_initial.py. It accepts the
same unbounded data as 4.55 and optional literal component-divisor vectors. A supplied vector
is checked against the integral equation (D.VC3); no rational correction is substituted. For an
original additive site it computes the orbit lengths and h, and applies the complete marked kernel
(D.IC7) only when h = 1. A nonzero whole-fibre change at a zero-degree original cap is also
retained as outside this implementation until its relative meridian marking is supplied.

4.3   Moving the zero of the linearization
Theorem 4.63 (the global moving-zero family). Let S → P1 be Engel’s rational elliptic
surface, with fibres IV ∗ , III, I1 at 0, 1, ∞, respectively. Put L = OS (P − O), T = t6P and
J = L ⊗ T ∗ L−1 ≃ π ∗ OP1 (1), with the direction of T fixed in Paper I, Theorem 20.2. We write
X log (u) for the logarithmically transformed sphere, and X(u) for the untwisted fibre of Paper I,
Theorem 20.2 and Paper I, Theorem 20.4. Choose sections φ0 , φ1 of O(1) with divisors ∞, 0,
respectively, normalized so that near infinity φ0 = qφ1 , q = 1/t. Set φs = π ∗ (φ0 − sφ1 ). For
every sufficiently small fixed u 6= 0 there is a proper flat holomorphic family Yu → ∆s , with
a holomorphic map to P1 , having the following properties. We perform the same logarithmic
transformations of multiplicities 3, 4 and the same admissible sphere twist data as for the chosen
X log (u). The central threefold Yu,0 has exactly one ordinary double point and is the contraction
of the diagonal (−1, −1)-curve of X log (u). Every fibre Yu,s for s 6= 0 is smooth. Its local change
at the contracted point is
                                     xy = u(zv − s),      q = zv.
This is the conifold transition described in Engel’s Remark 8.5. It is transverse to the u → 0
degeneration of Paper I, Theorem 20.2.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; Engel (2026c).

Proof. The equality defining J and its normalization are checked in Paper I, Theorem 20.2, using
Engel’s Lemma 2.1 and Corollary 2.2 Engel (2026c). We retain that equality, but allow the
section of J to vary. Here are the charts and their identifications. Choose Hermitian norms and
0 < r < 1/4. On the compact surface S, after restricting both parameters there is a uniform
inequality |u|kφs (x)k < r2 . Take a core

                              C = {(x, a, s) : a ∈ Lx , r < kak < r−1 }

and a node chart

               N = {(x, a, b, s) : a ∈ Lx , b ∈ L−1
                                                 T x , a ⊗ b = uφs (x), kak, kbk < 2r}.

On the collar r < kak < 2r, identify N with C by (x, a, b, s) 7→ (x, a, s). On r < kbk < 2r,
identify it by (x, a, b, s) 7→ (T x, b−1 , s). These maps and their inverses are holomorphic; on the
first collar b = uφs /a, and on the second a = uφs b−1 . The two node collars are disjoint by the
uniform inequality. A change of local line frames multiplies both sides of the node equation by
the same unit, so the construction is intrinsic.
     The quotient is Hausdorff. At each end of an attaching collar one chart contains the limiting
circle and the other omits it; there is no pair of distinct unpaired limits of the gluing graph.
The two node collars are separated, so no new chain of identifications changes this conclusion.
For properness, the closed core 3r/2 ≤ kak ≤ 2/(3r) and the closed node subset kak, kbk ≤ 7r/4
cover the quotient. Over any compact set of parameters their preimages are compact because S
is compact. This proves properness, also for the joint map to P1 × ∆s .
     On the core, flatness over s is immediate. On the node chart, the local rings are hypersurface
rings over the smooth surface S; the equation ab = uφs is not divisible by s − s0 , so multiplication
by s − s0 is injective. A coherent module over the one-dimensional regular local parameter ring
is flat precisely when it is torsion free; hence the family is flat. Alternatively, for the joint map to
(t, s) the fibres all have pure dimension two, and the Cohen–Macaulay regular-sequence criterion
gives flatness over the smooth two-dimensional base.
     Away from the zero of φs , the collar relation gives exactly L× /huφs i, with the contracting
generator covering T −1 . The uniform norm inequality ensures that every orbit meets a core
or node representative, so this is an actual biholomorphic comparison. Near 0 and 1 the ratio

φs /φ0 is a holomorphic unit, uniformly for small s. A local logarithm changes the scalar period
by a holomorphic function. Thus the same good-reduction torus cover and the same finite
affine translation data extend holomorphically in s. Their finite cyclic actions stay free, by
the unchanged primitive invariant translation coordinate. We replace the two corresponding
pieces by these smooth logarithmic-transform models and glue on the punctured overlaps by
the just-described period comparison. This is precisely the original finite gluing when s = 0.
Properness and flatness persist, since the replacements are proper families with the same compact
annular boundaries and are locally finite free quotients of smooth families.
    At the node of S∞ write q = zv. A unit change in a line coordinate gives xy = u(zv − s).
The relative gradient in (x, y, z, v) is (y, x, −uv, −uz), so the only possible critical point is the
origin, and it lies on the fibre exactly when s = 0. At a smooth point of a zero fibre of φs , its

other nodes are absent because the elliptic surface has only its stated three exceptional fibres,

such diagonal modulo the deck periods. The comparison with Paper I, Theorem 20.2 and Paper I,

    Before the finite logarithmic replacements, both constructions sit in the global core/node

slice s = 0 and varies u towards zero; the present construction fixes u 6= 0 and varies s. At u = 0

Proof. We first compute the canonical bundle by actual transition forms. On the core over a

da/a, which wedges to zero with ΩS . On the second plumbing collar the transition covers T
and changes the line coordinate by the scalar uφs ; its logarithmic derivative again contributes
only a base form. Translation on the elliptic surface preserves its invariant relative differential.
Thus the canonical transition functions are those of KS = π ∗ O(−1). On xy = u(q − s) the
residue expression dq ∧ dr ∧ dx/x becomes, using the equation, a nonzero constant multiple
of dy ∧ dr ∧ dx; it extends across the node-chart loci where a line coordinate vanishes. The

expression over q = zv has the same residue interpretation. For s 6= 0 it is regular wherever the

Indeed, for good reduction at IV ∗ write t = ζ 3 , x = ζ 4 X, y = ζ 6 Y ; then dt ∧ dx/y has order

on the regular locus, by the identity theorem, and it descends to a meromorphic function on

holomorphic disc and the bounded-pole criterion. Therefore C(Y ) = g ∗ C(B) and a(Y ) = 1.

proper derived direct image over a small parameter disc. Its value here is zero; connectedness
gives h0,0 = 1, and hence h0,1 = 1.

Proposition 5.1 (Counterexample: the proposed normalization). The local space (F ×∆       e E)/µm
in Lead 6 is not the normalization of the literal fibre product X ×B S at an additive fibre. It is a
different proper model of its punctured family.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. The reduced fibres of S of types IV* and III have respectively seven and two irreducible
components. In the literal fibre product the inverse image of each such component contains an
irreducible component which dominates it: at a general smooth point of the component, the
base-change equation is sm = ua , times smooth factors. Each branch of its normalization still
dominates that component. A finite normalization cannot contract any of these components.
Consequently the normalized central fibre has at least seven, respectively two, components. In
the proposed replacement the reduced central fibre is (F0 × E0 )/µm , which is irreducible. The
component counts disprove the asserted identification. Good reduction of the elliptic surface uses
contraction as well as normalization; omitting that contraction is the exact error in the reader’s
argument.

    The integral differential onto the first group in (E.I5) is surjective by naturality from the
sphere fibration: its own corresponding Leray quotient must vanish because H 3 (X) = 0. The
differential onto the second group is surjective as well. The X summand is killed by the differential
transported from H 4 (X) = 0; the elliptic orientation summand is killed by multiplying the
primitive degree-one transgression of X by the permanent class of the elliptic zero-section divisor.
That divisor has degree one on each elliptic fibre. Thus these are two primitive independent
target generators, not merely two independent rational images.
    Now H 0 (B, R3 g∗ Z) and H 0 (B, R4 g∗ Z) are free: in the first degree specialization has no
kernel, and in the second its only kernel is the free cusp class. There is no later Leray differential,
since the base has cohomological dimension two. Equation (E.I4) and the first surjectivity in
(E.I5) show that H 3 (Z; Z) is a free group, of rank one by 5.4. Equation (E.I4) and the second
surjectivity show that H 4 (Z; Z) is an extension of two free groups of rank one, and hence is
Z2 . Simple connectivity makes H 2 (Z; Z) torsion free. The universal coefficient theorem now
proves successively that H2 (Z; Z) = Z2 and H3 (Z; Z) = Z. Poincare duality determines the other
degrees and gives exactly the displayed groups.

Proof. Theorem A.8 proves smoothness. At each special value the other factor is a smooth
four-torus. The Euler characteristic of every fibre is therefore zero, and Euler additivity gives
χ(P ) = 0. We give van Kampen with the actual cusp relations, rather than deducing simple
connectivity from that of the factors. Over the six-punctured sphere the fibre group is ΛX ⊕ ΛX 0
and the base is free on five peripheral loops. Each monodromy acts on its own direct summand.
Filling the first cusp kills its angular generators w,   b δb and its cusp meridian. Their normal closure
under A1 also kills u b, since A1 w  b=u       b The same calculation in the other summand leaves
                                          b − w.
only h1 = γ  b and h2 = γ  b . The finite monodromies now act trivially on them. The four finite
                            0

filling relations are precisely those in (E.16), since γ(v1 ) = 1 and γ(v2 ) = −1. Both cusp collars
are untwisted; their meridians are killed. The product of the remaining four meridians gives the
last relation. These are all relations introduced by the six fillings, so van Kampen gives exactly
(E.16).
     Quotienting by h1 , h2 gives the orbifold group of the sphere with cone orders 3, 4, 3, 4. Its
orbifold Euler characteristic is −5/6, so its universal orbifold cover is the disc and the group is
infinite. Equivalently one can build the Seifert T 2 -bundle with these four primitive translation
vectors; over the disc it is a trivial torus bundle. Its exact sequence shows that the central subgroup
in (E.16) is Z2 . The abelianized five-by-six relation matrix has Smith factors (1, 1, 1, 1, 1), as
printed in the code, proving Gab = Z.
     For the rational homology there is no extra cusp kernel: each cusp is the original rank-two
cusp times a smooth torus, and its specialization is an isomorphism onto invariants over Q. The
two monodromy groups act on independent summands. In exterior degrees q = 0, . . . , 8, the H 0
and H 2 rows are both
                                           (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1),
and the H 1 row is
                                      (0, 0, 18, 60, 86, 60, 18, 0, 0).
To verify this without a matrix-size guess, the local invariant polynomials of the first factor are
A(z) = 1 + 2z + 2z 2 + 2z 3 + z 4 at a finite point and C(z) = A(z) + 2z 2 at its cusp. Hence the
Euler polynomial of the direct-image rows is

                               −4(1 + z)8 + (4A(z) + 2C(z))(1 + z)4 .

Formula (E.9), with six point strata, gives the displayed rows.
     Each invariant algebra of a factor has one generator in degrees zero through four. Its
invariant-to-coinvariant map is nonzero in even degrees and zero in odd degrees. In the marking
used above, this follows from the invariant form 6γ ∧ δ + u ∧ w and its exterior products: the
odd invariant classes pair to zero with every invariant complementary class, and the even ones
have nonzero square or top pairing. Its four transgressions are all nonzero, as the factor is a
sphere. The derivation rule therefore sends a tensor of bidegree (i, j) into bidegrees (i − 1, j) and
(i, j − 1), with the first term nonzero exactly when i > 0 and j is even, and the second exactly
when j > 0 and i is even. The nonzero column supports are disjoint except for pairs in a single
row, so their scalar normalizations do not affect ranks. This gives

                                  (r1 , . . . , r8 ) = (1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 2, 2, 1).

The exact program forms these matrices and takes their ranks. There are no later differentials.

    Finally, the admissible set of ϕ is the complement of finitely many proper complex
hypersurfaces in the connected complex manifold PGL2 (C), so it is path connected. The
universal pullback over this set is a proper smooth submersion: transversality was checked
pointwise above. Parallel transport along a path gives an oriented diffeomorphism of its
fibres.

Proposition 5.8 (the shifted product’s smooth type). The shifted product in (E.16) is the
closed oriented ten-manifold H10 specified by the 2432 ordinary framed handles of 5.25. Its
regular-fibre complement is, relative to its entire marked boundary, the 76-handle six-manifold
H6 of that theorem. The full attaching embeddings, their ordered normal coordinates, and every
dual belt embedding are prescribed by finite coordinate formulas. The identification follows by an
actual relative diffeomorphism of the cusp, core and finite caps, and then by the handle-by-handle
comparison of 5.25 using Milnor’s Theorems 1.4, 3.13 and 5.8. Top attaching maps are retained,
so there is no uncomputed sphere-capping ambiguity.
    Together with 5.6–3, 5.9–20, this supplies the complex invariants, the general smooth compact
pullback construction, the product case S 6 × N , and the shifted product’s fundamental group and
full integral homology. The smooth type is given by the explicit framed-handle presentation, not
by an inference from its homology or by an asserted connected-sum normal form. 5.22’s actual
quadratic obstruction is consistent with this presentation. The former open paragraph is retained
in the research records.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (E.16); theorem 5.25;
theorem 5.6; proposition 5.9; proposition 5.22.

Proof. Use subscripts one and two for the two rank-four cohomology local systems. At a critical

and their products. Together with b1 b2 these give an integral kernel basis in degree two; their
products give integral bases in degrees three and four. Both the central-fibre and invariant
lattices have ranks (1, 2, 4, 2, 1), as follows also from the normalization matrix in 4.2 at d = 1.
Thus the specialization is onto between free groups of equal ranks in every V      degree, proving the
claimed isomorphism. Thus the only difference between Rq g∗ Z and Jq = j∗ q (V1 ⊕ V2 ) is their

                         α ⊗ β 7−→ (ip α ⊗ β, −α ⊗ i0q β),              p + q = k.                    (E.MV7)

For a swept tensor, place the normal circle first. Then

                                                                                                      (E.MV8)
                                                       

The second sign contains the Koszul sign from moving the circle past α, the reversal of the two
boundary-circle orientations, and the second minus in Mayer–Vietoris. The last two cancel. This
specifies every integer entry of Dk .

Proposition 5.11 (a unique transverse family type and its stable tangent bundle). For fixed
marked sphere fibrations, all Möbius transformations whose critical triples are disjoint give
orientation-preservingly diffeomorphic shifted products. The same conclusion holds while either
sphere varies in its proper smooth marked period family. For every such fivefold P there is an
isomorphism of real vector bundles
                                        T P ⊕ R4 ≃ R14 .                             (E.MV9)
Thus all its positive-degree Stiefel–Whitney and Pontryagin classes vanish. For its given complex
tangent bundle, c1 (P ) = c2 (P ) = 0 integrally. These assertions and 5.10 do not identify the
complete smooth structure from its ordinary homology and fundamental group.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 5.10.

Proof. The allowed transformations form the complement in PGL2 (C) of the nine analytic
hypersurfaces imposing an equality of one critical value from each triple. This complement is
path connected: a piecewise smooth path between two points can be perturbed relative to its
endpoints to avoid these sets, which have real codimension two. Equivalently, use local complex
coordinate balls and perturb each segment there. Choose a smooth such path.
    The corresponding fibre products form a compact smooth family over its parameter interval.
Indeed the vertical derivative of f1 (x) − f2 (y) is surjective at every point, since its two factors
cannot be critical at the same base value. The same surjectivity solves the equation for a lift of
the interval coordinate vector field. A partition of unity supplies a global smooth lift; compactness
makes its flow exist for the whole interval. This flow gives the claimed diffeomorphisms. The
complex orientations vary continuously and hence are preserved. The identical argument applies
to smooth proper period families of either factor, keeping the critical triples disjoint throughout.
    View P as the transverse inverse image of the diagonal in B × B under f1 × f2 . Its real
oriented normal two-plane bundle is the underlying bundle of g ∗ TB , where g : P → B is the
common base map. It is trivial: its first Chern class is

                             c1 (g ∗ TB ) = 2g ∗ [B]∨ = 2 pr∗1 f1∗ [B]∨ = 0,

because H 2 (X; Z) = 0, and complex line bundles are classified by their first Chern class. The
tangent bundles of the two six-spheres become trivial after adding one real line each. Restriction
of their product tangent bundle gives

                                      (T P ⊕ R2 ) ⊕ R2 ≃ R14 ,

proving (E.MV9) and the characteristic-class assertions for the real tangent bundle. Finally the
holomorphic tangent sequence is

                        0 −→ T P −→ pr∗1 T X ⊕ pr∗2 T X 0 −→ g ∗ TB −→ 0.

Both sphere factors have integral c1 = c2 = 0, since their cohomology in degrees two and four
vanishes. The last line has zero first Chern class, as just proved. Multiplying total Chern classes
in this exact sequence gives c1 (P ) = c2 (P ) = 0 integrally.

Proposition 5.12 (the shifted product bounds with its natural stable framing). Equip the two
oriented six-spheres with their standard bounding stable tangent framings. Trivialize the oriented
two-plane bundle f1∗ T P1 on the first sphere, and equip the transverse shifted product P with the


                                                  234
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                     Paper III


induced stable framing in (E.MV9). Then there is a compact smooth oriented eleven-manifold V
with
                      ∂V = P,     T V ⊕ R3 ≃ R14 ,     [P ] = 0 in Ωfr
                                                                    10 .              (E.B1)
The boundary framing is the stated one. In particular its induced spin structure bounds. This
supplies a framed bordism invariant; it does not identify the smooth type from ordinary homology.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (E.MV9); theorem 2.4;
(Hirsch, 1976, Chapter 3, Section 2, Theorems 2.1 and 2.5); equation (E.B2); proposition 5.11;
theorem 5.13.

Proof. Write f2 : S 6 → P1 for the shifted map of the second factor. By 2.4 the first map
f1 : S 6 → P1 is null-homotopic. It therefore extends to a smooth map F : D7 → P1 , which can
be chosen to equal f1 on each sphere of a collar of the boundary. To see this with the boundary
fixed, first use the null-homotopy to obtain a continuous extension constant in the collar direction.
Smooth its interior in coordinate charts, with cutoffs supported away from the collar; on the
overlap the extension is already smooth.
    Let C2 be the three critical values of f2 . The restriction f1 is transverse to each point of
C2 , since the two critical triples are disjoint. Perturb F only in the interior to be transverse to
all these points. The applicable finite simultaneous transversality statement is (Hirsch, 1976,
Chapter 3, Section 2, Theorems 2.1 and 2.5). For the relative assertion, the proof of that
theorem uses local perturbations multiplied by cutoff functions. Their supports may be restricted
to the complement of the collar, where transversality has not already been secured; the open
condition on the collar persists. Compactness permits finitely many such perturbations. Thus no
assumption that F is a submersion everywhere is needed.
    Define the smooth fibre product

                             V = {(x, y) ∈ D7 × S 6 : F (x) = f2 (y)}.                       (E.B2)

At a point whose common value is outside C2 , the differential df2 is onto. At a point over C2 ,
the differential dF is onto. Consequently dF − df2 is onto everywhere on (E.B2). The same
argument holds on its boundary, using df1 there. The implicit-function theorem, including its
boundary version, makes V a smooth eleven-manifold with boundary exactly P . It is compact as
a closed subset of D7 × S 6 . The inverse-image orientation using the complex orientation of T P1
induces the complex orientation of P at the boundary, because the collar keeps the first map
fixed.
    Let g : V → P1 be the common map. The real normal two-plane bundle of (E.B2) is g ∗ T P1 ,
identified by dF − df2 . This is the pullback from D7 of F ∗ T P1 , which is trivial because the
disc is contractible. A choice of its oriented framing restricts on the boundary to the chosen
framing of f1∗ T P1 up to homotopy: two oriented framings of this two-plane bundle differ by a
map S 6 → SO(2), and H 1 (S 6 ; Z) = 0. The tangent exact sequence and the bounding stable
framing of the second sphere now give

                              T V ⊕ R2 ≃ T (D7 × S 6 )|V ,
                              T V ⊕ R3 ≃ R7 ⊕ (T S 6 ⊕ R)|V ≃ R14 .

At the boundary, the outward normal of D7 supplies the additional real line in T V |P = T P ⊕ R.
The resulting framing is precisely the stable tangent framing obtained from the two sphere
framings and the normal framing in 5.11. This proves (E.B1) by the definition of framed bordism.
It also proves the assertion about the induced spin structure, by forgetting the framing.
    This disc-extension construction does not by itself extend a classifying map P → Bπ1 (P )
over V . The different filling in 5.13 below does extend that map. Both are bordism statements;
the higher equivariant surgery data required for the smooth classification remain separate.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (E.16); proposition 5.12;

Proof. The aspherical target. The repaired quotient maps of Paper I, Theorem 17.4 are smooth

              N = {(u, v) ∈ S 3 × S 3 : h1 (u) = h2 (v)},                 c(x, y) = (e1 (x), e2 (y)).     (E.B5)

                                              B = S 2 (3, 4, 3, 4).

At a cone of order m, its uniformizing chart is (D2 × T 2 )/Cm , with the generator rotating the

    The orbifold has Euler characteristic 2 − 2(1 − 1/3) − 2(1 − 1/4) = −5/6. It is good and has

    Using the marked fibre generators h1 , h2 and the four positive peripheral generators gives

Proposition 5.14 (the fibre complement and a spinning obstruction). Let F = T 4 be a regular
fibre of the original sphere fibration and E = S 6 \ int(F × D2 ), with the marking of 5.10. Its
group and peripheral homomorphism are

                       K = π1 (E) = ha, b, h | h central, a3 = h, b4 = h−1 i,
                                                                                              (E.S1)
                                 g 7−→ h,       u, w, d 7−→ 1,    µ 7−→ ab.

Here µ is the normal meridian, with the peripheral orientation chosen so that [a] = 4[µ],
[b] = −3[µ] and [h] = 12[µ]. The image of the boundary group is the embedded copy hh, µi ≃ Z2 .
In the unique homotopy class of normal framings for which every pushed-off loop of F has linking
number zero, the image of g is

                         λ = hµ−12 ,        ker{π1 (F ) −→ K} = Zhu, w, di.                   (E.S2)

In particular the peripheral structure is that of the (3, 4) torus knot, with its regular Seifert
fibre rather than its preferred longitude as the original g coordinate. Nevertheless the embedded
four-torus F ⊂ S 6 is not the ordinary threefold closed spin of that classical knot, even allowing
ambient orientation reversal and arbitrary changes of its normal framing. More strongly, it is
not a single ordinary closed spin of any embedded T 3 ⊂ S 5 .

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 5.10; theorem 2.10;
equation (E.MV4); equation (E.MV6); (Winter, 2008, Section 3, immediately before Theorem
3.4); (Winter, 2008, Theorem 4.5); equation (E.S5); equation (E.S4).

Proof. Apply the van Kampen presentation in 2.10 with the regular base disc removed. The
cusp kills w, d and its peripheral loop. Conjugating w by the order-three generator also kills u.
The two finite caps impose a3 = h and b4 = h−1 ; there is now no relation ab = 1, since the outer
boundary has not been filled. The outer meridian is ab in the stated orientation. This proves
(E.S1), including the actual peripheral map, rather than only an abstract group isomorphism.
Eliminating h gives ha, b | a3 b4 = 1i. Its quotient by h is C3 ∗ C4 . The word ab has infinite order
in that free product, so a relation hr µs = 1 forces s = 0. Abelianization then forces r = 0. This
proves peripheral injectivity. It also shows that λ has infinite order: its image in C3 ∗ C4 is
(ab)−12 .
    Write θ ∈ H 1 (∂E; Z) for the normal-circle covector and retain (γ, u, w, δ) for H 1 (F ; Z). The
generator ξ ∈ H 1 (E; Z) restricts to θ + 12γ. Homotopy classes of normal framings differ by
H 1 (F ; Z). Consequently there is a unique framing for which the associated section s : F → ∂E
satisfies s∗ ξ = 0: it has s∗ θ = −12γ. Its induced peripheral map is exactly (E.S2). Simultaneously
reversing the meridian conventions changes the displayed signs and preserves all the following
assertions.
     For this section set

    R = im{H 2 (E; Z) −→ H 2 (F ; Z)},      rad(R) = {v ∈ H1 (F ; Z) : ιv ω = 0 for all ω ∈ R}.
                                                                                             (E.S3)
This uses the canonical identification of the cohomology of a torus with the exterior algebra of
its first cohomology. Equations (E.MV4)–(E.MV6) give classes whose boundary restrictions are
θu and θw: their unswept terms are zero because uγuw = wγuw = 0. Restricting them along s
proves
                                      −12γu, −12γw ∈ R.                                      (E.S4)
The simultaneous contraction kernel of these two forms is Zd. Indeed their contractions force
successively γ(v) = u(v) = w(v) = 0. Thus

                              rad(R) ⊆ ker γ = ker{π1 (F ) −→ K}.                             (E.S5)

Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                         Paper III


Both the zero-linking framing and this inclusion are invariants of the embedded pair, with no
choice of the original torus coordinates.
    We define the comparison construction precisely. For a closed submanifold L ⊂ int Dn , its
ordinary closed spin is L × S 1 in Dn × S 1 ⊂ ∂(Dn × D2 ) = S n+1 . Start with the closed classical
knot K0 ⊂ int D3 and repeat this operation three times, each time placing the previous compact
pair in the interior of a disc. This is the ordinary torus spinning construction reviewed in (Winter,
2008, Section 3, immediately before Theorem 3.4); no turning, twisting, or family of deformations
is inserted. If Σ is a Seifert surface for K0 , the same three spins give the embedded Seifert
hypersurface Σ × T 3 with boundary K0 × T 3 . Pushing the latter off using the normal of this
hypersurface gives its zero-linking framing.
    Let v be the original knot-circle class and let v1 , v2 , v3 be the spinning circles. Each pushed-off
two-cycle v ∧ vi bounds the corresponding copy of Σ × S 1 in a parallel copy of that hypersurface,
disjoint from the knot. Hence every restriction of a complement two-class vanishes on v ∧ H1 (F ):
v belongs to rad(R). On the other hand its pushed-off loop is the original preferred longitude
and is nontrivial for K0 = T (3, 4), whereas the spinning circles are trivial in the complement
group. These peripheral claims also follow directly at each spin: its complement is

                           ((Dn \ int νL) × S 1 ) ∪S n−1 ×S 1 (S n−1 × D2 ),

so van Kampen kills precisely the new spinning circle and preserves the old complement group.
They agree with the primary peripheral calculation (Winter, 2008, Theorem 4.5) in the first
spin. Thus the ordinary spun torus violates (E.S5). An identification of embedded pairs would
preserve its two sides, giving a contradiction.
    For the stronger assertion, let L = T 3 ⊂ S 5 be arbitrary and suppose that its ordinary closed
spin were our four-torus. Write EL for its exterior. Deleting a ball disjoint from L changes
cohomology only in degrees at least four. In the displayed spun-complement decomposition, with
n = 5, the cap and intersection are S 4 ×D2 and S 4 ×S 1 . Mayer–Vietoris and the surjectivity onto
the latter first cohomology therefore give, in degrees two and three, precisely the cohomology of
(EL \ D5 ) × S 1 . Let s be the spinning-circle covector and vs its primitive homology generator. Put
RjL = im{H j (EL ) → H j (L)}, using the zero-linking framing. One has R1L = 0. Also R3L = 0: the
pushed-off L bounds a parallel Seifert hypersurface in its exterior, so every top-degree restriction
evaluates to zero. The product restrictions consequently satisfy

                                    R2 = R2L ,       R3 = R2L ∧ s.                              (E.S12)

In particular vs ∈ rad(R2 ), and contraction by vs is injective on R3 . For our actual four-torus,
(E.S4) forces vs = ±d. But (E.MV4)–(E.MV6), now applied to α = γδ in degree three, show
that R3 contains ±2γuw. Its swept term vanishes in the zero-linking framing, and this is a
nonzero class annihilated by d. This contradicts that injectivity. No ordinary closed spin is
possible. Turned or deform-spun constructions insert additional data and are not excluded by
this argument.

Theorem 5.15 (exact second-homotopy coinvariants). For the classifying map c : P → N =
K(G, 1) of 5.13, one has

    c∗ : H3 (P ; Z) −→ H3 (N ; Z) = Z equal to zero, π2 (P ) G ≃ Z2 ⊕ (Z/12)6 .   (E.S6)

The pullback of a generator of H 3 (N ; Z) has exact order twelve in H 3 (P ; Z). In particular π2 (P )
is not a projective ZG-module. The fivefold cannot be diffeomorphic, or homotopy equivalent, to

ten-sphere. This computes coinvariants and a definite module obstruction; it does not assert a
presentation or a classification of the full ZG-module.

Proof. Use the separating base circle in 5.10 also in the target of 5.13. There M denotes the

    We first check the homological statement, retaining the full integer boundary maps. In

                                 c∗ (∂v) = ∂v     has exact order 12.                          (E.S9)

This uses the actual Mayer–Vietoris image; no splitting of a torsion filtration has been assumed.

                                 0 −→ Zz −→ L −→ Z ⊕ A −→ 0.                                  (E.S10)

The zero on the left uses c∗ H3 (P ) = 0, just proved. To determine this extension, replace c by its

Theorem 5.17 (an actual circle fibration and infinite-order return). The shifted fivefold admits
a smooth fibre bundle
                                                  ρ
                                      Y 9 −→ P −→ S 1                                    (E.S22)
with connected closed fibre, inducing the primitive character

                          χ(a1 , a2 , b1 , b2 , h1 , h2 ) = (4, −3, −4, 3, 12, −12)         (E.S23)

on the presentation of 5.13. Its fibre group is the fundamental group of the oriented principal
circle bundle of Euler number −1 over a surface of genus six. Here the base has its complex
orientation and the positive circle is h1 h2 ; reversing that circle changes the Euler number to +1.
In particular
                               π1 (Y ) = ker χ,       H1 (Y ; Z) = Z12 .                     (E.S24)
The return diffeomorphism of (E.S22) has infinite order even among unbased homotopy classes of
self-equivalences of Y , although its induced outer automorphism of π1 (Y ) has exact order twelve.
No connected finite cover of P is homotopy equivalent to a product S 1 × Z. These assertions
give a geometric mapping-torus description; they do not identify the smooth nine-dimensional
fibre or the full return diffeomorphism up to classification.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 5.13; (Scott, 1983, Theorem

Proof. A closed one-form with a nonzero derivative at every point. Use the actual smooth map
c = (e1 , e2 ) : P → N in 5.13, not an arbitrary representative of its classifying homotopy class.

closed one-form representing the primitive integral class χ on N and average it over this compact
torus. Its average α is closed, represents the same integral class, and is invariant. If Vi is the

along an ordinary orbit therefore gives

                                   α(V1 ) = 12,         α(V2 ) = −12.                       (E.S25)

The integrality of the periods integrates α to a smooth map ρN : N → R/Z.
    Choose the two cusp replacements defining ei in disjoint base discs, themselves disjoint from

invariant part of (E.S41). At the unchanged cusp the system is trivial, because g has character

degree one the image is hγ, ui; their products with those two degree-two classes give the two
independent invariant classes in degree three and the top class in degree four. Thus all the
specialization maps have the asserted ranks, with no additional skyscraper summand. The
paragraph following (B.5.16) also proves these specialization assertions integrally in all degrees
by the actual honeycomb quotient map.

which ` is one. This gives (E.S49). The same calculation proves identity on every other integral
cohomology group, including its torsion.

extensions must not be split by assumption. Instead use the nondegenerate integral torsion

the degree-three torsion to be (Z/6)2 , and the fixed degree-four torsion forces the same answer

to (E.S51). The order 72n in the middle groups distinguishes the covers for distinct n.

In the splitting f AΠ ⊕ ker r, the mixed component of (E.Q11) is f vj (z − 1) ⊗ ti(j) . If all these
mixed components were zero, every integer coefficient of vj (z − 1) would be divisible by six,
by (E.Q10). The group-ring basis makes this implication immediate even if ti has larger or
infinite order. Multiplication by z − 1 is also injective on (Z/6)[Π]: along an infinite z orbit a
finitely supported coefficient function with zero difference is zero. Hence every vj belongs to
6AΠ , contradicting (E.Q12).
    Finally, a connected sum with S 2 × S 7 has, through dimension four in its universal cover, the
original space wedged with a free deck orbit of two-spheres. All images of its four-dimensional
Whitehead map consequently have zero mixed component with that free summand. The preceding
argument rules this out for every free summand of the actual module. This proves the assertion
for Y .

   This computes a specified part of the actual quadratic attaching data. It does not identify
every higher handle attachment or the smooth type of the shifted fivefold.

Proof. We first construct the comparison by a smooth family, rather than use the logarithmic
homeomorphism in (B.5.7). Set Cs (q) = (1 − s)C(q) for 0 ≤ s ≤ 1. The affine toric cover is fixed.
On its dense torus the deck translation for λ ∈ Z2 becomes

                          (x, q, s) 7−→ q B0 λ exp(2πiCs (q)λ)x, q, s .                   (E.T3)
                                                                     

Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                      Paper III


The exponential is componentwise. The powers of q permute the toric charts by translation
of the A2 triangulation, while the exponential factors are nowhere-zero analytic units on every
chart. Thus (E.T3) defines a smooth family of holomorphic deck actions on a fixed smooth
toric covering space. On a central stratum the lattice translation permutes its bounded fan cells
without fixed points. Off the central fibre, freeness and properness are exactly the nondegeneracy
of the real period lattice.
    These assertions hold uniformly after shrinking η. Indeed put T = − log |q|/(2π), and let
K bound k Im Cs (q)k on the compact parameter interval and closed disc. For T > K + 1 the
matrix T B0 + Im Cs (q) is invertible, since B0 is orthogonal. A fundamental parallelogram has
logarithmic position B0 a + T −1 Im Cs (q)a with a ∈ [0, 1]2 ; it meets a uniformly bounded number
of toric charts. More explicitly choose a triangle containing the unperturbed point B0 a and
let P be its unimodular vertex matrix. Its barycentric coordinates tj are nonnegative,
                                                                                 √            and the
corresponding chart coordinates satisfy log |z√   j | = tj log |q| + O(2πkP −1 kK 2). There are only

finitely many such triangles, so with c = 2π 2 max kP −1 k every chosen chart coordinate has
modulus at most exp(cK), uniformly in q, s and all compact phases. Their closed polydiscs
have compact closure in the affine charts. These finitely many compact chart images prove
compactness of the quotient over [0, 1] and |q| ≤ η. The central charts and their incidence
relations are fixed. Projection of this quotient to s is consequently a proper smooth submersion,
including on every normal-crossings stratum. Its only boundary is |q| = η together with the
parameter end faces, and its boundary restriction is also a submersion.
    On |q| = η prescribe the marked real coordinates x = exp(2πi(Zs (q)a + b)), (a, b) ∈ T 4 . They
give a smooth product trivialization in s and precisely the prescribed mapping-torus marking.
Extend its horizontal vector field over a collar, and then over the compact family. Local toric
product charts provide extensions tangent to every central stratum; a partition of unity preserves
that property and the lift of ∂s . Integrating this field proves the asserted relative diffeomorphism.
Its orientation is the complex orientation on each fibre. This is relative Ehresmann transport in
an actual smooth family; no smoothness is inferred from a logarithmic formula at q = 0.
    It remains to identify the endpoint C = 0 with the framed plumbing data. In the lattice Z2
use cyclic rays
                          (1, 0), (0, 1), (−1, 1), (−1, 0), (0, −1), (1, −1).                  (E.T4)
The star of the vertex zero in the A2 triangulation consists of the six triangles spanned by zero
and consecutive rays. The corresponding three-dimensional cones have primitive rays (v, 1) and
determinant one. Their common divisor at the central ray is the toric surface S. A principal
central fibre has normal line
                                   OS (−C0 − · · · − C5 ) = KS .                           (E.T5)
The cyclic surface fan in (E.T4) also proves this identification directly: it is the fan of the three
torus-fixed blow-ups of CP2 , and each neighboring-ray relation gives Ci2 = −1. In the Picard

    Near a double curve the two adjacent unimodular charts give the total space of O(−1)⊕O(−1).

                   (z, a, b),    (w, A, B) = (z −1 , za, zb),   q = zab = wAB.                (E.T6)

so it extends smoothly over the endpoint. The map is involutive, preserves q, and its complex

sign and angular twisting.

Proof. The main geometric point is that the first three steps give actual smooth blocks of the cusp

(E.H4). Substituting the two cyclic permutations gives exactly (E.H3). This checks all six ends,
not just one representative. Triviality of a normal bundle over the annulus is not being used to
replace its relative endpoint framing by a constant framing.

face of the dense block. On the normalized toric surface take a small collar of its hexagonal toric
boundary, choosing the corner neighborhoods first and the edge strips second. Choose the strips

can be done directly with six inward parallel affine inequalities in (E.H5), smoothing each corner

     We finish by stating precisely why these data determine the smooth type, including its top
handles. The relevant relative uniqueness results are Milnor’s Theorem 3.13, which identifies an
elementary cobordism from its full characteristic embedding, Theorem 1.4, which makes smooth
composition unique with the marked boundary fixed, and the isotopy-extension Theorem 5.8
Milnor (1965a). In the present notation the characteristic embedding is the whole map S j−1 ×
Dn−j −→ ∂W , not just the attaching sphere or its homology class. Its normal coordinates are
part of (E.H3)–(E.H11). The elementary consequence needed here can also be seen directly. If
φ0 , φ1 are joined by the specified isotopy of full attaching embeddings, extend the velocity field
on their images to a slightly larger boundary collar and multiply it by a cutoff which is zero on
the protected marked boundary. Its flow extends the attaching isotopy to an ambient boundary
isotopy. Extending this flow across a product collar of W , and using the identity on the new
coordinate handle, identifies W ∪φ0 (Dj × Dn−j ) with W ∪φ1 (Dj × Dn−j ). The same cutoff
argument applies to the small radial corner changes above. This derives the relative, framed
version from the stated isotopy-extension theorem, without assuming an extension of an arbitrary
sphere diffeomorphism over a disk.
     Apply this comparison successively in the displayed block and sector order. The initial ball
comparisons are their coordinate identifications. At each next stage the actual attaching map
and the prescribed attaching map agree in the computed normal coordinates, or differ by the
explicitly described positive collar isotopy. The comparison of that stage is consequently the
identity on the new coordinate handle and the product-collar extension on the previous stages.
Theorems 3.13 and 1.4 give an inductive relative diffeomorphism of the whole six-manifold. The
final ordinary boundary coordinates are unchanged. The same argument, with the actual belt
embeddings and the specified boundary flip, applies to every handle on the dual ten-dimensional
side. In particular a top handle retains its entire attaching map S n−1 → ∂W ; none is replaced by
an arbitrary capping disk after forgetting that map. There is therefore no remaining disk-gluing
or exotic-sphere ambiguity. The computed ordered full framed attaching data, under this relative
uniqueness theorem, are the classifying data used for (E.H0); the preceding algebraic invariants
are not being used as a smooth classification.


6    The rank-three search and a parity obstruction
Theorem 6.1 (Euler number of a Kuhn cusp). Let g : M 8 → S 2 be a proper triangulable map, a
T 6 -bundle off finitely many values. Suppose its unique non-quotient special fibre is the rank-three
Kuhn toroidal fibre with period-lattice index d, and all its other special reduced fibres are free
finite quotients of T 6 . Then χ(M ) = 6d.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. A fundamental cube has six unimodular tetrahedra. Taking the quotient by an index-d
sublattice multiplies every cell count by d, so the quotient cell counts are d(1, 7, 12, 6). A cell
of dimension r corresponds to a torus stratum (C∗ )3−r . Only the 6d point strata contribute to
Euler characteristic. Euler integration over the regular base gives zero since χ(T 6 ) = 0, and a
finite free torus quotient has Euler characteristic 0/|G| = 0. Additivity now gives the formula.
This checks the rank-three instance of the localization mechanism in Paper II, Proposition 9.5
and Paper II, Proposition 9.7. It requires the specified toroidal filling, not just its unipotent
monodromy matrix.

    The complete credited statement and re-derivation are in theorem A.9. The complete credited

Proposition 6.2 (the diagonal obstruction). If A ∈ GLn (Z) has no eigenvalue one, every affine
map x 7→ Ax + b of Rn /Zn has a fixed point. Thus the diagonal elliptic finite monodromies in
Lead 7 admit no free affine lifts.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. The real map I − A is invertible. A real solution of (I − A)x = b maps to a fixed
point in the torus. The diagonal copies of the order-four and order-six elliptic rotations have
no eigenvalue one, so the conclusion applies to every translation part, not only to integral or
invariant choices.

Proposition 6.5 (Counterexample: determination by peripheral data alone). Monodromy
matrices and affine twist vectors alone do not determine the homology of a compact glued
manifold. A cusp filling, or an equivalent relative topological specification, is additional data.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. Use the constructed fourfold Z and blow up a smooth point of the smooth locus of its
cusp fibre. The operation takes place entirely inside that filling. It leaves every regular fibre,
every finite quotient model, every peripheral monodromy and every affine twist unchanged. The
total space remains smooth and compact, and its map to the same base remains holomorphic.
Blowing up a point in complex dimension four replaces a ball by the disc bundle of OP3 (−1).
Mayer–Vietoris along their common S 7 boundary adds a copy of Z in degrees two, four and six.
Thus the Euler number increases by three and the homology changes. The peripheral index-one
unipotent matrix is unaffected. The stronger specification of a particular height-one Kuhn
filling excludes this example. With that extra specification the question remains a substantive
classification problem; we do not claim to refute it.

Theorem 6.6 (the self-dual parity obstruction). Suppose a compact smooth eight-manifold has
the torus fibration and the specified Kuhn cusp of 6.1 with index one, and its other reduced fibres
are free quotients of complex three-tori by finite holomorphic affine actions. If its rational H 1
monodromy representation is self-dual, then it cannot satisfy b1 = b2 = 0. In particular no
symplectic-monodromy datum of F.2 can give the three-connected fourfold required in F.4, for
either k = 2 or k = 3 (or any number k of finite points).

annihilating the angular lattice, exactly the three-dimensional monodromy invariant subspace.
Hence the same equality holds at the cusp. It holds everywhere.
     Put a = dim H 0 (B, j∗ V) and b = dim H 2 (B, j∗ V). The only differential that can kill a class in
H 0 (R1 ) or in H 2 (R0 ) is d2 : H 0 (R1 ) → H 2 (R0 ) = Q. If b1 = b2 = 0, it must be an isomorphism,
so a = 1. Moreover H 1 (B, j∗ V) must vanish because its position (1, 1) has no possible incoming
or outgoing differential. Self-duality and compactly supported duality give b = a = 1.

Proof. Let W be the rank-four rational homology local system of the abelian surfaces. It

     The rank-six rational homology system T after the two Engel operations has a natural

                     0 ⊂ L ⊂ E ⊂ T,      L ≃ Q, E/L ≃ W, T /E ≃ Q.

Theorem 6.12 (the orbifold quotient). For the specified torus fillings in F.2, with affine
multiplicities m1 , . . . , mk , the fundamental group of the total space has a canonical surjection
onto
                                    hx1 , . . . , xk | xm

                                                         i

Consequently a simply connected example with k = 2 requires gcd(m1 , m2 ) = 1. There is no
simply connected example with k = 3 and m1 , m2 , m3 ≥ 2. An affine multiplicity-one point is an
ordinary smooth point and reduces to the problem with one fewer multiple fibre.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. Over the complement of small discs at the special values, the torus bundle projects
surjectively on fundamental groups to the punctured base. Quotient its fundamental group by
the normal closure of all regular-fibre loops. At a finite filling its root cover is a smooth torus
bundle over a disc, and its free deck group is cyclic of order mi . The covering exact sequence
shows that the quotient of the filling group by its fibre subgroup is precisely this cyclic group.
The boundary base meridian maps to its generator. Thus adjoining that filling imposes exactly
xmi = 1 after the fibre loops have been killed. At the index-one Kuhn cusp the fundamental
   i

group is generated by the three deck loops of its dual torus; these are regular fibre loops. Its
base meridian contracts. Hence its filling imposes the ordinary meridian relation and leaves no
extra generator in this quotient. The base relation gives the product relation in (F.27). Van
Kampen proves that (F.27) is the resulting quotient, in particular the asserted surjection.
     For two points, substitute x2 = x−1  1 ; the quotient is Z/ gcd(m1 , m2 ). For three points of

in the sphere, Euclidean plane or hyperbolic plane according as their sum is greater

than, equal to or less than π. In the spherical case the possible orders are, after sorting,

therefore give a nontrivial representation of (F.27) into the orientation-preserving isometry group.
