Proposition 6.13 (automatic local complex compatibility). Every simply connected datum of
F.2 with two finite affine fillings automatically has finite linear actions commuting with real
complex structures. This assertion concerns the individual finite actions and does not produce
simultaneous global periods.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 6.12; proposition 6.2.

Proof. Let mi be the order of the free cyclic affine action defining the ith filling. Its linear
order divides mi . By 6.12 the integers m1 , m2 are coprime, so at least one of them is odd.
The corresponding linear determinant is one, because a finite real matrix of odd order cannot
have determinant minus one. The relation M1 M2 M0 = I and the unipotence of M0 imply
det M1 det M2 = 1, so both determinants are one.
    A finite-order real matrix is semisimple. Its nonreal eigenvalues occur in conjugate pairs, and
its only possible real eigenvalues are 1 and −1. Determinant one says that the −1 eigenspace
has even real dimension. Since the total dimension is six, the 1 eigenspace also has even real
dimension. Choose a complex structure on each of these real eigenspaces by pairing a real basis.
On each nonreal isotypical real summand, multiplication by i in its complex eigenspace supplies
a commuting complex structure. Their direct sum commutes with Mi . The fixed eigenspace is
nonzero because the affine action is free, as in 6.2, so its even dimension is at least two.
    Each chosen structure makes R6 /Z6 a complex torus and the given affine map holomorphic;
thus it supplies precisely the local complex-compatibility hypothesis used in the subsequent
reductions. For three genuine finite fillings 6.12 has already excluded simple connectivity without
this argument.

Proposition 6.14 (exclusion of an involutory finite part). A simply connected datum with
b2 = 0, k = 2 and the stated finite affine fillings has neither finite linear monodromy of order
one or two. Its unordered pair of finite linear orders must therefore belong to

                       {(3, 4), (3, 5), (3, 8), (3, 10), (4, 5), (5, 6), (5, 8), (5, 12)}.        (F.28)

The affine multiplicities may still be larger than these linear orders.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 6.12; proposition 6.13;
theorem 6.6; equation (F.3).

Proof. An identity finite generator would make the product of the two finite matrices finite,
contrary to its nontrivial unipotent cusp. Suppose the cohomology generators are A, B with
A2 = I, where the other finite linear order is odd. It must be odd because the linear orders
divide the coprime affine multiplicities of Theorem 6.12. Write U = AB; the cusp condition gives
(U − I)2 = 0. Multiplication of this identity on the left by A and on the right by B −1 gives

                                            BA + AB −1 = 2I.                                      (F.29)

For v ∈ ker(B − I) we obtain (B + I)Av = 2v. As B has odd order, B + I is invertible, so Av = v.
Every B-fixed vector is therefore globally fixed. The finite free affine action has a nonzero fixed

                                                      282
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                       Paper III


linear subspace, and 6.13 makes its real dimension even; it is at least two. Consequently the
global cohomology invariant rank is at least two. The Leray argument of Theorem 6.6 shows
that b1 = b2 = 0 requires that rank to be exactly one, a contradiction. Inverse or transpose
monodromy conventions give the same identity and fixed-space conclusion.
    Finally take the complete finite-order list (F.3), discard one and two, and keep its coprime

Proposition 6.15 (the only first-cohomology pattern for two points). For a simply connected
two-multiple-fibre datum with b2 = 0, the rational cohomology system V has one invariant, no
coinvariants, and fixed rank two at each finite generator. Its quotient W = V /Qe by the invariant
line has neither invariants nor coinvariants. If one finite characteristic polynomial on W is
(T − 1)Φd (T ) with deg Φd = 4, then W is irreducible over Q.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 6.6; proposition 6.13.

Proof. Write a = dim V Γ , b = dim(V ∗ )Γ and fi for the finite fixed ranks. Theorem 6.6 gives
a = 1, vanishing first parabolic cohomology, and f1 + f2 = 4 + b. By 6.13 each fi is positive
and even, so b is even. The maximal square-zero cusp has ker N = im N . Therefore every
globally fixed vector belongs to im N , whereas every globally fixed covector kills im N . The
global invariant and coinvariant spaces pair to zero.
    Restriction of a globally invariant covector to the fixed space of a finite generator is injective:
averaging that generator is the projection onto its fixed space, and the covector is unchanged by
averaging. Its restriction kills the a global invariants in that space. Hence a + b ≤ fi for each i.
If b ≥ 2 is even, the even ranks satisfy fi ≥ b + 2, so 4 + b = f1 + f2 ≥ 2b + 4, a contradiction.
Thus b = 0 and f1 = f2 = 2.
    The quotient W has no invariant covectors, since its dual embeds into V ∗ . If it had a fixed
line, its preimage in V would be an extension of the trivial line by the trivial line. Every finite
generator on this two-dimensional space would be unipotent of finite order, hence identity. This
would give two invariants in V , a contradiction. Thus W also has no invariant vectors.
    If one finite characteristic polynomial is (T − 1)Φd (T ) with the second factor irreducible of
degree four, every proper nonzero rational submodule has dimension one or four. In dimension
one that generator acts as the identity. Since the product of the two finite generators is unipotent,
their induced one-dimensional characters are inverse; hence the other generator also acts trivially.
This would be an invariant line. In dimension four the one-dimensional quotient is trivial by the
same argument, giving a coinvariant. Both have just been excluded.

The primitive exterior-square bridge used in the proof. Here is an elementary
construction of the classical five-dimensional orthogonal representation, with the precise
unipotent comparison. Let E = C4 have a symplectic basis e1 , e2 , f1 , f2V
                                                                          . The invariant bivector
ω = e1 ∧ f1 + e2 ∧ f2 has nonzero square. The wedge pairing on 2 E is symmetric and
nondegenerate. Its orthogonal complement E0 = ω ⊥ therefore has          V2dimension five  and is
nondegenerate. Preservation of ω gives determinant one on E; det( g) = (det g) and the
                                   2                                                    3

fixed line Cω therefore give determinant one on E0 . The action gives

                                       ρ : Sp(E) −→ SO(E0 ).

Its differential is injective. Indeed, a symplectic infinitesimal transformation acting trivially on E0
also acts trivially on Cω, hence on all of 2 E. In a basis, the equations Xei ∧ ej + ei ∧ Xej = 0
                                            V
for every i < j first make every off-diagonal coefficient of X zero, and then give Xii + Xjj = 0 for
every distinct pair. Since there are four indices, these equations make every diagonal coefficient
zero. Both Lie algebras have dimension ten, so the image contains a neighbourhood of the identity

                                                 283
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                     Paper III


in SO(E0 ). That complex special orthogonal group is connected. For completeness, orthogonal
elimination expresses an orthogonal matrix as a product of reflections in vectors of nonzero
norm: to fix a nonisotropic vector, reflection in the difference of its image and itself works when
that difference is nonisotropic; otherwise reflection in their sum followed by reflection in the
vector works. At least one of sum and difference is nonisotropic. Continue on its nondegenerate
orthogonal complement. Determinant one makes the number of reflections even. The nonisotropic
vectors of a complex vector space of dimension at least two form a path-connected set, since two
generic complex line segments can avoid the zero set of the norm polynomial except at finitely
many parameter values, around which the paths can be detoured. Varying one vector in a pair of
reflections to the other connects that pair to the identity. The one-dimensional final complement
contributes only the already accounted-for sign. This proves connectedness. Thus the open image
of ρ is the whole special orthogonal group.
    The kernel is {I, −I}. If an element acts trivially on E0 , it also fixes ω and hence every
bivector. It preserves every two-plane, as follows by applying it to a nonzero decomposable
bivector of that plane. Intersections of two-planes show that it preserves every line. A linear
map preserving every line is scalar: apply it to the coordinate lines and their pairwise sums. Its
scalar has square one. In particular every finite orthogonal element of order m has lifts whose
mth powers belong to {I, −I}; the lifts are finite and semisimple.
    The symplectic transvection fixing e1 , e2 , f2 and sending f1 to f1 + e1 acts on the following
primitive basis:

                    e1 ∧ e2 ,   e1 ∧ f2 ,   e2 ∧ f1 ,   f1 ∧ f2 ,    e1 ∧ f1 − e2 ∧ f2 .

Its difference from the identity sends the third vector to the negative of the first and the fourth
to the second, and annihilates the other three. Its orthogonal Jordan type is therefore (2, 2, 1).
Conversely, for an orthogonal unipotent I + N of that type, N 2 = 0 implies N ∗ = −N , because
(I + N )∗ = (I + N )−1 = I − N . Its image is an isotropic plane. After choosing a basis of that
plane and a dual isotropic plane, use the isometry on their residual nondegenerate line to make
the identification of two such decompositions have determinant one. Changing its sign changes
that determinant and commutes with N , which kills the residual line. In these decompositions, N
is determined by a nonzero alternating form on the dual two-dimensional space. All such forms
are equivalent under its general linear group. Extending that change by the inverse transpose on
the first plane gives an orthogonal change of basis; its determinant is one. Thus these unipotents
form one special-orthogonal conjugacy class. Surjectivity of ρ lifts the conjugacy. The two lifts
of I + N are a symplectic transvection and its negative. Hence, after changing one lift’s sign, the
product of the two finite lifts in the argument is precisely a rank-one symplectic transvection.
    Finally a symplectic diagonal element with eigenvalues x, x−1 , y, y −1 acts on E0 with
eigenvalues
                                  1, xy, x/y, y/x, (xy)−1 .
This gives the exact eigenvalue comparison used above and completes the required bridge without
changing any assertion about rational or integral conjugacy.

Theorem 6.16 (exclusion of three further order pairs). No simply connected datum with k = 2,
b2 = 0, and finite linear orders (3, 5), (3, 8) or (3, 10) has the required maximal square-zero cusp.
Among such data, the remaining necessary unordered linear order pairs are

                                  {(3, 4), (4, 5), (5, 6), (5, 8), (5, 12)}.                  (F.30)

When one order is five, the other finite characteristic polynomial cannot be (T − 1)2 Φ4 (T )2 or
(T − 1)2 Φ6 (T )2 .

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 6.15; equation (F.31).


                                                    284
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                          Paper III


Proof. Let the second order be d ∈ {5, 8, 10}. Proposition 6.15 gives an irreducible rational
rank-five quotient W , with finite characteristic polynomials

                              (T − 1)(T 2 + T + 1)2 ,      (T − 1)Φd (T ).

Since the invariant line of V lies in im NV , the quotient cusp has Jordan type (2, 2, 1). All three
local conjugacy classes are self-dual. Their centralizer dimensions are respectively 9, 5, 13. For
the last value, the conjugate partition is (3, 2), so the dimension is 32 + 22 ; the finite values are
the sums of squares of their eigenvalue multiplicities. Consequently the invariant-sheaf Euler
formula applied to Hom(W, W ∗ ) gives

                         χ P1 , j∗ Hom(W, W ∗ ) = −25 + 9 + 5 + 13 = 2.                         (F.31)
                                                


If W were not self-dual, irreducibility would make both HomΓ (W, W ∗ ) and HomΓ (W ∗ , W )
zero. These are the degree-zero group and the dual of the degree-two group in (F.31). The
Euler characteristic would then be nonpositive, a contradiction. Thus W has an invariant
nondegenerate rational bilinear form. Its symmetric part is nonzero, since an alternating form
cannot be nondegenerate in odd dimension; irreducibility then makes that symmetric part
nondegenerate. Both generators have determinant one.
     Over C use Spin5 ≃ Sp4 and its explicit degree-two representation on the primitive exterior
square. Choose finite semisimple lifts R, S of the two orthogonal generators, choosing one of their
signs so that RS is the unipotent lift of their unipotent product. The orthogonal Jordan type
(2, 2, 1) lifts to a rank-one transvection. This can be verified directly, as follows. For a rank-two
square-zero skew-adjoint operator on a five-dimensional quadratic space, its image is a maximal
isotropic plane, and its nonzero skew form on the dual plane determines one orbit under the
complex orthogonal group. A rank-one symplectic transvection in dimension four maps, under
the primitive exterior square, to precisely that orbit: its logarithm has two length-two blocks and
one trivial block. The exact exterior matrices checking these ranks and square zero are included
in fourfolds_order_pairs.py.
     The first lift has, up to a common sign, eigenvalues 1, 1, ζ3 , ζ3−1 . Indeed a symplectic torus with
eigenvalues x, x−1 , y, y −1 has primitive exterior eigenvalues 1, xy, x/y, y/x, (xy)−1 ; substitution
of the two equal primitive-third pairs gives the asserted list. In particular R has a repeated
eigenvalue. The lift S has order dividing 2d, so it has no eigenvalue of order three or six. Nor can
it have eigenvalue 1 or −1: a symplectic pair x = x−1 = ±1 would make two of the nontrivial
primitive exterior eigenvalues repeat, whereas Φd has four distinct roots. Thus R−1 and S have
coprime characteristic polynomials.
     We finish with an elementary consequence of the rank-one companion argument. Two matrices
with coprime characteristic polynomials whose difference has rank one are both cyclic. To prove
this, let u span the difference image. A common invariant subspace either meets the image
nontrivially, in which case the two induced quotient matrices agree, or is killed by the difference,
in which case their restrictions agree. Coprimality forces that subspace to be respectively the
whole space or zero. The span of the iterates of u under either matrix is stable under both
and is nonzero; it is therefore the whole space, proving cyclicity. Apply this to R−1 , S, since
R−1 − S = R−1 (I − RS) has rank one. But a finite semisimple matrix with a repeated eigenvalue
is not cyclic. This contradicts the displayed spectrum of R, and excludes all three order pairs.
The same proof gives the final assertion: replace the two primitive-third pairs on W by two
primitive-fourth or primitive-sixth pairs. The local centralizer dimension is still nine, so the
Hom Euler characteristic is again two. The spin lift has, up to sign, eigenvalues 1, 1, ζj , ζj−1 for
j = 4 or 6. The other lift has order dividing ten and has no eigenvalue 1 or −1 because its
primitive exterior spectrum is simple. Their spectra are disjoint, and cyclicity gives the same
contradiction.

Proposition 6.17 (rational uniqueness of the extension). Let W be a rational rank-five
representation of a twice-punctured affine line, with two finite generators having fixed rank one and
product with unipotent Jordan type (2, 2, 1). Suppose W has neither invariants nor coinvariants.
Up to rescaling the invariant line, there is exactly one rational extension 0 → Qe → V → W → 0
in which the two finite generators retain their finite orders and the cusp has square-zero logarithm
of rank three. Thus, for the two-point candidates of 6.15, the remaining rational representation
problem is exactly the problem of the rank-five quotients. This statement does not identify integral
lattices in those representations.

Proof. All matrix identities and integral lattices used below are printed and checked exactly in

          u1 = (1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0)t ,    u2 = (1, −1, 1, −1, 0, −1)t ,      ` = (1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0).

They are invariant vectors with `(ui ) = 1. The cusp vanishing lattice and its two finite translates
generate the saturated lattice ker `. Choose twists v1 = −2u1 , v2 = 5u2 . Their `-values are units
modulo five and twelve, proving every nonidentity affine power free. After killing the vanishing

for the invariant sheaves, and the same rational Leray argument as in 6.8 gives the asserted Betti
vector.
    We first prove that changing the lattice cannot remove the obstruction at the prime three.
Write R = Z3 and K = Q3 . The standard quotient lattice WR defined by A5 , B5 has irreducible
reduction modulo three. Indeed Φ5 is irreducible over F3 , since three has order four modulo
five. Every proper nonzero A5 -stable subspace therefore has dimension one or four. On a
one-dimensional subrepresentation or quotient its A5 character is one; the unipotent product
forces the B5 character to be one too. The stacked and horizontal matrices for A5 − I, B5 − I
both have rank five modulo three, as certified in the code, ruling out those two possibilities.
    This irreducible reduction makes WR the unique stable R-lattice up to homothety. To see this,
rescale another lattice into WR but not into 3WR . Its reduction is a nonzero invariant subspace,
hence all of WR /3WR . Nakayama’s lemma, or the elementary Smith form of the inclusion, then
makes it equal to WR .
    Normalize the quotient of any stable lattice in VK to be WR . Its intersection with the invariant
line is 3r Re for some integer r. The representation of the free group on the two generators has
extension class α ∈ H 1 (Γ, WR∗ ). This cohomology group is torsion free: the coboundary map
from WR∗ into two copies has full column rank modulo three, since WR∗ has no invariants modulo
three. The class α is primitive in this free R-module. Otherwise the extension would split modulo
three and V would have a trivial quotient there. The horizontal matrix [A − I B − I] instead
has Smith factors (1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2), so it has full rank modulo three.
    In a basis starting with 3r e, the extension class is 3−r α. Integrality is therefore possible
exactly when r ≤ 0. Changes of splitting introduce no further classes: the coboundary image is
primitive, so an integral coboundary over K is already an integral coboundary over R. Thus these
lattices are represented by multiplying the extension rows by 3−r . On the quotient cusp NW has
primitive rank-two image. The extra cusp map is the nonzero map ker NW / im NW → Re. It is
a unit for the displayed lattice, because its full cusp has Smith factors (1, 1, 1); for the lattice
indexed by r it is multiplied by 3−r . Hence the full cusp is primitive exactly when r = 0. We
have proved uniqueness of the primitive-cusp lattice over R, without relying on a bounded lattice
search.
    It remains to compute the obstruction on that lattice. We first justify the arbitrary-twist
comparison integrally. For any global invariant lattice take the primitive invariant homology
covector ` and quotient the van Kampen group by every fibre loop in ker `. The finite presentations
become [a, h] = [b, h] = 1, am1 = hr1 , bm2 = hr2 , where ri = `(vi ). The cusp meridian gives
ab = h−κ for an integer κ determined by its translation clutching (κ = 0 for the stated standard

                                                   287
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                       Paper III


clutching). The cusp angular lattice lies in ker `, so it adds no further relation to this quotient. In
particular this is an abelian quotient with determinant m1 m2 κ+m2 r1 +m1 r2 . Simple connectivity
makes that determinant ±1. Reduction modulo each mi proves both gcd(m1 , m2 ) = 1 and
gcd(ri , mi ) = 1.
    The two finite fillings have free R-cohomology in the degrees needed here. In the invariant
marking whose first homology vector over R has `-value one, the map mi ` from the reduced finite
fibre to R/Z has connected fibre T 5 : the affine generator permutes its mi preimage components
by addition of ri modulo mi , transitively by the proved coprimality. Its monodromy on vertical

mapping torus of a power prime to the linear order. The translation is isotopic to the identity
and does not change its Wang maps. At the second point, over R we may take the invariant
first vector to be v2 /r2 ; its denominator is prime to three and does not change the R-homology
lattice. At the first point the covering degree m1 is prime to three, so averaging and the transfer

    The finite degree-two covering cokernel is read from integral periods. Vertical cycles have
integral periods. The remaining primitive two-cycle is the commuting torus formed by a base
suspension and a primitive fixed vertical loop λi ; its covering period is ω(ui , λi )/mi for an

      0 −→ coker(Disi − I | H2 (T 5 ; R)) −→ H2 (Bi ; R) −→ ker(Disi − I | H1 (T 5 ; R)) −→ 0.

                                        (0, 0, 5),    (3, 1, 1).                              (F.35)
The vertical Wang quotient has no torsion, so those cycles generate the full free second homology

    Since 3 | m2 , the already-proved coprimality gives 3 - m1 and makes r2 a unit in R. Changing

is primitive, with vanishing rational parabolic first cohomology. Therefore H 1 (P1 , R2 g∗ R) =

would be zero. Their two supporting planes in W ∗ would be distinct stable planes meeting in

orthogonal and N ∗ = −N , so I + tN is orthogonal for every t. The odd-dimensional characteristic
polynomial of (I + tN )A is then anti-reciprocal. Its quadratic coefficient in t is

                                      x2 (det H)x − det H 0 ,
                                                           


by the determinant lemma, so anti-reciprocity forces det H = det H 0 . Formula (F.U8) contradicts
this whenever v 6= 0.
    All the matrix identities, coefficient integrality, both mod-two checks, and the affine formula are
checked symbolically by code/fourfolds_unbounded_family.py. Its separate Smith diagnostics
over −6 ≤ v ≤ 10 are explicitly bounded and are not the basis for the universal assertions
above.

Theorem 6.24 (a residual obstruction for every lattice). Let a rational rank-six datum have finite
linear orders five and four, a primitive maximal cusp on a stable integral lattice, and invariant
line L, with irreducible rank-five quotient W and no rational global coinvariants. Suppose that at
a prime p 6= 2, 5 the semisimplified reduction of a stable lattice in W is the sum of the trivial
module and an absolutely irreducible module of dimension four. Then no stable integral lattice in
that rational datum, with primitive maximal cusp, and no free finite affine twists can give π1 = 1
and H2 = 0 simultaneously.
    For every v ∈/ {0, 1}, the rational family in 6.21 satisfies this hypothesis at each prime dividing
v − v + 1. Consequently the exclusion of those parameters holds for all stable lattices and all
  2

twists, not just the lattice in (F.U6). The two remaining parameters are the verified survivors of
6.10 and 6.23.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 6.21; equation (F.U6);
theorem 6.10; theorem 6.23; equation (F.U12); proposition 6.22; equation (F.U1).




                                                    295
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                    Paper III


Proof. We first give the lattice-independent mechanism. For any stable lattice VZ , use its
primitive invariant line LZ and quotient lattice WZ . The semisimplified reduction of a rational
representation is independent of its stable lattice. One elementary way to see this is to compare
two commensurable lattices by their finite quotient T . The exact sequence obtained by reduction
modulo p has end terms T [p] and T /pT , which have the same composition factors by the filtration
of T by powers of p. Hence the two lattice reductions have equal classes in the Grothendieck
group of finite-length modules. Chaining such comparisons proves the assertion for any two
lattices.
    Thus WZ /pWZ has length two, with one trivial constituent and one irreducible four-
dimensional constituent. It has either a trivial submodule or a trivial quotient (and possibly
both).
    Suppose first that it has a trivial submodule. Its inverse image in VZ /pVZ is an extension of
a trivial module by a trivial module. Each finite generator acts on this two-dimensional space by
a unipotent matrix. Since its order is five or four, prime to p, it acts as the identity. There are
therefore at least two global invariant vectors in degree-one fibre cohomology modulo p. Write
their dimension as ap ≥ 2; this is also the dimension of the global coinvariants of fibre homology
over Fp , by the perfect pairing between fibre homology and cohomology.
    The abelianized van Kampen presentation now shows

                                         b1 (M ; Fp ) ≥ ap − 1.                            (F.U12)

Indeed, after the monodromy relations the fibre contributes ap dimensions, and the two finite
meridians contribute two more. The two finite power relations and the single base relation
impose at most three linear relations. The cusp introduces no further fibre relation in this
abelianization. On the dual homology lattice its nilpotent operator is still primitive and maximal,
so its angular lattice is ker(M0 − I) = im(M0 − I) by primitivity, and the latter image already
vanishes among the global monodromy relations. Its base meridian is the base relation just
counted. Changing affine twists changes coefficients of these three relations, not their number.
Thus (F.U12) contradicts simple connectivity.
    Suppose instead that the reduction of W has a trivial quotient. Its integral global coinvariants
have nonzero p-primary torsion, since they have rational rank zero. The natural map from
the global coinvariants of V to those of W is an isomorphism. To check its kernel, a primitive
generator e of LZ lies in ker(M0 − I) = im(M0 − I), and hence is already zero among global
coinvariants. Therefore H 2 (R1 ) has nonzero p-primary torsion. If the total space were simply
connected, the finite-cap argument of 6.22 would make every V2 possible torsion source in H (R )
                                                                                              0   2

supported only at two and five. The invariant part of          V is zero by irreducibility of the
odd-dimensional quotient. Consequently the nonzero p-primary subgroup survives to H 3 (M ; Z)
and then to Tor H2 (M ; Z), again a contradiction. This proves the general criterion.
    For its application to 6.21, let p | q = v 2 − v + 1. We have p 6= 2, 5. In the original cycle
lattice of (F.U1), Y 1 = 2q(−1, 1 − v)t , so 1 gives a trivial submodule after reduction. On
the four-dimensional quotient the first finite generator has characteristic polynomial Φ5 , and
C = B −1 has polynomial (x + 1)2 (x2 + 1). This quotient is absolutely irreducible. Here is a
characteristic-independent proof over Fp .
    A one-dimensional composition factor would make the eigenvalues of A and C equal, because
CA−1 is unipotent. An eigenvalue of order dividing both five and four must be one, which is
absent from Φ5 . If the quotient were reducible, its only remaining possible composition-factor
dimensions would be two and two. On each factor, the determinants of A and C must agree
and have orders dividing five and four, so both determinants are one. The two C eigenvalue
pairs must therefore be (−1, −1) and (i, −i) in some order. On the former factor C = −I, since
its order is prime to p. Then the unipotence of CA−1 = −A−1 would force the eigenvalues of
A to be −1, impossible for Φ5 . This proves absolute irreducibility and establishes the required


                                                  296
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                     Paper III


residual composition factors at every p | q. When v ∈/ {0, 1}, the integer q is greater than one
and has such a prime divisor. The criterion applies.

Corollary 6.26 (all good-prime lattices are forced). For a (5, 4) datum with π1 = 1 and H2 = 0,
the rank-five quotient has absolutely irreducible reduction at every prime p 6= 2, 5. At each such
prime its stable Zp -lattice is unique up to homothety. The same is true of the rank-six extension
among lattices with primitive maximal cusp. Thus, once a rational pair in 6.25 admits one
survivor, all remaining integral-lattice ambiguity is supported at the primes two and five. This
assertion supplies no finite bound on those bad-prime lattices or on the rational parameters.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 6.25; theorem 6.24.

Proof. Work first over an algebraic closure of Fp . Both finite generators are semisimple because
p 6= 2, 5. A one-dimensional composition factor must be trivial: its A and C eigenvalues agree by
the unipotent product, and their orders divide five and four. There can be at most one such
factor, since the 1 eigenvalue of A occurs once. If it occurs, the remaining four-dimensional
module is absolutely irreducible by the spectral argument in 6.24. The only other possible
reducible composition pattern is 2 + 3. On each factor, determinants of A and C agree and
have orders dividing five and four, hence are one. The two-dimensional C eigenvalue pair is
therefore (−1, −1) or (i, −i). The first would give C = −I on that factor, contradicting the
unipotence of CA−1 and the absence of −1 among the eigenvalues of A. In the second case the
three-dimensional factor has C eigenvalues 1, −1, −1, so C 2 = I there; it has an A-fixed vector
because the other factor has determinant one and cannot contain the simple 1 eigenvalue of A.
    Here is the required elementary involutory identity in the present characteristic. Put B = A−1
on this factor. From (CB − I)2 = 0 and C 2 = I one obtains

                                          BC + CB −1 = 2I.

For Bv = v this says (B + I)Cv = 2v. The operator B + I is invertible, since B 5 = I and p 6= 2,
so Cv = v. The resulting common fixed line contradicts simplicity of the three-dimensional
factor. We have proved that any reducible residual representation has exactly the constituents 1
and an absolutely irreducible four-dimensional module. Theorem 6.24 excludes that possibility
for a survivor, proving absolute irreducibility at every indicated prime.
    Let R = Zp and Kp = Qp . For two stable quotient lattices, multiply one by a power of p
until it is contained in the other but not in its p-multiple. Its nonzero residual image must then


                                                  299
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                       Paper III


be the whole quotient by absolute irreducibility. Nakayama’s lemma, or the Smith form of the
inclusion, makes the lattices equal. This proves quotient-lattice uniqueness.
    For completeness the extension-lattice comparison is also integral. Fix a primitive-cusp lattice
VR , with invariant line Re and quotient WR . The coboundary map

                                         WR∗ −→ WR∗ ⊕ WR∗

is primitive, because its reduction has trivial kernel. Thus its cokernel, the degree-one cohomology
of the free group on the two generators, is torsion free, and an integral coboundary over Kp is
already integral over R. The extension class α is primitive in this cokernel. Indeed, divisibility
by p would make the extra cusp map

                                      ker NW / im NW −→ Re

divisible by p, contrary to the three unit Smith factors of the full cusp. Here NW has primitive
image: it is the quotient of the primitive image of NV by Re ⊂ im NV .
    Normalize any other stable lattice by the already proved quotient homothety so that its
quotient is WR . Its invariant line is pr Re for some integer r. The extension class in that basis
is p−r α; primitivity makes it integral only when r ≤ 0. Primitivity of the coboundary map
eliminates any additional rational change of splitting. The extra cusp map is then multiplied by
p−r , so its Smith factor is a unit exactly when r = 0. The lattices coincide after the common
homothety. This proves the full assertion and retains the bad-prime and rational-parameter
problems explicitly.

Theorem 6.27 (a terminating lattice algorithm for each rational pair). Let (A, C) be any
irreducible rational rank-five pair in one of the eight spectral cases of 6.20, with A5 = I, B = C −1 ,
and (AB − I)2 = 0 of rank two. There is an explicit terminating algorithm which decides whether
the pair preserves an integral lattice, and, if so, lists all such lattices up to simultaneous integral
conjugacy. It then lists all rank-six extensions with the same finite orders and primitive maximal
square-zero cusp, up to simultaneous integral conjugacy. The bounds below depend on the input
rational pair and are proved to lose no lattice. They do not bound the rational parameter space
or classify all affine twists and resulting homology.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 6.20; equation (F.L3);
equation (F.L5); proposition 6.17; equation (F.L6); equation (F.L7).

Proof. We give the algorithm and its termination proof. The fixed line of A has dimension one.
Choose a nonzero vector e on it and a nonzero fixed covector ϕ. Irreducibility implies that the
vectors ge, with g a word in A, C, span the whole rational space; the analogous statement holds
for the covectors ϕh. In fact words of length at most four suffice. The spans of words of lengths
at most j increase from dimension one; if one step does not increase the span, it is invariant
under both generators and hence already the whole space. There are only four possible increases.
    Choose words g1 , . . . , g5 and h1 , . . . , h5 giving bases in this way, and put

                              P = I + A + · · · + A4 ,     Tij = gi P hj .                     (F.L1)

The rank-one operator P is a nonzero scalar multiple of eϕ. Hence the 25 matrices Tij are a
rational basis of Mat5 (Q). Each belongs to R = Z[A, C]. Let R0 be their integral span and set

Theorem 6.33 (universal fundamental group and twist normalization). In the remaining (5, 4)
locus, fix the marked standard Kuhn cap and allow affine translation clutching. Let Λ = Z6 be
fibre homology and let ΛΓ be its global monodromy coinvariants. Write ΛΓ = Zh ⊕ T , with T
finite, and let ` be the primitive invariant covector detecting the free factor. The following are
complete reductions for any datum that could satisfy π1 = 1 and H2 = H3 = 0.
    The actual multiplicities must be (5, 4), and the local vertical fixed pairings must be h1 =
5, h2 = 4, as in 6.30. For any affine twists and clutching the fundamental group is abelian. If its
free presentation determinant is nonzero, its order is

                               |π1 | = |20κ + 4r1 + 5r2 | |T |,     ri = `(vi ).              (F.T11)

If that determinant is zero the group is infinite. In particular simple connectivity is equivalent to

                                    T = 0,       20κ + 4r1 + 5r2 = ±1.                        (F.T12)

Whenever these conditions and h1 = 5, h2 = 4 hold, every such twist choice is oriented
diffeomorphic to the normalized filling with twists (u1 , −u2 ) and zero cusp clutching, where
ui is any integral fixed vector with `(ui ) = 1. Thus each eligible integral linear datum has exactly
one normalized smooth filling to test for the remaining homology conditions; no affine-twist
enumeration remains.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 6.30; equation (F.S5);
equation (F.T8); theorem 6.29.

Proof. The image of the fibre fundamental group is a normal abelian subgroup in the van Kampen
presentation. After quotienting by it, the two finite meridians satisfy a5 = b4 = ab = 1. That
quotient is trivial, because five and four are coprime. The entire fundamental group is therefore
equal to the image of the fibre group and is abelian. This argument does not assume that the
normal closure of cusp vanishing cycles already exhausts ker `.
   In abelianization the monodromy relations give ΛΓ . The primitive cusp angular lattice is the
image of its nilpotent operator, and this image is already zero among those monodromy relations.
The remaining presentation is

                   5a = v1 ,        4b = v2 ,      a + b + v0 = 0    in ΛΓ ⊕ Za ⊕ Zb,         (F.T13)

where `(v0 ) = κ fixes the sign convention. Use any Smith presentation of T and split the free part
Zh. The full relation matrix is block triangular, with the presentation of T as one diagonal block
and the three-by-three free matrix of determinant ±(20κ+4r1 +5r2 ) as the other. Its determinant
gives (F.T11); when the latter free matrix has rank less than three the group has positive rank
and is infinite. For determinant ±1, elimination of the three free variables leaves precisely T ,
even if the twists have nonzero torsion components. This proves the exact simple-connectivity
criterion.
    We give the global twist comparison to make its scope precise. Under (F.T12), the finite fixed
covector image is one at each point, so choose integral fixed ui with `(ui ) = 1. The primitive
vertical fixed vector λi and invariant covector ϕi satisfy ϕi (λi ) = mi , by the assumed maximal
local pairings. Formula (F.S5) makes the finite norm onto Zλi . Consequently every vertical
numerator component si λi is removed by the explicit cap translation (F.T8), whose boundary
residue has `-coordinate zero.

Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                           Paper III


     For the complementary pair of pants the full relative obstruction group for extending boundary
translation sections is H 2 (P, ∂P ; Λ) = ΛΓ . Now T = 0, so it is exactly Z detected by `, not just a
rational or free quotient. Prescribing the identity translation at the cusp therefore allows all the
vertical finite changes to extend over P . The same argument removes the zero-` component of any
cusp translation clutching. For determinant −1, write r1 = 1 + 5a, r2 = −1 + 4b; then (F.T12)
says a + b + κ = 0. The two integer changes of finite boundary marking and the remaining cusp

fibre inversion extending over the Kuhn fan, proved in 6.29, identifies the two choices. All maps
used in the comparison are cap translations or translations by smooth torus-bundle sections
over P ; the prescribed cusp is retained throughout. This proves the claimed complete twist
normalization.

Corollary 6.35 (constructive classification of all survivors). For the marked Kuhn cap and affine
translation clutchings used throughout F.2, the following is a complete constructive classification
of the data with π1 = 1 and H2 = H3 = 0, up to integral conjugacy of their linear tuples and
oriented diffeomorphism of their fillings.
    There are no data with three genuine finite fillings. With two fillings their actual affine orders
are five and four. Order the order-five point first. The complete, unbounded parameter set is
the rational projective normal form of 6.25 together with its exceptional rational affine line. For
each parameter, run the terminating order, conductor, stable-lattice, and primitive-extension
algorithm of 6.27. Discard precisely the integral classes failing (F.HC1) or one of (F.HC3). The
classes retained by this procedure are exactly all surviving integral linear tuples. For each retained
class all simply connected affine twists are exactly the choices satisfying (F.T12); their fillings
are all oriented diffeomorphic to its normalized filling. If ordered labels with the order-four point
first are desired, interchange the finite labels and recompute M0 = (M1 M2 )−1 .

Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                     Paper III


   Every retained datum has
                                                 
                                                 Z, j = 0, 8,
                                                 
                               π1 = 1,       Hj = Z4 , j = 4,                             (F.HC13)
                                                       otherwise,
                                                 
                                                  0,
                                                 

and its oriented smooth manifold is 3HP2 #(−HP2 ). It has bounded-cusp holomorphic periods in
the literal sense of F.3, by 6.51. The classification here concerns the survivor subproblem. It does
not classify the nonsurviving tuples or compute their full integral homology, as also requested in
F.2.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 6.25; theorem 6.27;
equation (F.HC1); equation (F.HC3); equation (F.T12); theorem 6.51; theorem 6.12;
theorem 6.20; theorem 6.30; theorem 6.32; theorem 6.33; theorem 6.34; theorem 5.3;
proposition 6.13; theorem 6.8; theorem A.9; theorem 6.52.

Proof. The exclusions 6.12, 6.20, 6.30, and 6.32 leave exactly the stated minimal orders and
rational quotient problem. The rational normal form is injective on conjugacy classes, including
the exceptional line. The finite interval and extension-coset enumeration in 6.27 gives every
integral class over each rational point, with all bounds proved for that input. No distinct rational
points can become integrally conjugate, since an integral conjugacy induces a rational quotient
conjugacy. Theorem 6.33 and the necessary-and-sufficient criterion 6.34 prove both directions
of the retention rule and account for every affine twist. This is also an exhaustive enumeration
if desired: enumerate primitive projective integer triples with first nonzero coordinate positive
by increasing height, and enumerate reduced rational exceptional parameters by increasing
numerator and denominator height. Every finite stage has finitely many inputs, each terminates
by 6.27, and every rational input occurs. No finite cutoff is imposed or needed.
    Hurewicz makes the retained simply connected manifolds three-connected. The only singular
contribution to Euler number is the Kuhn cusp, whose value is six by 5.3; torus bundles and the
free finite caps have Euler number zero. Integral Poincare duality and the universal coefficient
theorem then give (F.HC13), including torsion freeness.
    For the smooth classification, 6.13 supplies a compatible complex structure at each finite cap,
and the cusp already has its complex model. Choose their common fibre orientation to be the
one induced by the cusp. Commuting complex structures at the finite caps can be chosen in that
component: their two-dimensional fixed real summands allow the orientation to be reversed when
necessary. The fibre of the bundle of orientation-compatible complex structures retracts to CP3 .
Its connectedness and simple connectivity extend the prescribed boundary structures across the
two-dimensional pair of pants, exactly as in 6.8. A compatible horizontal distribution gives an
almost complex structure on the total manifold. Theorem A.9 therefore gives signature two,
intersection lattice I3,1 , and c22 = 2. Since H 2 = 0, p1 /2 = −c2 is primitive, characteristic, and
has square two. The complete Wall–Nikulin–Nagy argument in 6.52 depends only on these almost
complex characteristic numbers and three-connectivity. It applies without alteration and gives
the claimed exact oriented diffeomorphism. Finally 6.51 applies to the resulting determinant-one
monodromy and primitive cusp. It asserts the requested punctured-base periods with bounded
correction, not an additional unproved simultaneous good extension at all finite points.

Proof. Actual finite and cusp caps. The affine lift on R6 has mi th power translation by wi , as
the displayed sum shows. It commutes with that power, so Mi wi = wi . The group generated by
lattice translations and this lift is the fundamental group of the reduced flat six-manifold. Its
presentation consists of the lattice, its si conjugation relations, and sm        i = wi . The finite cap
                                                                                   i

deformation retracts onto that reduced manifold by the equivariant radial contraction of its root
disc. Thus these are the actual cap relations, even for a numerator which is not an invariant
lattice vector.
    For the primitive Kuhn cap, the compact toric strata in its normalization and all their
intersection components are simply connected. Applying van Kampen successively to their
tubular neighborhoods identifies the fundamental group of the central fibre with that of its dual
three-torus. The nearby fibre map kills the angular lattice U and sends the long-period lattice
Λ/U isomorphically onto this dual-torus group. This is also the explicit toric collapse used in
5.3. The primitive index-one condition gives U = ker(M0 − I) and makes Λ/U free of rank three.
A section through a smooth central stratum bounds the base meridian by its parameter disc.
The smooth cap retracts onto the central fibre, so it adds exactly these relations, with no extra
meridian relation left unspecified.
    Over the punctured sphere the bundle has a section up to homotopy, because the base retracts
to a graph. Its group is the appropriate semidirect product. Choose the cap sections and retain
their relative translation clutching as κ. Van Kampen with the actual boundary maps just
described gives exactly (F.G3). Changing the transport convention causes no group ambiguity:
reverse the ordered list and replace each affine map by its inverse, and replace κ by −κ. The
new linear matrices are Mk−1 , . . . , M1−1 , the power vectors are −wk , . . . , −w1 , and the cusp image
lattice is unchanged. The substitutions si 7→ s−1      k+1−i give the explicit isomorphism between
these two presentations. This supplies the dictionary when geometric transport is recorded with
opposite path-composition order.
    Integral closure and two-point elimination. In a normal abelian fibre subgroup, the normal
closure of U is precisely the integer sum (F.G4). Start with its column Hermite basis and
repeatedly append its images under every Mi and Mi−1 , then take Hermite normal form again. If
the rational rank increases, it can do so at most three times. At the first nonincrease the rational
span is invariant under every generator and its inverse, hence never increases again. If the current
lattice has saturation index D in that span, every subsequent strict enlargement divides this
index by an integer at least two. There can therefore be at most blog2 Dc such enlargements.
This proves termination and gives the computable bound used by the code; it never replaces a
finite-index lattice by its saturation.
    On A one has M2 = M −1 in the two-point case. The product relation eliminates s2 = t−1 x−κ ,
where t = s1 . Multiplying this word m2 times gives
                                    (t−1 x−κ )m2 = t−m2 x−Sm2 (M )κ .
Thus the two power relations become tm1 = w1 and tm2 = w20 . Both right sides are fixed by M
on A. Also M m1 = M m2 = 1, hence M d = 1 there. Bezout elimination gives exactly e = 0 and
td = z in (F.G5). Replacing the Bezout pair changes z by a multiple of e and therefore changes
no extension datum.
    To prove the asserted injection, construct A oM Z and quotient by its central element td z −1 .
This cyclic subgroup has nonzero projection dZ to the infinite cyclic factor, so it intersects
A trivially. The quotient has precisely the presentation obtained by elimination. This proves
(F.G6), including the absence of any further hidden fibre relation.

additional kernel is exactly hei. This proves the spherical assertion, with the orientation fixed by
this cell calculation.
    There is no implicit infinite search for a spherical group. After sorting its orders the
possibilities are (2, 2, n), (2, 3, 3), (2, 3, 4), (2, 3, 5), with groups of orders 2n, 12, 24, 60, respectively.
These follow directly from the positive spherical-triangle angle condition. The code constructs
the dihedral, tetrahedral, octahedral, or icosahedral permutation group and finds the marked
peripheral generators in that finite group. Breadth-first words supply their actions on A; every
generator edge is checked modulo the actual lattice L. It then computes the two finite sums in
(F.G9) and their integer Smith form.

Theorem 6.37 (a complete three-point logarithmic family). Start with the compact complex
fourfold of 6.47 and its normalized order-five and order-four affine fillings. Let ` be the primitive
invariant covector on fibre homology, with the sign chosen in 6.33. At any additional ordinary
fibre choose v ∈ Z6 and an integer m ≥ 2 such that

                                    r = `(v),      gcd(r, m) = 1.                             (F.LT1)

fillings, whose linear orders are five, four and one and whose actual affine orders are five, four
and m. Its fundamental group is

         π1 (Xm,v ) = ha, b, c, h | h central, a5 = h, b4 = h−1 , cm = hr , abc = 1i.         (F.LT2)

the convention xαi i hβi = 1 and product xi = 1. Its base orbifold is hyperbolic, and its central fibre
h has infinite order.

    One may verify the Seifert identification directly: take a product circle bundle on a three-
holed sphere and attach its three solid tori with primitive meridian slopes (5, −1), (4, 1), (m, −r).

hyperbolic orbifold cover gives a circle bundle on the plane, hence the trivial circle bundle. The
subsequent universal cover is the plane times R, and the fibre subgroup is infinite cyclic. This
also proves directly that none of these groups is trivial. The rational Euler number in these
conventions is r/m − 1/20.
    In abelianization the relations 5a = h, 4b = −h give a = 4x, b = −5x, h = 20x because five
and four are coprime. The product relation gives c = x. The remaining relation is (m − 20r)x = 0.
Thus H1 = Cm,r exactly, including its integral generator and the exceptional infinite-cyclic case.

    Proof and exact algorithm. Let K be the periodic Kuhn triangulation of R3 . Normalize every
simplex by translating its lexicographically first vertex to zero. The objects are its simplex orbits;
a morphism τ → σ is every strict translated face inclusion τ + w ⊂ σ. Keep distinct translated
inclusions as distinct morphisms. Composition adds the translation vectors. Enumerating all
nonempty faces of the six chains in the unit cube gives (1, 7, 12, 6) simplex orbits in dimensions
zero through three, and the displayed morphism and flag counts. The category nerve is the
barycentric cell model of the dual decomposition of R3 /Z3 ; the direction of the face order is
reversed when interpreted as dual cells.
    For an object τ let Lτ ⊂ Z3 be the primitive span of its vertex differences. Its primitivity

retains their quotient by the vertex differences. The finite face identifications give (F.CK2), so
there are no further gluing constants in this fixed marked cap.

Hypotheses and marking of the logarithmic comparison.                     Give the small disc its

central fibre. In a unimodular chart the characteristic monoid map is
                                   N −→ Nk+1 ,        1 7−→ (1, . . . , 1).
Both monoids are fine and saturated. The group cokernel is free, and the underlying chart is the
monomial semistable map x0 · · · xk = t with additional smooth coordinates; this is log smooth.

the other generators after the diagonal generator is killed. The morphism is therefore vertical.
The periodic toric construction is proper over the sufficiently small disc.

the resulting radial boundary identification and its stated angular and tropical generators. This
suffices to model the pair and its inclusion up to marked homotopy. It does not replace the
supplied cusp marking by another integral basis.

    Scope of the chain result. The local finite pairs and the full cusp pair now have effective
marked chain models. To turn them into a universal integral homology calculation for arbitrary
nonsurviving F.2 data, one must also implement the maps from these boundary models to the
common torus-bundle complement, with its specified peripheral word and clutching translation.
The local results alone do not assert that this remaining global comparison has been completed.
    The periodic toric quotient used for the cusp is the construction in Yang’s theorem Higher-
dimensional periodic quotient, and its Kuhn-grid Euler number is the formula in his corollary The
standard grid family (Yang, 2026, section on periodic toroidal quotients in arbitrary dimension).
For the present primitive rank-three grid, this gives Euler number 3! = 6. The full cap and
boundary complexes, their integral inclusion, and the torsion groups are calculated in the proof
above.

Theorem 6.41 (simultaneous integral conjugacy for every input). There is an unconditional
exact algorithm which decides simultaneous GL6 (Z) conjugacy of any two marked matrix tuples of
F.2 and returns a conjugating matrix when one exists. The algorithm does not impose a bound on
their entries, on the affine multiplicities, or on the integral conjugator. More generally it applies
to any integral tuple containing a matrix 1 + N with N 2 = 0 and rank N = 3; the primitive-image
assumption is unnecessary for this statement.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; (Bley et al., 2022, Algorithm 8.3);
Bley et al. (2022); (Bley et al., 2022, Theorem 3.4 and Propositions 8.1–8.2).

Proof. We use column vectors and seek P satisfying P Xi = Yi P for every marked index, including
the cusp index. Put

                      H = {P ∈ Mat6 (Z) : P Xi = Yi P (∀i)},
                                                                                               (F.IC1)
                       O = {C ∈ Mat6 (Z) : CXi = Xi C (∀i)},           E = QO.

Both lattices are saturated integer kernels of explicitly displayed linear equations in thirty-six
unknowns. Thus Hermite or Smith reduction computes full bases, rather than sublattices of
finite index.
    We first Pdecide rational isomorphism. For a basis h1 , . . . , hs of H, form the polynomial
f (c) = det( cj hj ). If it is zero, there is no rational isomorphism. Otherwise successively
substitute one of 0, 1, . . . , 6 for each variable while keeping the remaining polynomial nonzero.
At each stage one of these seven values works, because the degree in that variable is at most
six. The final matrix D ∈ H is invertible over Q. This is a terminating exact test, including the
negative case, and not a search for a lucky invertible intertwiner.

    For clarity this decomposition is effective without a split-algebra oracle. Rational linear
algebra computes J as the radical of the regular trace pairing and computes the quotient
multiplication table. Its simple factors are obtained from its centre. A commutative factor is a
number field. In a noncommutative factor of dimension n2 , we enumerate integral combinations
e of a rational basis until the left ideal Be has dimension n. Such an e exists because the factor is
Matn (Q), so its rank-one matrices are rational points; clearing denominators expresses one among
the enumerated combinations. Left multiplication on Be then supplies an explicit isomorphism
to Matn (Q). The program verifies multiplication on every pair of basis elements.
    The images O and L are a full order and a full right lattice in B. If the right order of L
differs from O, this lattice cannot be principal over that order. Otherwise Algorithm 8.3 of Bley
et al. (2022), in its right-ideal form, decides principality and returns a generator α when one
exists. The cited algorithm passes through a maximal order and its central conductor, tests
local freeness and principality over the maximal order, and solves the remaining reduced-norm
congruence in a finite quotient. Its correctness proof uses its Theorem 4.5(b) and Theorem 7.9; its
Theorem 8.4 specifies the number-field, finite-field and integer factorization subproblems. These
have unconditional exact algorithms. In the recorded implementation the class and unit groups
of every number-field component are certified with GRH=false before the principal-ideal decision
is used. The negative decision thus does not presume the generalized Riemann hypothesis.
    If L is not principal, L cannot be principal. If it is principal, solve the integer linear equations
expressing α as a combination of the images of the chosen basis of L. This produces a lift α ∈ L
and an integral intertwiner P = Dα ∈ H. We claim that a simultaneous integral conjugacy exists
if and only if | det P | = 1.
    The sufficient direction is immediate. For the necessary direction, suppose P0 ∈ H is
unimodular. Every h ∈ H has P0−1 h ∈ O, so L = α0 O, where α0 = D−1 P0 . Write α = α0 u
with u ∈ O. Because both image elements generate L, u is a unit of O. Lift its inverse to
v ∈ O. Then uv = 1 + j with j ∈ J ∩ O, and the finite geometric series for (1 + j)−1 shows that
u−1 = v(1 + j)−1 ∈ O. Thus u is an integral unimodular matrix and P = P0 u is unimodular.
This also proves that any chosen lift of the image generator gives the same yes-or-no answer. It
is the right-module form of (Bley et al., 2022, Theorem 3.4 and Propositions 8.1–8.2), with the
needed determinant condition written out.
    Every branch either proves nonexistence or returns a matrix whose integrality, determinant
and all intertwining equations are verified exactly. This completes the decision procedure.

comparison algorithm is distinct from a completed tabulation of all nonsurviving tuples or from
an arbitrary-height truncation of such a tabulation.

Theorem 6.42 (a complete canonical-representative algorithm). Every marked linear tuple in
F.2, for either k = 2 or k = 3, has a computable canonical integral representative and a returned
simultaneous unimodular conjugator. Two inputs have the same representative if and only if they
are simultaneously GL6 (Z) conjugate. The algorithm uses a proved finite bound depending on the
input. No fixed global entry bound can represent every class.
    This is an effective classification, not a claim that its infinite output has been printed in a
finite table. The ordered involution sector has the separate complete finite normal form 6.43,
and all of its 56 classes have been computed. The general bounded fallback is potentially very
expensive; its finiteness is a theorem, not a runtime estimate.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 6.43; equation (F.CN1);
theorem 6.41; equation (F.CN2); theorem 6.21.

Proof. We first remove the existential condition about affine lifts from the admissibility test
for a linear tuple. A finite-order matrix M admits a free finite affine lift on T 6 if and only if
ker(M − 1) 6= 0. If this kernel is zero, 1 − M is a surjective endomorphism of the torus, so every
affine map with linear part M has a fixed point. Conversely let the order of M be d > 1 and
choose a primitive u ∈ ker(M − 1) ∩ Z6 . The map x 7→ M x + u/d2 has actual order d2 : its dth
power is translation by u/d, of exact order d. For each prime p | d, the generator of its order-p
subgroup is translation by u/p, which has no fixed point. Every nontrivial stabilizer contains a
prime-order subgroup, so the whole cyclic action is free. If M = 1, translation by a primitive
half-vector is a free lift of order two. The invariant integral kernel is primitive, so such a primitive
vector is obtained by Smith reduction.
    Finite order is also effectively bounded at this linear stage. Its minimal polynomial is a
product of distinct cyclotomic polynomials, and eigenvalue one uses at least one of the six
dimensions. Every other cyclotomic factor therefore has degree at most five and their total degree
is at most five. For a cyclotomic index d, each prime divisor p has p − 1 ≤ 5, and its prime-power
factors satisfy pa−1 (p − 1) ≤ 5. Enumerating these factors and the possible degree sums gives
exactly
                                      d ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12}.                        (F.CN1)
Here d is the order of the matrix, the least common multiple of its cyclotomic indices. Multiplicities
of a factor can only increase the dimension and introduce no new orders. Each listed order occurs
with a fixed vector after adding trivial summands. Thus taking the powers in (F.CN1), checking
the fixed kernel, the product relation, and the cusp Smith factors gives an exact admissibility
test. The unbounded actual affine multiplicities are not bounded by (F.CN1).
    For an admissible full tuple T = (M1 , . . . , Mk , M0 ) let H(T ) be its maximum absolute entry.
If a three-point linear tuple has an identity at a finite position, temporarily delete that identity,
classify the remaining two-point tuple, and reinsert the identity at the same marked position.
There can be only one such identity, since otherwise a finite matrix would equal the inverse of the
nontrivial unipotent cusp. Deleting a fixed identity changes neither height nor the lexicographic
comparison of tuples in that conjugacy-invariant sector. This is only a linear normalization:
a nontrivial affine order at the identity-linear site is retained in the gluing datum. In the
two-involution sector use the canonical representative defined in 6.43. This sector is invariant
under simultaneous conjugacy. In every other sector, order full integer tuples first by H, then
lexicographically by their row-major entries in the displayed marked order. Define the canonical
representative to be the first admissible tuple in the simultaneous conjugacy class.

    Every simultaneous orbit has a least element in this order. Its height is at most the height of

Theorem 6.47 (compact holomorphic filling). The smooth eight-manifold of Theorem 6.10
carries an integrable complex structure. There is a proper holomorphic map to P1 whose regular
fibres are complex three-tori, whose two finite reduced fibres are the free affine quotients of
orders five and four specified in Theorem 6.8, and whose remaining fibre is the index-one Kuhn
degeneration.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 6.10; theorem 6.8;
equation (F.24); equation (F.13); equation (E.4); equation (E.5); theorem 5.2; theorem 5.3.

Proof. We first fix the dual convention. The preceding construction has cohomology monodromies
A, B; Theorem 6.8 uses homology monodromies At , B t . All three special values are real. Choose
a positive real basepoint and paths along the positive real circle to infinity and to zero. Complex
conjugation fixes these paths and reverses the respective peripheral meridians. Pull back the
preceding period family by conjugation of the base and conjugate its complex fibres. Its Hodge
subbundle is holomorphic, with local expression F(λ̄), and its cohomology monodromies are
A−1 , B −1 . Its homology monodromies are therefore exactly At , B t . The third monodromy is fixed
by the product relation, so this also fixes its cusp marking. The primitive index-one condition
and the bounded holomorphic cusp correction are preserved, after replacing the real angular
basis by its negative if necessary.
    For a holomorphic Hodge subbundle F with F ∩ F̄ = 0, restriction of integral homology
functionals embeds the homology lattice discretely in F ∗ . Real transversality makes its real
span the whole real vector space. The quotient F ∗ /VZ∗ is consequently a holomorphic family of
compact complex three-tori over U , with its zero section. This also proves local properness, by a
smoothly varying fundamental parallelepiped.
    On the root disc at the finite point of order mi , the family extends smoothly and its deck
map has linear part Mi . The invariant vector vi of Theorem 6.8 gives a holomorphic torsion
section vi /mi . Use the diagonal affine deck action

                                  (z, s) 7−→ (Mi z + vi /mi , ζmi s).                          (F.24)

not multiplication of a complex three-vector by a six-by-six matrix. Likewise vi /mi means its

Every nonidentity power is fixed-point-free on the central torus: the invariant integral covector `
takes vi to 1 or −1, so a fixed point would require the noninteger ±j/mi to vanish in R/Z. Away

Theorem 6.49 (holomorphic periods on every open base). Let B be an open connected Riemann
surface and ρ : π1 (B) → GL+ (6, R) any representation. Its associated flat D3 -bundle admits
a holomorphic section. More generally, every continuous section which is holomorphic near a
compact Runge set can be deformed through sections to a holomorphic section, with arbitrary
uniform approximation there and any prescribed finite-order interpolation at finitely many points
of that set. For an integral representation, this gives a holomorphic family of complex three-tori
with the prescribed lattice local system and a zero section over B.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 6.48; (Alarcón and
Forstnerič, 2025, Proposition 7.13(d)).

Proof. The flat bundle D = B    e ×ρ D3 → B is a holomorphic fibre bundle: its transition maps are
constant real linear transformations, acting holomorphically on the Grassmannian. Its fibre has
LSAP by Theorem 6.48, so the bundle map is an Oka–1 map by (Alarcón and Forstnerič, 2025,
Proposition 7.13(d)). The lifting property in Definition 7.7 of that paper, applied to the identity
map of B, gives precisely the stated section deformation and approximation, including the finite
jets. This uses the section theorem, rather than an inference from the Oka–1 property for maps
to the fibre alone.
    There is a continuous section to start with. An open Riemann surface has the homotopy type
of a one-dimensional CW complex; a bundle with connected fibre admits a section over its vertices
and edges, and the homotopy lifting property transports this section to B. Connectedness holds
for the chosen component D3 . Taking the Runge set empty therefore proves existence.
    For an integral representation let VZ be its lattice local system and let F ⊂ VZ ⊗ OB be the
resulting holomorphic rank-three subbundle. Real transversality says that projection identifies
the real vector bundle with the underlying real bundle of Q = (VZ ⊗ OB )/F. Hence the image of
VZ is a full lattice in every fibre of Q. Locally it is uniformly discrete and acts by holomorphic
translations. The quotient Q/VZ → B is consequently a smooth proper holomorphic family of
compact complex three-tori, with its evident zero section and the required marking.

Scope of 6.48–6.49. Taking B = P1 \ {singular values} settles existence of nondegenerate
holomorphic periods on the smooth locus for every oriented rank-six datum. It does not impose
good reduction after the finite root changes or the bounded correction to the logarithmic cusp
period. Those are conditions at points missing from B, whereas the interpolation theorem
controls only finite jets at points lying in B. Exact agreement with a prescribed germ on an
annulus cannot be requested either: the identity theorem would then determine its analytic
continuation. Thus this theorem advances the unrestricted F.3 problem but does not decide all
its compactification conditions.

Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                     Paper III


Lemma 6.50 (retaining isolated extension points). Let R be an open Riemann surface, V → R a
holomorphic vector bundle, and U ⊂ Grr (V ) an open subset whose projection onto R is surjective.
Let S ⊂ R be finite. Suppose that over R \ S this projection is a holomorphic fibre bundle with an
LSAP fibre. Let K ⊂ R be a compact Runge set containing S in its interior. Every continuous
section of U which is holomorphic near K can be deformed through sections to a holomorphic
section, with arbitrary uniform approximation on K and interpolation of any given finite jets at
finitely many points of its interior. No fibre-bundle or Serre-fibration assertion is required at the
points of S.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (F.O5); (Forstnerič and
Prezelj, 2002, Theorem 1.2); (Alarcón and Forstnerič, 2025, Theorem 2.13).

Proof. Here are the details of the relative version of the LSAP argument in (Alarcón and
Forstnerič, 2025, Lemma 5.1, Theorem 6.1 and Proposition 7.13(d)). They also specify why
isolated extension points cause no new analytic step. Enlarge K slightly inside the domain of
holomorphicity, retaining the Runge property. Choose a strongly subharmonic Morse exhaustion
of R starting with this compact set. All subsequent boundary arcs, attached discs and critical
one-handles can and will be chosen disjoint from S. On them U is an ordinary holomorphic
bundle with LSAP fibre.
    The global spray on the old compact set can be taken to be vertical even though the fibres at
S differ. Indeed, let f be the current holomorphic section on a Stein neighborhood W of that set.
Put A equal to the finite interpolation set, including S, and choose an ideal sheaf I vanishing
to one more than the prescribed jet orders at its points. Cartan’s theorem A supplies finitely
many holomorphic sections T1 , . . . , TN of End(V )|W ⊗ I which generate End(V ) on the compact
attaching arcs, after shrinking W if needed. The formula
                                                              
                                                  N
                                 F (z, a) = exp                                           (F.O5)
                                                  X
                                                      aj Tj (z) f (z)
                                                 j=1

defines a holomorphic spray of sections of the Grassmannian bundle. Its differential in a surjects
onto the vertical tangent space at every attaching point, since End(Vz ) → Hom(f (z), Vz /f (z)) is
onto. For a sufficiently small it has range in U on a neighborhood of the old compact set, by
openness and compactness. Every parameter value preserves all the chosen jets. Domination at
A is neither asserted nor used.
    For a noncritical extension, subdivide the new annular regions into small discs lying in bundle
trivializations over R \ S. Restrict (F.O5) to a thin attaching disc. LSAP of the fibre extends
this spray across the attached disc, approximating the old spray as closely as desired on the
intersection. The spray gluing used in the proof of (Alarcón and Forstnerič, 2025, Lemma 5.1,
equations (5.6)–(5.8)) now applies verbatim to vertical sprays: the inverse-function step is needed
only on the attaching intersection, where (F.O5) is dominating. It produces reparametrizations
of the two sprays and a glued section. The old part remains in U because it is evaluated in
(F.O5); the new part remains in U because the LSAP spray takes values in the bundle fibre.
The fixed jets survive the reparametrizations, being independent of the spray parameters on the
old side.
    For a critical extension, first extend over the attached real arc using the given continuous
section and the homotopy already constructed on the old compact set. Apply Mergelyan
approximation with the same finite jets to a neighborhood of the union of the old set and this
arc, and then apply the noncritical step. To see explicitly that this approximation is by sections,
trivialize V holomorphically on the open Riemann surface: its underlying complex bundle is
trivial over a graph spine, and the frame bundle therefore has a continuous section. Its fibre
GL(rank V, C) has the dominating spray (g, A) 7→ g exp A, so (Forstnerič and Prezelj, 2002,

                                                344
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                     Paper III


Theorem 1.2) gives a holomorphic frame. The section is then a map to the fixed Grassmannian,
to which (Alarcón and Forstnerič, 2025, Theorem 2.13) applies. The base coordinate is kept
unchanged. Close approximation on the compact arc and old set, followed by shrinking its
neighborhood, preserves membership in the open subset U . This is the critical case of Theorem
6.1 of that paper, with no approximation performed at a singular point of the projection: here
the projection is a submersion everywhere, as U is open in a Grassmannian bundle.
    Choose successive errors summably small on the preceding compact sets and smaller than
their distances to the complement of U . The sections converge uniformly on every compact
set to a holomorphic section with range in U . The finite jets persist. The close homotopies on
successive stages concatenate in the usual exhaustion construction. All new attachment regions
lie outside S; the old section remains holomorphic on a full neighborhood of each point of S at
every stage. This proves the lemma.

neighborhood of (0, C0 ) lies in the adjoined set, proving openness. The projection is consequently

    Start with a polynomial C0 (t) realizing the desired finite jet. Formula (F.O7) makes it a

continuously over B. To justify the relative extension, D3 is connected and simply connected: it

complex coordinate is a generator of the real two-plane rotation loop. A cellular decomposition of
the surface outside the cusp disc now extends its boundary section over edges by connectedness
and over two-cells by simple connectivity. The flat bundle is trivial over each cell. This argument
uses no fibration property at p0 .
    Over B \ {p0 } the fibre is the LSAP manifold D3 from Theorem 6.48. Lemma 6.50, with
S = {p0 }, produces a holomorphic section of U over all of B, with the chosen jet at p0 . Since
its value at p0 lies in the affine chart just adjoined, it has a holomorphic matrix C(t) there.
Undoing the canonical frame gives exactly (F.O6), with a bounded holomorphic correction.
Everywhere else membership in U is precisely nondegeneracy of the complex-torus periods. More
explicitly, choose three members of a real lattice basis whose projected periods are complex-
linearly independent, and normalize them to I3 . The remaining three periods form a matrix
Z, and real transversality is exactly det Im Z 6= 0. This normalization persists locally. A single
Schubert chart is not imposed globally, and none is needed to define a marked torus period
family.
    For F.2 survivors, Theorem 6.12 excludes k = 3 and Proposition 6.13 proves orientation
preservation of the finite matrices for k = 2. The cusp determinant is also one. Thus all survivors
satisfy the hypotheses. This is a universal existence decision and does not require completion of
their simultaneous integral classification.

Finite good reduction remains a distinct requirement. Theorem 6.51 resolves the period-
existence clause of F.3 as written: its base is the punctured sphere, and its specified end condition
is the bounded cusp correction. It does not claim that every such family extends at the other
punctures after the finite root changes. Requiring that stronger simultaneous extension would
retain every puncture and leave a compact base, to which the Runge exhaustion used above does
not apply. The specific compact fourfold in F.4 already has all its finite extensions by Theorems
6.45–6.47; its existence does not depend on this stronger unresolved general compactification
question.

Proposition 7.3 (a global scalar gauge would be trivial). Let a smooth circle act on a simply
connected smooth manifold Z. If g : Z → S 1 is smooth and invariant under the circle, then
z 7→ g(z) · z is smoothly isotopic to the identity. The primitive coordinate θ detecting γ on a
regular fibre of Xc has no continuous extension to Xc .

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. Since Z is simply connected, g lifts to a smooth real function a with g = e2πia . Invariance
implies a(λz) − a(z) ∈ Z. This difference is continuous in the connected circle and is zero
at its identity, so it is zero everywhere. The maps z 7→ e2πita(z) · z are diffeomorphisms with
inverses obtained by replacing t by −t. They give the isotopy. In the present application a
loop representing γb in a regular torus fibre has degree one under θ. If θ extended to the simply
connected S 6 , that degree would be zero. The contradiction shows why the proposed local scalar
twist is not a global scalar-gauge calculation.

      The credited statement and complete re-derivation are in proposition A.15.

Proposition 7.5 (independence of the equivariant lift). Let X = Xc carry the effective semifree
circle action of A.14, with fixed surface F ∼
                                            = S 2 . If two smooth equivariant diffeomorphisms of X
induce the same map of its orbit space, they are smoothly isotopic. More generally, a smooth

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition A.14.
