C    Thom, Euler and orientation comparisons
The following complete arguments are retained as re-derivations of their classical prerequisites.
Source-specific calculations and their hypotheses are stated explicitly.

Lemma C.1. Every subgroup of a free abelian group is free.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. Well-order a basis of F . Let Fα be generated by the basis elements preceding α, and put
Jα = J ∩ Fα for the subgroup J. At a successor stage, Jα+1 /Jα embeds in Fα+1 /Fα = Z. It is
either zero or generated by a least positive integer; in the latter case choose a lift in Jα+1 . At a
limit stage take the union. These chosen lifts form a basis: subtracting a multiple of the lift at
the last nonzero coordinate reduces that last coordinate, and induction in the well-order gives
spanning; the last nonzero coordinate also proves independence. All elements have finite support,
and no infinite strictly decreasing sequence of ordinals occurs.

    For an abelian group M , choose a free presentation 0 → J → F → M → 0 and define
Ext(M, G) = coker(Hom(F, G) → Hom(J, G)). This group does not depend on the presentation.
Indeed a map between the quotient groups lifts to a map of the free groups by choosing preimages
of their basis elements, and carries kernels to kernels. Two lifts differ by a map into the target
kernel; precomposition by that difference becomes a restriction from the target free group and
hence vanishes in the cokernel. Lifts of identity maps between two presentations therefore induce
inverse cokernel maps. This also proves functoriality.

Theorem C.2 (universal coefficient exact sequence). For a free abelian chain complex K there
is a natural exact sequence

             0 → Ext(Hm−1 (K), G) → H m (Hom(K, G)) → Hom(Hm (K), G) → 0.

    The last map evaluates a cocycle on cycles. In particular it is an isomorphism if Hm−1 (K) = 0.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; lemma C.1.

Proof. Put Zm = ker ∂ and Bm = im ∂. These groups are free by lemma C.1. The surjection
Km → Bm−1 splits because Bm−1 is free, so Km = Zm ⊕Lm . A homomorphism Hm = Zm /Bm →
G extends to Km by zero on Lm and is a cocycle. This proves surjectivity of the evaluation map.
    A cocycle in its kernel vanishes on Zm , so it factors through Km /Zm = Bm−1 . Two such
cochains differ by a coboundary exactly when their maps on Bm−1 differ by the restriction of a
map on Km−1 , equivalently of a map on Zm−1 , since that summand splits too. Their quotient
is the cokernel for the free presentation 0 → Bm−1 → Zm−1 → Hm−1 → 0. This identifies the
kernel with the stated Ext group. Evaluation, factorization and the presentation comparison
above commute with chain maps, so the sequence is natural; the chosen splittings are used only
to prove surjectivity.



                                                477
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                    Paper III


   Over a field k, the corresponding statement reduces to H m (Homk (K, k)) = Homk (Hm (K), k).
The same splitting proof applies to vector spaces, and every linear map from a subspace extends
by choosing a basis, so there is no Ext term. These statements apply to the singular relative
complexes defined in Paper I, Subsection F.1.

C.1    The relative generator in a vector space
The pair (R, R \ 0) has homology Z in degree one and zero elsewhere. Indeed the two components
of the punctured line and the contractibility of the line, together with the pair sequence, identify
H1 with the kernel of Z ⊕ Z → Z, (a, b) 7→ a + b. The positively directed interval from −1 to 1
represents the generator whose boundary is the positive point minus the negative point.
    A free chain complex with this homology is chain homotopy equivalent to Z concentrated
in degree one. Here is the required algebra. Split Km → Bm−1 by freeness, as in theorem C.2,
and split Zm → Hm , since these homology groups are free. Then Km = Bm ⊕ Hm ⊕ Lm , with
∂ : Lm → Bm−1 an isomorphism. Projection to H∗ and its inclusion are inverse up to the
homotopy sending Bm to its inverse image in Lm+1 and vanishing on the other summands. This
proves the assertion, including a cocycle u1 evaluating to one on the chosen interval.
    Apply Paper I, Lemma F.4 repeatedly to the product of r punctured-line pairs. Their
exceptional union is exactly Rr \ 0; all of its factor subspaces are open. The relative complex is
therefore chain homotopy equivalent to Z concentrated in degree r. Its positive generator is the
product of the r positive intervals, with coordinate axes in their listed order. Write ur for its
dual integral class. In particular the relative cohomology is G in degree r and zero otherwise for
every abelian group G.
    An invertible real linear map acts on this generator by the sign of its determinant. To verify
the sign, Gram–Schmidt writes a positive-determinant matrix as QR, with Q ∈ SO(r) and R
triangular with positive diagonal. Interpolating R to the identity stays invertible. A rotation
in the plane spanned by a unit vector and the first coordinate vector takes that vector to the
coordinate vector; for its antipode use a half-turn in a coordinate plane. This reduces an element
of SO(r) to an element of SO(r − 1), and induction gives a path to the identity. The cases
r = 1 and SO(1) = {1} start the argument. A reflection in one coordinate exchanges the two
components in the punctured-line calculation and acts by −1. Every negative-determinant matrix
is the product of a positive-determinant one and this reflection. Homotopy invariance proves the
claim.
    Thus an orientation determines an integral generator uV for each fibre vector space V . Modulo
two the determinant sign disappears, giving a canonical generator without an orientation.
Proposition C.3 (trivial Thom isomorphism). For every space B, the class pulled back from ur
gives isomorphisms

              H j (B; G) −→ H j+r (B × Rr , B × (Rr \ 0); G),      a 7−→ π ∗ a ^ ur .
    The corresponding homology map π∗ Rur is an isomorphism too. The same assertions hold
with the mod-two fibre class and F2 coefficients.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. The relative product chain equivalence identifies the source relative complex with C∗ (B) ⊗
C∗ (Rr , Rr \ 0). Replace the second factor by its chain homotopy equivalent Z[r]. Tensoring the
equivalence and its homotopy is legitimate for these free complexes; the graded tensor differential
verifies the homotopy formula. On the original relative complex the projection to this shifted
base complex is (1 ⊗ ur )A. In degree j + r it evaluates ur on the last r vertices and retains the

                                                478
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                      Paper III


first j + 1 vertices projected to B. It is exactly π∗ Rur . Dualizing with values in G gives the
displayed cup-product formula. This proves both isomorphisms and also proves that the fibre
value one characterizes the trivial-bundle Thom class uniquely.

C.2    A global Thom class, including integral coefficients
Let π : E → B be a real rank-r bundle, r > 0, over a Hausdorff base. Write E0 = E \ zero section,
an open subset. We use either integral coefficients with a chosen orientation, or F2 without one.
These alternatives will be called the chosen coefficients. In the integral case an orientation means
continuous choices of oriented local frames; the preceding section explains the corresponding
fibre generators.

Theorem C.4 (Thom isomorphism). There is a unique class uE ∈ H r (E, E0 ) whose restriction
to every fibre pair is its chosen generator. The groups H i (E, E0 ) vanish for i < r. Multiplication
gives an isomorphism
                                     ∼
                                     =
                       ΦE : H j (B) −
                                    → H j+r (E, E0 ),      a 7−→ π ∗ a ^ uE .

    The homology map π∗ RuE : Hj+r (E, E0 ) → Hj (B) is also an isomorphism. In the oriented
integral case the cohomology isomorphism holds with any abelian coefficient group G, multiplying
by the integral class uE .

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition C.3; theorem C.2.

Proof, finite covers and passage to arbitrary bases. Finite covers. A bundle trivial on one open
set satisfies all assertions by proposition C.3. Suppose they hold over U, V, U ∩ V . The two
degree-r Thom classes agree on the intersection, because they have the same fibre values. Relative
Mayer–Vietoris gives a common class on U ∪ V , uniquely since H r−1 (EU ∩V , (EU ∩V )0 ) = 0. It
still has the required fibre values.
     Right multiplication by this class maps the base cohomological Mayer–Vietoris sequence to
the relative total-space sequence. It commutes with coboundaries and restrictions by the cup
differential formula, hence with the connecting maps from Paper I, Subsection F.3. The five
lemma proves the cohomological isomorphism in every degree, including vanishing below r. For
integral orientation, the same diagram works with every group G, multiplying on the right by
the integral class.
     On homology use small chains for the two inverse-image open sets. The operator π∗ Ru takes
a simplex supported above U to a simplex in U , and likewise for V and their intersection. It
commutes with boundaries, so it defines a map of their split exact chain sequences and their
connecting maps. The homological five lemma gives the asserted isomorphism. Its induced map
is independent of the cocycle representing u, by the cap homotopy of Paper I, Subsection F.4.
     Induction proves these statements for any finite trivializing cover. At the inductive step, the
intersection of the last chart with the union of the earlier charts has a cover by fewer trivializing
sets, so its assertion is already available. No infinite-cover induction has been assumed.
     Passage to arbitrary bases. For each compact subset C ⊂ B, the restricted bundle has
a finite trivializing cover. Denote its Thom class by uC . If C ⊂ D, uniqueness shows that uD
restricts to uC .
     Every singular chain in E projects to a compact subset of B. The same holds for a finite
collection of chains, including chains that witness a boundary. Consequently

               Hm (E, E0 ) = colim Hm (EC , (EC )0 ),         Hj (B) = colim Hj (C).
                                C⊂B                                       C
                              C compact



                                                479
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                    Paper III


    For surjectivity a representing cycle has compact projected support; for injectivity a bounding
chain has compact projected support too. Finite unions of compact subsets are compact, so these
are filtered limits. This argument is valid for integral homology and for field homology.
    The compatible maps π∗ RuC therefore give isomorphisms Tj : Hj+r (E, E0 ) → Hj (B). In
particular Hr−1 (E, E0 ) = 0, and T0 identifies Hr (E, E0 ) with H0 (B). Positive fibre generators
map to their component generators under T0 . In the integral case compose T0 with the
homomorphism H0 (B) → Z sending every component generator to one. theorem C.2 identifies
this functional with a unique class uE ∈ H r (E, E0 ; Z). In the mod-two case use the field version
of that theorem and the analogous functional with values in F2 .
    On every compact C, this class restricts to uC : their evaluation functionals agree, and the
degree-r evaluation maps there are isomorphisms. Thus uE has exactly the desired fibre values.
Those values also characterize its evaluation functional, since the fibre generators generate
Hr (E, E0 ) by its identification with H0 (B). This proves global uniqueness.
    The global cap map is now Tj , because its restriction to each compact projected support is
the already constructed cap map. It is therefore an isomorphism. Apply the natural universal
coefficient exact sequences to this map of free complexes, reindexed by r. It gives isomorphisms
on the Hom and Ext terms because it is an isomorphism on homology. Exactness, or the five
lemma with zero end terms, then gives an isomorphism on cohomology with every group G in
the oriented case. By the cap evaluation identity this dual map is precisely a 7→ π ∗ a ^ uE . In
the mod-two case field duality gives the same conclusion with F2 . This also proves the stated
low-degree vanishing.

    For rank zero, E = B, E0 = ∅, and uE = 1; the theorem is the identity map. No
paracompactness or CW assumption was needed in theorem C.4. Those hypotheses will be useful
for metrics and obstruction theory, but the compact-support chain argument already proves this
theorem on every Hausdorff base.
    The zero section z : B → E and π are homotopy inverses: (b, v, t) 7→ (b, tv) contracts each
fibre. Thus the theorem can equivalently be stated as the isomorphism H j (E) → H j+r (E, E0 ),
given by multiplication by uE .

C.3    Euler classes and their product rule
Let j : H r (E, E0 ) → H r (E) forget the relative condition. Define

                                         e(E) = z ∗ j(uE ).

     With integral coefficients this is the Euler class of an oriented bundle. With F2 coefficients
it is defined for every real bundle. Naturality of the Thom class is immediate from its uniqueness,
with the following precise assumptions: a fibrewise linear isomorphism over a base map pulls the
Thom class back to the Thom class, preserving the chosen orientation in the integral case. It
induces a map of the nonzero-vector pairs. Consequently Euler classes are natural for pullbacks
and oriented bundle isomorphisms.
     The homotopy inverses above imply j(uE ) = π ∗ e(E). Therefore

                     uE ^ uE = π ∗ e(E) ^ uE ,        Φ−1
                                                       E (uE ^ uE ) = e(E).

   In this formula the first relative factor can be forgotten before multiplying: both versions use
the same cocycle on the same front face, so they agree.
   Reversing the orientation replaces every fibre generator by its negative, hence replaces both the
Thom class and the Euler class by their negatives. The automorphism v 7→ −v has determinant
(−1)r and fixes the zero section. For odd r, pulling back by it yields e(E) = −e(E), so 2e(E) = 0.


                                                480
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                        Paper III


This proves only the two-torsion assertion; it does not allow dropping torsion in an arbitrary
base cohomology group.

Proposition C.5. If a positive-rank oriented bundle has a nowhere-zero section, its Euler class
is zero. The same conclusion holds for the mod-two Euler class without orientation.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. A section s : B → E0 has zero pullback of j(uE ), because that class restricts to zero on
E0 . The sections s and z are homotopic as maps into E by scalar multiplication along each fibre.
Paper I, Lemma F.1 gives e(E) = z ∗ j(uE ) = s∗ j(uE ) = 0.

Proposition C.6 (Whitney product). If E, F are oriented bundles on one base, orient E ⊕ F
by an oriented basis of E followed by one of F . Then

                                   e(E ⊕ F ) = e(E) ^ e(F ).

    The same formula holds modulo two without orientations.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; section C.1.

Proof. First use the external product bundle over B × C. Its nonzero set is E0 × F ∪ E × F0 , a
union of open subspaces. The external product uE × uF is defined by Paper I, Subsection F.4
and restricts to the positive generator on each ordered product fibre, by the product calculation
of section C.1. Uniqueness identifies it with uE×F . Pull back to the product zero section to
obtain e(E × F ) = e(E) × e(F ). For a common base, pull back along its diagonal. The pullback
bundle is E ⊕ F , and diagonal pullback of the external product is the cup product by the defining
Alexander–Whitney formula.

D.2    Finite projective spaces and their full integral groups
Define CPn as the set of complex lines in Cn+1 , with its topology of rank-one orthogonal
projections. It is a closed bounded set of matrices satisfying P ∗ = P , P 2 = P , tr P = 1, hence
compact Hausdorff. Near a fixed line, projection to that line is invertible on any sufficiently
close line; its graph is a continuous complex coordinate. These graph charts also trivialize the
tautological line Q.
    There is one cell in each real dimension 0, 2, . . . , 2n. More explicitly the attaching map of the
closed unit ball in Cq is

                                                                                                 (230)
                                                    p
                                       z 7−→ [z :    1 − kzk2 ].
    Its boundary maps p to CP . The interior maps bijectively to its complementary affineq chart
                               q−1

with coordinate z/ 1 − kzk2 . Thus the attachment quotient is homeomorphic to CP : the
resulting continuous bijection is from a compact space to a Hausdorff space, and images of closed
sets are compact and closed.
    Here is the singular-group calculation behind this cell argument. In a finite disk attachment,
the preceding skeleton together with the outer collars kzk > 1/2 is an open neighbourhood that
retracts to that skeleton by radial motion in each collar. The homotopy is continuous on the
attachment quotient because its quotient map is a closed surjection of compact Hausdorff spaces,
and its product with the interval is still closed and quotient. The triple exact sequence permits
replacing the skeleton by this neighbourhood in relative homology. Excision then removes the
skeleton and leaves the disjoint disk-interior/collar pairs. Each pair has the groups of (Dd , S d−1 ):
the sphere and pair calculation in the Thom/Euler provider gives one copy of Z in degree d,
and zero otherwise. The same argument gives the relative cohomology with any coefficients.
Induction over the finite attachments proves vanishing above the dimension. Because all cells here
are even-dimensional, the intervening odd homology groups vanish. At each even attachment,
the exact sequence therefore adds a free copy of Z in precisely that degree and preserves lower
groups. Hence H2i (CPn ; Z) = Z for 0 ≤ i ≤ n, and all other homology groups vanish.
    The unit sphere of Q is S 2n+1 , via v 7→ ([v], v), with inverse forgetting the line. A complex
line has its real orientation (v, iv); multiplication by a nonzero complex scalar has positive real
determinant. Put x = −e(QR ). For 1 ≤ j ≤ 2n, the positive sphere groups appearing beside the
multiplication maps in (228) vanish. In degree one its degree-zero connecting map lands in a
negative-degree group and is zero. It follows successively that the odd base cohomology groups
vanish and multiplication by e(QR ) is an isomorphism between successive even groups through
degree 2n. Starting at H 0 = Z, and using the dimension bound above, this proves

                                    H ∗ (CPn ; Z) = Z[x]/(xn+1 ).                                (231)
    The sign is fixed as follows. A Hermitian metric, linear in the first variable, gives the
anti-complex-linear map w 7→ h−, wi from a line to its dual. Its real determinant is negative,
so e(Q∗R ) = −e(QR ) = x. On CP1 , the functional (z0 , z1 ) 7→ z1 is a section of Q∗ with one
zero at [1 : 0]. In the frame (1, ζ) its value is ζ, with positive local index. The sphere zero
formula gives hx, [CP1 ]i = 1, in the complex orientation. The stereographic map [1 : ζ] 7→
(2<ζ, 2=ζ, 1 − |ζ|2 )/(1 + |ζ|2 ) preserves that orientation: at ζ = 0, its two coordinate derivatives
followed by the outward normal have positive determinant. This is the sign used in lesson 11.

D.3    The integral projective-bundle map
For a complex rank-n bundle V over a Hausdorff base, let p : P (V ) → B be its bundle of
lines. The chart construction gives a locally trivial Hausdorff bundle with fibre CPn−1 and a
tautological line S ⊂ p∗ V . Set z = −e(SR ). For every abelian group G, the map

                 n−1                                                         n−1
                                                                                                    (232)
                 M                                                           X
                       H m−2i (B; G) −→ H m (P (V ); G),         (bi ) 7−→         p∗ bi ^ z i
                 i=0                                                         i=0

   is an isomorphism. In particular p∗ is injective, including on integral torsion.
   To prove this without a cohomological limit assumption, choose integral cocycles ci for z i ,
with c0 = 1. The unshifted right cap operation of the Thom/Euler provider gives the chain map

                                               n−1
                                                                                                    (233)
                                               M
                       T : Cm (P (V ); Z) −→         Cm−2i (B; Z),      Ti = p∗ Rci .
                                               i=0

    Its cap identity proves commutation with the differentials; replacing a cocycle by a coboundary
changes this map by the cap homotopy proved there. On a trivializing open set, z i is the L pullback
of the fibre class in (231). The fibre singular complex is chain homotopy equivalent to n−1 i=0 Z[2i]:
split its free boundary groups off the chain groups, split the free homology off its cycles, and
contract each remaining boundary/preimage pair. Its projection to Z[2i] can be chosen to be the
cocycle dual to xi . The Alexander–Whitney and shuffle equivalence supplied in the Thom/Euler
provider then identifies the product complex with the right side of (233). The projection is
precisely p∗ Rci , since it evaluates on the last 2i-face and retains the first face projected to the
base. Thus (233) is a homology isomorphism on each such open set.
    The maps preserve projected support. Apply them to the small-chain Mayer–Vietoris
sequences for two base open sets and their inverse images. Their connecting maps commute
because these are maps of exact chain sequences. The five lemma makes T an isomorphism
over a union whenever it is one on the two sets and their intersection. Induction over a finite
trivializing cover works: the intersection with the last chart has a cover by fewer trivializing
sets. In particular this proves the assertion on every compact restricted base. Every cycle
upstairs, downstairs, or witnessing a boundary has compact projected support; finite unions of
such compact sets are compact. Therefore the global homology map is an isomorphism as well.
This is a direct argument about finite chains, with no inverse limit of cohomology groups.
    Apply the natural universal coefficient exact sequences, proved in the Thom/Euler provider, to
the map of free complexes (233). Its Hom and Ext maps are isomorphisms because its homology
maps are. Exactness therefore makes the dual cohomology map an isomorphism for every G.
Evaluation of a cochain on p∗ Rci is exactly p∗ bi ^ ci ; there are finitely many summands, so
dualization retains their direct sum. This proves exactly (232). Associativity of cup product
proves its compatibility with the base module structure.

D.4    Actual flag bundles over compact bases
Now let B be compact Hausdorff. The finite embedding and orthogonal-projection construction
in section AI.10.1, supplies a Hermitian metric on every bundle in use. Over P (V ), take the
orthogonal complement Q1 of its tautological line, so p∗1 V = S1 ⊕ Q1 . Projectivize Q1 , take the
next tautological line and its complement, and repeat until rank one. Orthogonal projection
matrices depend continuously on the base and have constant rank; a fixed maximal independent
set of columns remains independent nearby, so these images and kernels are actual local bundles.
This constructs

                            f : Flag(V ) −→ B,         f ∗ V = L1 ⊕ · · · ⊕ Ln .                    (234)

                                                     483
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                      Paper III


    Each projection in the tower has injective cohomology pullback by (232), so the composite
does too, with integral or any other constant coefficients. Its total spaces are compact Hausdorff.
For compactness, given an open cover upstairs, trivialize near a base point and cover its compact
projective fibre by finitely many product neighbourhoods in that cover. Intersect their base
neighbourhoods. These products cover all the fibres over this smaller neighbourhood. Finitely
many such base neighbourhoods cover the compact base, yielding a finite subcover upstairs. The
Hausdorff assertion follows by separating distinct base points downstairs or points over the same
base point in a chart. Thus a second bundle can be split by a second flag tower over the first;
the resulting common pullback is still injective and the space is still compact. Ranks zero and
one require no tower.

D.5    Line tensor products, with a finite classifying map
Define c1 (L) = e(LR ) for a complex line. Conjugation reverses its real orientation, so c1 (L̄) =
−c1 (L); the metric dual map above gives c1 (L∗ ) = −c1 (L).
    For lines L, M on a compact Hausdorff base, choose finite embeddings L ,→ B × CN ,
M ,→ B × CK . Their image projections give continuous maps g : B → CPN −1 , h : B → CPK−1 .
The embedding itself identifies L with g ∗ QN and M with h∗ QK , complex linearly on every fibre.
Adding a trivial coordinate if necessary makes N, K ≥ 2.
    The product chain equivalence in Paper I, Lemma F.4 and the free even homology in
section D.2 give H1 (CPN −1 × CPK−1 ; Z) = 0 and H2 = Z ⊕ Z, with generators the projective
lines in the two axes. The universal coefficient sequence therefore shows that a degree-two
integral class is determined by restriction to these two axes. Let Q1 , Q2 be the two pulled-back
tautological lines. On the first axis Q2 is a fixed one-dimensional vector space, so Q1 ⊗ Q2 is
isomorphic to Q1 ; on the second it is isomorphic to Q2 . These isomorphisms preserve complex
orientations. Euler naturality and this degree-two detection prove

F     Singular duality, the diagonal and the Euler class
The following complete arguments are retained as re-derivations of their classical prerequisites.
Source-specific calculations and their hypotheses are stated explicitly.
   A manifold’s tangent characteristic classes can be recovered from its cohomology and its
cohomology operations. The bridge is the diagonal: its normal bundle is the tangent bundle,


                                                     486
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                              Paper III


while its cohomology class is determined by the cup-product pairing. We prove the bridge,
including the compact-support duality and tubular-neighbourhood foundations, and then derive
the Euler characteristic and Wu formula.
    Manifolds here are smooth, Hausdorff and second countable, without boundary unless stated.
Dimension-zero orientation statements use the canonical point orientation and the established
rank-zero Thom convention. The section C proves singular excision, Mayer–Vietoris, products,
coefficient theorems and the Thom isomorphism. The section D and section E prove the mod-two
and signed compact-set fundamental classes. These are the precise prerequisites used below.

F.1   Compact supports and the duality map
Fix a commutative coefficient ring R. Use an orientation of M d when R 6= F2 ; for R = F2 no
orientation is required. The fundamental-class results just cited give a compatible class

                                          µK ∈ Hd (M, M \ K; R)

   for every compact K ⊂ M : it has the prescribed local orientation at every point of K, and is
uniquely determined by these local restrictions. With an orientation, this class is the coefficient
image of the integer class. With mod-two coefficients it is the corresponding unsigned class. The
compact-set construction works over R by the same proof: coordinate relative homology is R in
top degree and zero above it; its Mayer–Vietoris gluing and local detection use only addition and
subtraction. Thus uniqueness is being proved over the chosen ring, rather than inferred from an
unsupported coefficient-change injection.
   Define

F.2   The full Poincaré duality proof
Lemma F.1 (The compact-support gluing square). If M = U ∪ V is an open cover, cap maps
identify the compact-support cohomology Mayer–Vietoris sequence with the ordinary homology
Mayer–Vietoris sequence, reversing degrees. Give its middle vertical map the signs (DU , −DV ),
matching the cohomological difference map with the homological sum map. Squares for the
inclusion maps then commute; the square of connecting maps in cohomological degree r commutes
up to the sign (−1)d−r .

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (251); equation (248).

Proof. For compact K ⊂ U, L ⊂ V , put A = M \ K, B = M \ L. On singular cochains the
sequence


                                                             (a,b)7→a−b
   0 → C ∗ (M, C∗ (A) + C∗ (B)) → C ∗ (M, A) ⊕ C ∗ (M, B) −−−−−−→ C ∗ (M, A ∩ B) → 0          (251)

    is degreewise split exact. In its first term the notation means cochains vanishing on both
indicated chain groups. To split the last arrow, assign each simplex’s value to the first cochain if
that simplex is not contained in A, and otherwise to the negative second cochain; a simplex in
both A, B has value zero. Since A, B are open, small-chain excision identifies the first term’s
cohomology with that of the pair (M, A ∪ B). Thus (251) gives the sequence for supports
K ∩ L, K, L, K ∪ L. Excision places these terms respectively in U ∩ V, U, V, M .
    The connecting square requires a chain check. Represent µK∪L , after subdivision, as

                                          α=x+y+z

    with x in U \ L, y in U ∩ V , and z in V \ K; these open sets cover M . Then x + y represents
µK , since its boundary is outside K, and y represents µK∩L . Their local values are the required
ones, so uniqueness of compact-set fundamental classes proves these assertions.
    Let a cocycle φ with support K ∪ L be written φ = φA − φB by (251). Its connecting cocycle
is δφA = δφB , supported on K ∩ L in the small-chain model. The homological Mayer–Vietoris
boundary of Rφ α is represented by ∂Rφ x: take its U part to be Rφ x and its V part to be
Rφ (y + z). Since φB vanishes on x, this boundary equals RφA ∂x. Also RφA ∂(x + y) = 0, because
that boundary is outside K. It is therefore −RφA ∂y. By (248), modulo boundaries in U ∩ V ,

                                   RδφA y = (−1)d−r+1 RφA ∂y.




                                                488
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                       Paper III


    The two connecting routes differ by exactly (−1)d−r , as asserted. All calculations can be
made after the same sufficiently fine subdivision; the proved small-chain homotopies identify
them with the original classes.
    Pass to the filtered limit over K, L. Each compact subset of U ∩ V lies in such an intersection,
and each compact subset of M lies in such a union: use a finite subcover and compact shrinkings
inside U, V . Filtered limits preserve exactness, since an element in a kernel has its zero image at
a later stage and then lifts there by stagewise exactness. This gives the stated diagram. The
other squares follow directly from local fundamental-class compatibility.

Theorem F.2 (Poincaré duality). The map (249) is an isomorphism for every r.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (249); lemma F.1.

Proof. On Rd , closed balls are cofinal compact supports. The relative cohomology of a ball and
its exterior is R in degree d and zero otherwise, by the sphere calculation and excision. Cap
with a positively oriented d-simplex sends its degree-d evaluation cocycle to the first vertex, with
coefficient one. Thus D is an isomorphism on Rd and on any open ball or nonempty convex open
subset homeomorphic to it.
    If duality holds on U, V, U ∩ V , lemma F.1 and the five lemma prove it on their union; signs
can be inserted in the vertical maps and do not change invertibility. If U1 ⊂ U2 ⊂ · · · are open
and cover M , compact supports lie in some Ui , and every finite singular cycle or bounding chain
also lies in some Ui . Hence both sides of (249) are their filtered direct limits and duality passes
to the union.
    An open subset of Rd is a countable union of open balls with closures inside it. Every
nonempty finite intersection is homeomorphic to Rd . To verify this detail, choose a point c in
the intersection. The distance Ri (θ) from c to the i-th ball’s boundary in unit direction θ is
the positive root of kc + tθ − ci k2 = ri2 ; its explicit quadratic formula is continuous and positive.
The minimum R(θ) of these finitely many roots is likewise continuous and positive. In polar
coordinates the map c + tθ 7→ tθ/(R(θ) − t) is a homeomorphism onto Rd , with continuous
inverse and the centre mapped to zero. Induction over finite unions, followed by the preceding
limit argument, proves duality for every open subset of Rd . Finally cover M by countably
many coordinate neighbourhoods. Intersections of any already formed union with a new chart
are open subsets of that chart, so their duality is established. Finite-union induction and the
countable-union argument now prove the theorem on M . The empty space and d = 0 follow
from the same definitions: a compact subset of a discrete manifold is finite and the cap map is
the identity on its point coefficients.

Corollary F.3 (Finite generation and perfect pairings). A closed oriented manifold has finitely
generated integer homology, zero above its dimension. Over a field F , with the stated orientation
or F = F2 , the pairing

                    H r (M ; F ) × H d−r (M ; F ) → F,     (a, b) 7→ ha ^ b, [M ]i               (252)

   is perfect.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (250).

Proof. Write the ordinary fundamental class as a finite singular cycle c. For each r, every cap Ra c
lies in the finite free subgroup of chains generated by the front ((d-r))-faces of the finitely many
simplices of c. Its subgroup of cycles is finitely generated over Z: a subgroup of a finite-rank
free abelian group is free of rank at most that rank, as proved in the coefficient chapter. Duality
says these caps represent every homology class. Thus homology is a quotient of this finitely


                                                 489
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                        Paper III


generated cycle subgroup. Over a field the same argument gives finite dimension. Duality in
negative cohomological degrees gives the vanishing above d.
    Field cohomology is the linear dual of homology by the proved coefficient theorem. Apply this
and (250) to the duality isomorphism. It makes (252) nondegenerate, and finite dimension makes
the induced maps to dual spaces isomorphisms. Graded commutativity accounts for changing
the order of its two factors.

    Define χ(M ) = r (−1)r rank Hr (M ; Z) when these groups are finitely generated and vanish
                      P
in sufficiently large degrees. It equals the alternating sum of dimensions over every coefficient field.
Indeed split the finitely generated integer groups into free and finite cyclic summands. Coefficient
change gives each free generator once; a torsion summand visible in the chosen characteristic
contributes in two consecutive homological degrees through tensor and Tor, so cancels in the
alternating sum. In characteristic zero no torsion contributes. The tensor/Tor coefficient
sequence follows from the same split cycle-boundary free presentation used for the already proved
cohomology coefficient theorem: tensor its two-term free resolution. The elementary two-term
resolution of Z/q is multiplication by q, yielding the claimed two adjacent contributions. For
nonorientable closed manifolds the finite-generation premise is proved in section F.3 below.

F.3    Tubular neighbourhoods, with the analytic prerequisites
We need a tubular neighbourhood in a smooth ambient manifold A, not an unexplained appeal
to a geodesic construction. The following elementary analytic facts supply one.

Lemma F.4 (Local inverse and local flows). A smooth map between open Euclidean sets with
invertible derivative at a point has a smooth inverse on neighbourhoods of that point. A smooth
finite-dimensional vector field has a unique local flow, smooth in time and its initial point.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. For the inverse assertion translate the point to zero and let its derivative be the invertible
matrix B. On a sufficiently small closed ball, continuity of the derivative gives kI−B −1 DF k ≤ 1/2.
Solving F (x) = y is the fixed-point problem x = x + B −1 (y − F (x)). For y sufficiently close to
F (0), this map preserves the ball and contracts distances by 1/2. Its iterates converge uniformly,
since successive distances form a geometric series; completeness gives a unique solution. The same
estimate bounds inverse differences by 2kB −1 kky − y 0 k, so the inverse is continuous. Inserting this
bound into the differentiability remainder for F proves its derivative is DF (x)−1 . This derivative
is continuous. Repeated differentiation of the inverse identity proves smoothness, inductively
using smoothness of matrix inversion where its determinant is nonzero. Shrinking the open ball
and its image provides the stated neighbourhoods.
    For a smooth field G, restrict to a coordinate ball where kGk ≤ C and kDGk ≤ L. Choose
(T>0) with T C smaller than the available margin and (TL<1/2). On continuous paths staying
in that ball, the map

estimate. The derivative in x0 solves the linear integral equation

    Its integral operator has norm at most (TL<1/2), so the Neumann series gives a unique

Theorem F.5 (Tubular neighbourhood). If M ⊂ A is a smooth embedded submanifold, its
normal quotient bundle ν = T A|M /T M has a neighbourhood of its zero section diffeomorphic
to an open neighbourhood of M in A, fixing M . The whole bundle is diffeomorphic to such a
neighbourhood by a radial fibre change. If M is closed as a subset of A, excision also identifies
the pairs’ cohomology

                               H ∗ (A, A \ M ; R) ∼
                                                  = H ∗ (ν, ν \ M ; R).                       (254)

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; lemma F.4.

Proof. First reduce the tubular assertion to a closed embedding. Local submanifold charts make
M locally closed: near each of its points, it is the zero set of the normal coordinates. Hence
every point of M has a neighbourhood disjoint from C = M \ M . Points outside M do also.
Thus C is closed in A, and A0 = A \ C is open with M closed in it. The normal quotient in A0 is
the same as in A, and an open tube in A0 is open in A. We can therefore assume M closed for
the construction. The relative-cohomology assertion (254) is asserted for the original ambient
space only when its embedding is closed.
     A smooth metric identifies ν with the orthogonal complement of T M , by the proved
complement theorem. Restrict L to this complement. At a zero vector its derivative sends
(a, b) ∈ Tx M ⊕ νx to a + b ∈ Tx A, an isomorphism. lemma F.4 makes it a local diffeomorphism
near each zero vector.
     Here is the global injectivity detail, including a noncompact base. A second-countable manifold
has a compact exhaustion: take a countable relatively compact chart cover and successively
enlarge finite unions of their closures to lie inside the interiors of the next such unions. Smooth
bumps equal to one on each compact stage and supported in the next produce a nonnegative
properPsmooth function h: if ψj = 1 on stage j and is supported in stage j + 1, the locally finite
sum j (1 − ψj ) is bounded on compact stages and tends to infinity off them. Its sublevel sets
are compact. Put Kj = M ∩ {h ≤ j}, compact because M is closed.

                                                 491
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                       Paper III


    For each Kj there is a radius j > 0 such that L is defined and locally invertible on all normal
vectors over Kj of smaller norm, satisfies |h(L(x, v)) − h(x)| < 1/2, and is injective between
any two such vectors. For the last claim, if no radius worked, two distinct vectors of norms
tending to zero would have equal images and bases in Kj . Pass to convergent base subsequences.
Their images tend to the bases, so both limiting bases agree. The local inverse at that common
zero vector contradicts the equality for sufficiently late terms. The other claims follow from
compactness and continuity. Take these radii positive and decreasing in j.
    Choose a continuous positive function g(t), t ≥ 0, by interpolating between j+4 /2 at
successive integers, and choose a smooth positive ρ(x) < g(h(x)) on M . Such a minorant
follows by a smooth locally finite chart partition and constants smaller than the positive lower
bound of g ◦ h on each chart closure. The normal disk domain kvk < ρ(x) is contained in the
local-diffeomorphism domain. If two of its points have the same image, their base heights differ
by less than one. With j the ceiling of the larger height, both bases lie in Kj , and both norms are
smaller than j by the decreasing-radius choice and the four-stage margin. The compact-stage
injectivity then makes them equal. Thus L is an injective local diffeomorphism on this domain
and has a smooth inverse on its open image.
    The fibre map v 7→ ρ(x)v/ 1 +p   kvk2 is a diffeomorphism from the whole normal bundle onto
                               p

that domain, with inverse w 7→ w/ ρ(x)2 − kwk2 . It fixes the zero section. The resulting open
neighbourhood and A \ M cover A; excision for this cover proves (254). In codimension zero M
is open and closed, and the statement reduces to its identity neighbourhood.

    The orientation of T M agrees with the local-homology orientation used above. In an oriented
coordinate chart this is the positive coordinate generator. If a transition has derivative B at a
point, the rescaled maps ht (v) = (h(tv) − h(0))/t extend at t = 0 to Bv, uniformly on a small
sphere; invertibility makes them avoid zero there. Hence their local degree is sign det B, by the
linear determinant calculation in the Thom chapter. This proves compatibility, including its
change on opposite orientations.

Lemma F.6 (Compact Euclidean embedding and finite domination). Every compact smooth
manifold embeds smoothly in some finite Euclidean space and is a retract of a neighbourhood
there. Its integer homology is finitely generated and vanishes in sufficiently large degrees, whether
or not it is oriented.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem F.5.

Proof. Take finitely many coordinate maps fi : Ui → Rd and smooth functions φi ≥ 0 supported
inside Ui , positive on sets covering M . Define the Euclidean map with blocks (φi , φi fi ), extending
the second component by zero. These extensions are smooth because their supports are inside the
charts. If two points have the same image, a block positive at the first is positive at the second,
and division by its common first coordinate gives identical chart coordinates; the points agree. If
its derivative vanishes on a tangent vector, a positive block gives first dφi = 0, then φi dfi = 0, so
the vector is zero. Thus it is an injective immersion; compactness makes it a homeomorphism
onto its image. The local inverse lemma, applied to any full-rank coordinate projection of its
derivative, shows its image is an embedded submanifold.
    In Euclidean space the normal map is simply (x, v) 7→ x + v. Its derivative at zero is the
tangent/normal direct-sum isomorphism. The compact version of the injectivity argument
in theorem F.5 gives a tubular neighbourhood N , and projection along its normal fibres is a
retraction r : N → M . Choose a sufficiently fine finite grid of closed Euclidean cubes meeting M .
Their union P lies inside N , since the distance from compact M to the closed complement of N
is positive. Include all faces, so P is a finite cubical CW complex. Inclusion and retraction give
M → P → M with composite identity. Thus homology of M is a direct summand of homology
of P . The finite cellular complex, proved from relative cells in the Schubert chapter, has finitely

                                                 492
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                    Paper III


generated integer groups in finitely many degrees. Its homology and their summands have the
same finiteness properties. This proves the claim.

   Together with the coefficient calculation following corollary F.3, this proves coefficient
independence of χ for every closed manifold. No triangulation of M was assumed.

F.4   A submanifold’s dual class and the diagonal
For a closed embedded codimension-k submanifold j : M ,→ A, the Thom class of its normal
bundle transfers by (254) to

                                     uM ∈ H k (A, A \ M ; R).

    Use mod-two coefficients without an orientation, or an orientation of the normal bundle
with any R. Its image in H k (A; R) is the dual cohomology class UM . Restriction back
to M is the Euler class of the normal bundle, or its top Stiefel–Whitney class modulo two:
restriction corresponds under the tube to zero-section pullback of the Thom class. This proves
the self-intersection formula directly from the Euler definition.
    If AD , M D−k are closed and oriented, orient the normal bundle by the convention that a
positive tangent basis of M , followed by a positive normal basis, is positive in A. In codimension
zero take j to preserve the given orientations, consistently with the rank-zero convention. Then
for z ∈ H D−k (A; R),

                                   hz ^ UM , [A]i = hj ∗ z, [M ]i.                            (255)

   The same formula holds without signs over F2 .

Proof of (255). Subdivide a fundamental cycle of A for the tube/complement cover. Cap with
a relative cocycle representing uM kills the complement pieces and gives a cycle in the tube.
Project it to M . In a local tangent/normal coordinate product, the ambient local generator
is the product of the positive tangent generator and positive normal generator, in that order.
The Thom cap calculation of the Thom chapter sends this product to the tangent generator: its
normal-factor evaluation is one. Thus the projected cycle has the required local value at every
point of M . Local fundamental-class detection makes its class [M ]. The cap evaluation identity
says its evaluation by j ∗ z is the left side of (255), because the tube retracts onto M .

    For example, a positive-codimension submanifold embedded as a closed subset of Euclidean
space has zero dual class in that ambient space. Therefore its normal top Stiefel–Whitney class,
and oriented normal Euler class if defined, vanish. Closedness and embeddedness are part of this
assertion; an immersion supplies no such ambient relative Thom class.
    Now take a closed d-manifold M and its diagonal ∆ : M ,→ M × M . With a product metric
its tangent space is {(v, v)} and its normal space is {(−v, v)}. Hence

based representatives constant near ∞, and smooth based homotopies constant on endpoint
collars, calculate the original continuous based homotopy classes. The norm factors in (307)–(308)
belong to the explicit retraction; no original sphere radius or input map is silently replaced.
    We now arrange regularity at the specified point q− . This keeps the target point and its
frame, rather than substituting a nearby regular value. The following argument applies either to
a single smooth map on S D or to a smooth homotopy on S D × [0, 1]. In the latter case suppose
that q− is already regular for the two endpoint maps, which are constant in their time collars.

G.7    The two constructions are inverse in each stated ambient dimension
Let Bn,r denote the set of compact smooth n-submanifolds without boundary in Rn+r , each
with an ordered Euclidean normal frame of rank r, modulo the embedded framed bordisms of
(295)–(296). Reparametrizing product collars allows smooth concatenation of two bordisms; the
constant cylinder supplies reflexivity. Reversing the height parameter and transporting its full
normal vectors by (x, t) 7→ (x, 1 − t) supplies symmetry. Thus this is an equivalence relation.
The induced boundary orientation is always the one calculated in (302)–(303).
    The collapse construction and the regular-inverse-image construction give mutually inverse
maps

                                         P
                                  Bn,r  [S n+r , S r ]∗ ,   r ≥ 1.                             (334)
                                         R

    Here the bracket denotes continuous based homotopy classes with the specified basepoints,
and the normal frame in R is exactly (314). We verify every choice and composite.
    For P, two valid collapse radii give homotopic maps by (301). A framed bordism gives a
based homotopy by section G.4. The linear tube is determined by the given embedding and full
normal frame; the construction makes no additional choice of orthonormal frame. Hence P is
well-defined.
    For R, equations (304)–(311) give a smooth transverse representative of any based class. Two
such representatives of one class have a continuous based homotopy. Apply (305)–(308) relative
its smooth endpoint collars, and then (309)–(311) relative those collars. The inverse image (316)
is an embedded framed bordism with precisely their frames (314). Thus both approximation and
transverse-parameter choices give the same element of Bn,r , and R is well-defined.



                                                  506
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                     Paper III


   The composite RP recovers the original submanifold as a set and as an embedded smooth
manifold, and recovers every original frame vector by (293) and the uniqueness after (316).
Therefore this composite is the identity. The other composite is the identity by the three explicit
homotopies of section G.6. This proves (334).
   The based null-homotopy case will be used directly later. If the collapse of a particular original
(M, E) is null-homotopic, section G.5 applied to a homotopy to the constant q+ map gives a
compact embedded (n + 1)-manifold with one boundary component, whose normal frame extends
exactly E. Conversely such a framed bounding manifold gives a null-homotopy by section G.4
with an empty upper endpoint. This statement retains the original boundary embedding, collar
and frame; it does not infer a bounding manifold merely from stable parallelizability.

G.8    Suspension, stable bounding and the original complex tangent framing
We specify the suspension coordinates before identifying its inverse image. The one-point

                                   (RD × R)+ −→ (RD )+ ∧ R+ .                                    (335)

because complements of neighborhoods there are compact subsets of that complement. This
proves (335) as a homeomorphism. The order of the new coordinate is spatial x, then u.

G.10     The relative embedding needed for tangent-framed bordism
The normal-framed Pontryagin–Thom construction is stated for embedded bordisms. To apply it
to the group defined using abstract stable tangent framings, the following relative construction is
needed. Every stabilization of an existing embedding uses identically zero appended coordinates.
The additional coordinates used in the relative extension vanish on the prescribed boundary
collars, as specified below. All changes of their order are specified.

Lemma G.1 (Relative Euclidean embedding with specified product collars). Let W be a compact
smooth manifold whose boundary is the disjoint union M0 t M1 . Fix disjoint collars and smooth
embeddings ji : Mi −→ RD . After appending finitely many zero spatial coordinates, there is a
smooth embedding
                                   J : W −→ RN × [0, 1]
whose restrictions in smaller collars are exactly (m, t) 7→ (j0 (m), 0, t) and (m, t) 7→ (j1 (m), 0, t),
respectively. Its interior is in RN × (0, 1). Here the coordinate in the upper collar is t = 1 − r,
where r is the prescribed inward collar coordinate.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. Choose a number a > 0 so that the two collars are defined for 0 ≤ r < 4a and 4a < 1/2.
Choose a smooth function t : W → [0, 1] equal to r in the lower collar for r < 3a, equal to 1 − r
in the upper collar for r < 3a, and taking values strictly between zero and one elsewhere. For
example, interpolate by a smooth cutoff between each indicated collar formula and the constant
1/2, completing the interpolation before the end of that collar. Convex combinations remain in
(0, 1) at every interior point.
     The boundary maps have a smooth extension f : W → RD which is exactly ji (m) for r < 3a:
multiply each ji in its collar by a cutoff equal to one there and zero near the far end of the collar,
extend by zero, and add the two terms. Their supports are disjoint.
     There is a smooth embedding e : W → RK given by finite coordinate blocks (χ` , χ` ψ` ), with
each cutoff supported in a coordinate chart and identically one on a smaller cover. Boundary
charts are charts in a half-space and their coordinate functions and cutoffs extend smoothly to
open Euclidean charts. A block with χ` = 1 separates points by ψ` and has injective tangent
derivative. The resulting map is an injective immersion, and compactness makes it an embedding.
This is the same finite-chart proof as the closed-manifold construction, with the half-space charts
retained.
     Choose a smooth function g ≥ 0 which is zero exactly on the two closed collar regions r ≤ a
and positive elsewhere. Such a function is obtained by a smooth flat step in each collar, equal to
one before its far end, and by setting it equal to one off those collars. Define

                                                                                              (RB.1)
                                                                    
                                J(w) = f (w), g(w), g(w)e(w), t(w) .

At a point with g > 0, the first scalar g and the block ge recover e by division. Equality of
two images therefore implies equality of the two points. Also dJ(v) = 0 gives dg(v) = 0, then
g de(v) = 0, so v = 0. Points with g = 0 cannot have the same image as points with g > 0. On
g = 0, formula (RB.1) is the prescribed product embedding; its two collar components have
disjoint height ranges. Its derivative is injective there because f = ji and t = r or 1 − r on
a larger collar. These observations prove injectivity and immersion everywhere, including the
flat joining locus r = a. Compactness again gives an embedding. The previously chosen height
function proves the assertion about the interior. One further zero spatial coordinate may be
appended if an even value of N is wanted.


                                                  513
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                        Paper III


Lemma G.2 (Exact boundary normal frame of a tangent-framed bordism). Let dim W = 7.
Suppose the stable tangent framing of W is a product in the specified collars and induces the
prescribed stable frames
                                  τi : T Mi ⊕ Rk −→ R6+k .
Append an identity line if necessary so that k is even. In a collar use the coordinate vector ∂t
directed from the lower end towards the upper end, and write the product framing as

                                    τW (v + a∂t , b) = (τi (v, b), a).                          (RB.2)

The embedding in the preceding lemma, after a further specified zero stabilization, has a normal
framing whose restriction is exactly the normal frame constructed from ji and τi , followed by one
identity normal vector. Hence it is an embedded normal-framed bordism between those stabilized
endpoint frames.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. Regard the derivative of J as a map K : T W → RN ⊕ Rt , put QW = (K T K)−1 K T in
any tangent chart, and put PW = I − KQW . The matrix PW is independent of the tangent
chart and is the orthogonal projection onto the normal bundle νW . The identities QW K = I,
QW PW = 0, PW + KQW = I prove all of these assertions directly.
    Add 7 + k zero ambient coordinates. The normal bundle is then νW ⊕ R7+k . Its following
trivialization and inverse are actual bundle maps:
                                                                          −1
                        AW (y, u) = (y + Kv, b),                (v, b) = τW  (u),
                                                                                                (RB.3)
                        A−1
                         W (z, b) = (PW z, τW (QW z, b)).

Substitution using the three projection identities proves both inverse identities. This also proves
that the formulas agree in overlapping tangent charts. The images under A−1   W of a fixed ordered
basis give a smooth full normal frame, with its actual Gram matrix; no orthonormal replacement
is needed.
    Put the new ambient coordinates before the height coordinate, so the ambient cylinder has
spatial order RN , R6+k , Ra and last coordinate t. Order the normal parameters as (z, b, a), with
respective dimensions N, k, 1. This parameter order is the explicitly recorded permutation of the
order (z, a, b) in the right side of (RB.3). In a product collar write Ji = Dji , Qi = (JiT Ji )−1 JiT ,
and Pi = I − Ji Qi . The derivative and projection of the original bordism embedding are block
diagonal there. Applying (RB.2)–(RB.3) gives the full collar frame

                                                                                              (RB.4)
                                                                        
                                  (z, b, a) 7−→ Pi z, τi (Qi z, b), a; 0 .

The final semicolon separates the height coordinate. The first two blocks in (RB.4) are precisely
the endpoint frame in the original tangent-to-normal construction. The third is its right-appended
unit vector. The last component is zero throughout the collar, so the embedding and the normal
frame have the exact product germs required by the embedded Pontryagin–Thom construction.
Formula (RB.4), rather than an orientation-only argument, verifies the asserted matching.
    If the initial definition of tangent-framed bordism supplies a framing homotopy on the
boundary instead of the exact product equality (RB.2), make that homotopy constant near both
endpoints and install it on a smaller collar. It is a homotopy through bundle isomorphisms,
equals the old frame on a neighbourhood of the inner seam, and hence pastes to the old framing
on the remaining manifold. This gives (RB.2) exactly and does not change the specified boundary
maps.

Lemma G.3 (The inverse normal-frame comparison). Starting with a framed normal bundle,
passing to its tangent-plus-normal stable tangent framing, and applying the preceding normal
construction recovers the original normal framing up to stabilization and an explicit homotopy
through full normal frames.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. Let j : M 6 → RD have derivative J and normal frame E : Rr → ν, where D = 6 + r.
Suspend once if necessary so that r and D are even. Put

                   Q = (J T J)−1 J T ,     P = I − JQ,           E + = (E T E)−1 E T .

Then EE + = P , and the stable tangent frame is τ (v, b) = Jv + Eb. Applying its normal
construction to (j, 0) gives

                              F (a, b) = (P a, JQa + Eb)       in ν ⊕ RD .                  (RB.5)

The original stabilized normal frame is Est (b, a) = (Eb, a). Decompose a = Jv +Ec using v = Qa,
c = E + a. On the fixed even-dimensional parameter space Rr choose the constant operator Ir
with square −I, acting on successive coordinate pairs by (x, y) 7→ (−y, x). For 0 ≤ s ≤ 1, set
θ = πs/2, ϕ = πs, and

                               bs = cos θ b + sin θ c,
                               cs = (cos ϕ I + sin ϕ Ir )(− sin θ b + cos θ c),             (RB.6)
                         Gs (b, a) = (Ebs , Jv + Ecs ).

Each factor in this formula is invertible: use the inverse plane rotation on (b, c) and replace the
sine by its negative in the factor involving Ir . Thus Gs is a full frame for every s. At s = 0 it
is Est ; at s = 1 it is (Ec, Jv + Eb) = F (a, b). The domain order (b, a) at this endpoint is the
recorded block permutation of the order (a, b) in (RB.5). Its sign is (−1)Dr = +1. It has a path
through constant orientation-preserving matrices to the identity: use plane rotations to reduce
its orthogonal matrix to a diagonal matrix, then rotate each pair of remaining negative diagonal
entries through angle π. Reversing the finite list gives the required path. This supplies the
parameter-order homotopy as well as the bundle-dependent homotopy (RB.6). All occurrences of
J, E, Q, E + remain the given point-dependent matrices. Smoothness follows from their displayed
formulas and matrix inversion on positive definite Gram matrices.

Proposition G.4 (The abstract tangent-framed Pontryagin–Thom comparison). The embedded
normal-framed Pontryagin–Thom bijection, together with the displayed stable tangent-to-normal
construction, induces an isomorphism Ωfr6 = π6 (S) for abstract stable tangent-framed bordism. It
                                          ∼
is independent of the embedding and the specified zero stabilizations, and preserves disjoint-union
addition.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. Choice of the original embedding. First consider appending d zero coordinates to
an embedding j : M → RD . Its canonical frame, in the displayed orders, is

                                   ((a, c), b) 7−→ (P a, c, τ (Qa, b)).

Move the middle ambient block c after the τ block and move its parameter block after b. The
result is exactly the original frame followed by d identity vectors. The two permutation signs

                                                  515
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                        Paper III


are (−1)d(6+k) and (−1)dk ; with the stipulated even k they are both positive. The constant
rotation construction in the preceding proof supplies both homotopies. Thus a zero-coordinate
enlargement of the original embedding agrees with the specified stable transition map, with the
complete block comparison retained.
    The same comparisons account for embedding choices. For two embeddings j0 , j1 of one
compact manifold, first place them in a common Euclidean space by zero coordinates. In its
double use js = (cos θ(s) j0 , sin θ(s) j1 ), where θ goes from zero to π/2 and is constant near the
endpoints. At every parameter at least one coefficient is nonzero, so injectivity and injectivity
of the tangent derivative follow from that embedding. Apply the actual Gram-matrix normal
construction, including its specified zero stabilization, to this family; write the resulting stabilized
embedding again as js . It gives a smooth family of full normal frames Es . A family Es orthogonal
to Djs yields the normal frame
                                   Es A 7−→ (Es A, −hEs A, ∂s js i)
on the embedded cylinder (m, s) 7→ (js (m), s): its scalar product with every vector (Djs v +
a∂s js , a) is zero. Its rank is unchanged because its spatial part is injective. It is a product
frame near the ends. An ambient plane rotation carries the second coordinate block to the first,
with its full normal derivative. Naturality of the canonical frame under a constant orthogonal
transformation R reads
                                  ERj (a, b) = (R ⊕ I)Ej (R−1 a, b).
This follows by substituting J 7→ RJ, P 7→ RP R−1 and Q 7→ QR−1 in its complete formula.
The plane rotation path consequently supplies the parameter comparison as well as the ambient
one. The positive block-order comparisons are the constant-matrix homotopies already recorded
above. This gives embedded framed bordisms for all embedding and ordering choices, after finite
stabilization.
    The group operation is also preserved. Place two disjoint compact embedded representatives
in disjoint Euclidean balls by translations and positive dilations, retaining their full transported
frames. Their tubes can be chosen inside those balls. The collapse of their disjoint union is the
map supported on those two balls, constant elsewhere. The based pinch description of addition
in the sphere homotopy group is exactly this map. The translations and dilations give framed
cylinders by the same family construction, so this comparison is independent of the placements.
    Consequently the two existing Pontryagin–Thom constructions descend to abstract tangent-
framed bordism in dimension six. The tangent composite is the explicit involution homotopy
already proved in the sphere-twist chapter, equations (7.9)–(7.19). The normal composite is
(RB.5)–(RB.6). Relative embedding and (RB.4) give bordism compatibility. Together with
the already proved embedded normal-framed bijection, these prove the asserted isomorphism
Ωfr
  6 = π6 (S) at the precise point where the geometric framing chapter uses it. This bridge does
    ∼
not compute the stable group and does not certify any still unread Adams prerequisite.


H     The six-dimensional bundle comparison and the stable framing
The following complete arguments are retained as re-derivations of their classical prerequisites.
Source-specific calculations and their hypotheses are stated explicitly.
    The classical framing and surgery context is credited to Michel–Weber, Sections 2–3 Michel and
Weber (2014); the actual compact-group maps, Euler calculation and unstable frame comparison
are proved here.
    We prove the following receiving result for lesson 7: for every oriented smooth homotopy
six-sphere Σ, the original rank-seven bundle T Σ ⊕ 1R is trivial. We retain the extra real line.
The original tangent bundle has Euler number two and is not trivial. A stable framing is also
not a framed null-cobordism; producing the latter is a further step in smooth sphere recognition.

                                                  516
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                    Paper III


    The proof uses the polynomial loop reduction already proved in section AI.10, and supplies
its injectivity argument for the compact bases actually needed here. We then construct the
full map SU (4) → SO(6), compute its Euler class, and use the actual frame fibration SO(6) →
SO(7) → S 6 . The human context is Françoise Michel and Claude Weber, Michel Kervaire work
on knots in higher dimensions, arXiv:1409.0704v1, Sections 2–3. Those original-author TeX
sections were read; their statements of stable parallelizability, surgery and stable groups are not
used as substitutes for the receiving proofs below.

H.1    A family index for the actual loops
Let Y be a compact space and let

                             g : Y × T −→ GLr (C),             g(y, 1) = Ir .                (367)

     Use increasing t in z = e2πit for the circle direction. Let H 2 ⊂ L2 (T) be the closed span of
1, z, z 2 , . . ., and let P be its orthogonal projection. Define

                                         Tgy = P Mgy |H 2 ⊗Cr .                              (368)

    The family is continuous in operator norm, since kTa − Tb k ≤ ka − bk∞ . For Laurent
polynomial symbols, direct multiplication of the unilateral shift and its adjoint shows that
Ta Tb − Tab has finite rank: all differences occur among finitely many initial Fourier modes.
Uniform approximation of continuous symbols by their Fejér polynomials, with the operator
bound just given, shows that this difference is compact for continuous matrix symbols. Therefore

                                  Tg Tg−1 − I    and     Tg−1 Tg − I                         (369)

     are compact, continuously in the parameter.
     Here are the Fredholm and family-index facts needed to use (369). Suppose a bounded
operator A : H → H has a bounded two-sided inverse modulo compact operators. Its kernel
is finite dimensional: an infinite orthonormal sequence there would contradict compactness in
BA − I. The same argument applied to the adjoint gives finite-dimensional cokernel once closed
range is proved. On the orthogonal complement of its kernel, A is bounded below. Otherwise
choose unit vectors vj ⊥ ker A with Avj → 0. The equation BA = I + K and compactness of K
give a convergent subsequence of vj , whose unit limit lies both in the kernel and its orthogonal
complement, a contradiction. This lower bound proves closed range, and the adjoint argument
completes the Fredholm assertion.
     For a continuous Fredholm family Ay , choose a finite-dimensional subspace E ⊂ H for which

                           ey : H ⊕ E −→ H,
                           A                            (v, e) 7−→ Ay v + e                  (370)

    is onto for every y. Such a space exists. At each point take a complement of the range;
surjectivity persists on a neighbourhood because a right inverse persists by a Neumann series.
Finitely many of these neighbourhoods cover Y ; the sum of their finite-dimensional complements
works everywhere.
    The kernels of (370) form a finite-rank vector bundle. To see the local construction, fix a
bounded right inverse R0 at y0 . Near y0 , set

                                                                                             (371)
                                                     −1
                                   ey − A
                      Ry = R0 I + (A    ey )R0             ,      Py = I − Ry A
                                                                              ey .
                                          0


  Then A ey Ry = I, P 2 = Py , and the image of Py is precisely the kernel. The projections here
                     y
may be oblique. For two sufficiently close finite-rank idempotents P, Q, the restrictions of Q to

Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                       Paper III


im P and of P to im Q are injective, by the estimate kQv − vk < kvk on im P , and its reverse.
Thus their finite ranks agree, and these restrictions supply continuous local trivializations.
   Define

                               Ind(A) = [ker A]
                                             e − [Y × E] ∈ K 0 (Y ).                             (372)

   This does not depend on E. If E ⊂ E 0 , projecting the added coordinate modulo E gives the
exact bundle sequence

                         0 −→ ker A
                                  eE −→ ker A
                                            eE 0 −→ Y × (E 0 /E) −→ 0.                           (373)

    It is onto because (370) with E is onto; a lift of any extra coordinate can be corrected using that

dimensions in (372) proves independence for nested choices, and a common containing subspace
proves it for arbitrary choices. The construction on Y × [0, 1] proves homotopy invariance, using

    For a projection e(y) ∈ MN (C), let Ee be its image bundle. The actual positive loop and its

                        fe (z) = ze + I − e,      Tfe = S ⊗ e + I ⊗ (I − e).                     (374)
