AE.3     Finite generation of the original unstable groups
We will use a CW comparison for the intermediate path fibres. Here are its maps and the facts
needed from it. For a space Y , let S(Y )n be the set of all continuous maps ∆n → Y , with the
original face and degeneracy pullbacks. Set

                    Q(Y ) = |S(Y )|,      eY : Q(Y ) −→ Y,        eY [σ; t] = σ(t).            (1715)


                                                   802
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                        Paper III


    Evaluation agrees on all identifications and is continuous by the quotient topology. The
realization argument of the Adams companion, section AC.9, makes Q(Y ) a CW complex.
    We recall the comparison proof to fix what (1715) preserves. An ordered triangulated map
f : P → Y from a finite polyhedron lifts to Q(Y ): on each oriented simplex a : ∆n → P , use
the characteristic simplex labelled f a. The lifts agree on their faces and evaluate to exactly f .
Subdivision changes this lift by a homotopy. To construct it, triangulate each simplex times
an interval with its original triangulation at the bottom and the chosen subdivision at the top,
extending the already chosen triangulations on side faces. Label every prism simplex by its
projection to that original simplex followed by f . Their characteristic maps into Q(Y ) give the
homotopy; every signed side face agrees with its neighbour. The construction is relative to a
subpolyhedron.
    We also need this comparison for a map g : P → Q(Y ) already given. A compact image
in a CW complex is contained in a finite subcomplex. For this realization, the subcomplex
is made from finitely many characteristic simplices and their face identifications. Subdivide
those simplices with their identifications retained. The open stars of the subdivided faces give a
finite cover. Subdivide P until the image of each closed simplex lies in one such star. Choose
the corresponding carrier faces on vertices; on a simplex use their common carrier and affine
barycentric interpolation. On a face the carrier restriction is the already chosen face map, since
its characteristic identifications are affine face maps or degeneracy collapses. Interpolating in the
same carrier gives a homotopy from g to this map, relative to a subpolyhedron where it was already
of this form. This is the simplicial-approximation argument in the actual characteristic simplices;
no injectivity of a boundary characteristic map is required. Apply the prism construction of the
preceding paragraph to each carrier simplex and its restrictions. It compares that map to the
characteristic lift of its evaluation in Y . Thus g is homotopic to a characteristic lift of eY g, after
the displayed subdivision.
    Apply these statements to spheres, and then to disks with their boundary prescribed. Every
sphere map to Y lifts; a nullhomotopy in Y lifts after subdivision and the relative prism restores
the original boundary map in Q(Y ). The same argument for an interval proves the component
assertion. Hence eY induces every homotopy isomorphism and a bijection on components. The
induced homology map is also an isomorphism. Indeed the cellular chain group of Q(Y ) is freely
generated by the nondegenerate singular simplices of Y , with exactly their original signed face
differential. The full singular chain complex of Y maps onto this complex by killing its degenerate
simplices. The degenerate subcomplex is contractible by the face/degeneracy contraction proved
in the included Thom/Euler companion: successively remove the first degeneracy, with its
alternating sign; the two matching face terms give the identity and all other terms cancel.
Therefore this quotient induces a homology isomorphism. On each characteristic cell, evaluation
(1715) gives precisely its original singular simplex, so its homology map is the inverse comparison.
We have proved

AE.4     The finite-range homology comparison
We require the range of a particular suspension map, so we prove the finite-range form of the
path-fibre argument. Let f : A → B be a map between simply connected spaces, let B be a CW

                        Hi (f ; Z) is an isomorphism for i ≤ D,        D ≥ 2.                 (1724)

connected total space joining two fibre points projects to a loop in B; lift a contraction of that
loop relative the endpoint lifts. The resulting top path joins the points inside K.

product, and obtains a framed nullbordism of the original homotopy six-sphere. The section AG.7

and gives the orientation-preserving diffeomorphism to the original six-sphere, homotopic to its
original degree-one map.

AF.1     The full rank-three framing map and its factor two
Use the original quaternion coordinates


q = q0 + q1 i + q2 j + q3 k,       i2 = j 2 = k 2 = −1,      ij = k,        |q|2 = q02 + q12 + q22 + q32 .
                                                                       ji = −k,
                                                                                                 (1767)
     The other two cyclic products are jk = i and ki = j, and reversing either order changes its
sign. Quaternion conjugation changes all three imaginary signs. Thus q q̄ = q̄q = |q|2 . Let S 3 be
the original unit sphere in these four ordered coordinates, with its positive boundary orientation.
     For a unit quaternion a, conjugation v 7→ avā preserves the imaginary subspace with
coordinates (i, j, k) and its Euclidean norm. It lies in SO(3), since S 3 is connected and at a = 1
it is the identity. Its kernel is {1, −1}: a quaternion commuting with i, j, k is real. The map
is onto. Indeed for a unit imaginary quaternion u, write a = cos t + u sin t. It fixes u; for an
imaginary v ⊥ u, direct multiplication using uv = −vu gives

                                        avā = cos(2t)v + sin(2t)uv.                              (1768)

   Every orientation-preserving rotation has an axis and such a rotation on its perpendicular
plane. The derivative of the map at 1 sends an imaginary h to v 7→ hv − vh; it is injective and
both Lie algebras have dimension three. Therefore this surjection is a local diffeomorphism with
the displayed two-element kernel, and is a covering map. Lifting spheres and homotopies gives

                               π3 (SO(3)) ∼
                                          = π3 (S 3 ) ∼
                                                      = Z,       π2 (SO(3)) = 0.                  (1769)

   The generator in (1769) is the original conjugation map on the positively oriented S 3 , not an
unspecified choice.
   The corresponding four-dimensional map is

                          ρ4 : S 3 × S 3 −→ SO(H),               ρ4 (a, b)(v) = av b̄.               (1770)

    It preserves the full norm (1767) and orientation. Its kernel consists of (1, 1) and (−1, −1):
apply the identity action to v = 1, then to every imaginary basis element. Its derivative sends
(α, β) to v 7→ αv −vβ; vanishing first gives α = β, then makes this imaginary quaternion commute
with every quaternion, hence zero. The derivative is an isomorphism onto so(4) by dimension.
Its compact image is both closed and open in the connected SO(4), so (1770) is onto and is the
indicated two-sheeted cover. Connectedness of SO(4) follows directly by successively rotating its
oriented orthonormal columns to the coordinate columns in coordinate two-planes. The stabilizer
of the first vector 1 ∈ H has a = b. Consequently the original inclusion fixing that first coordinate
is exactly

    Here [a] denotes the rotation (1768); the equality records the actual diagonal lift.

the divisor is |w − v(v ∗ w)|, which is nonzero on that neighbourhood. Its fibre over (1, 0)T is

sequence therefore proves that the displayed fibre map induces an isomorphism on π3 .

                                  P (v1 , v2 , v3 , t, s) = (t, v1 , v2 , v3 , −s).

right-stabilized matrix diag(Ad(a), 1, 1) to diag(1, Ad(a), 1), exactly the map (1771) followed by
(1777). Successive coordinate-plane rotations, as in the connectedness proof above, give a path
from I5 to this specified P . Conjugation along that path is a based homotopy, so the two original
maps induce the same stable π3 -map. The last-coordinate sign and the intervening coordinate
permutation have both been retained and proved harmless by this actual homotopy.

over its positive unit sphere. The two in (1780) is the sum of the two actual diagonal factors in
(1771); it has not been absorbed into a generator.

AF.2     The obstruction for an actual embedded three-sphere
Let M be an oriented smooth six-manifold, and retain a specified stable tangent framing

                                        τ : T M ⊕ R s −→ R 6+s .                               (1782)
    Here a framing is the displayed fibrewise linear isomorphism, in the displayed order. Fix an
orientation-preserving parametrized embedding f : S 3 ,→ M , where the sphere has the quaternion
coordinates (1767). Its normal bundle has rank three. Give it the orientation for which the
ordered sum T S 3 ⊕ νf has the pullback orientation of T M .
    This oriented normal bundle is trivial. To prove this without replacing it by its stable class,
choose trivializations over the two hemispheres of S 3 . Their transition on the equatorial S 2 is a
map to GL+ (3, R), and the positive polar deformation retracts that group to SO(3). Equation
(1769) says the transition is nullhomotopic. Extending that nullhomotopy over one hemisphere
changes its trivialization so that the two agree on the equator. The resulting three sections
trivialize the original normal bundle. Denote an oriented normal frame by

                                            φq : R3 −→ (νf )q .                                (1783)
    Choose a metric only to view the normal vectors in Tf (q) M . Write the inner product on H as
hq, zi = Re(q̄z). For q ∈ S 3 and z ∈ H, retain both parts of its orthogonal decomposition:

                      r = Re(q̄z),        zT = z − qr ∈ Tq S 3 ,        z = zT + qr.           (1784)
   The actual matrix to be compared is


                    Af,φ (q) : H ⊕ R3 ⊕ Rs −→ R6+s ⊕ R,
                                                                                              (1785)
                                     (z, w, u) 7−→ τf (q) (dfq (zT ) + φq (w), u), −r .

    Every map in (1785) is specified. Its inverse first recovers r as the negative last coordinate,
applies τ −1 to recover the tangent vector and u, decomposes that tangent vector uniquely into
df (T S 3 ) and νf , and finally returns z = zT + qr and w = φ−1 of its normal part. Thus (1785) is
an invertible real matrix at every q.
    The last minus sign records the collar of the handle trace. Form the incoming cylinder with
coordinate t increasing toward the handle. The attaching part of D4 × D3 is ∂D4 × D3 ; its
outward radial coordinate points back into the cylinder, hence to −∂t . The trace framing on the
cylinder sends a vector (v, u, c∂t ) to (τ (v, u), c). At the central attaching sphere, its expression
in the handle coordinates is exactly (1785). Neither the collar sign nor the order of its final
coordinate has been suppressed.
    Take the basepoint q0 = 1 and set

                                      Bf,φ (q) = Af,φ (1)−1 Af,φ (q).                          (1786)
   This is a based map into GL+ (7 + s, R): the determinant sign of A is constant on the
connected sphere, so its quotient has positive determinant. For definiteness the deformation to
SO(7 + s) is the positive polar homotopy

                                                    816
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                       Paper III




                               B 7−→ B(B T B)−t/2 ,          0 ≤ t ≤ 1.                        (1787)

   The positive definite power exists by the spectral theorem, varies continuously, and fixes
B = I. Use the stable generator specified after (1780), and define the integer and its parity

              kτ (f, φ) = [Bf,φ ] ∈ π3 SO(7 + s) = Z,       ετ (f ) = kτ (f, φ)   (mod 2).     (1788)

    The equality with the stable group in (1788) is proved by the sphere bundles at the end of
section AF.1, since 7 + s ≥ 5.
    We now prove all choice statements needed for this definition at a fixed parametrized
embedding. First change its oriented normal frame to φ0q = φq h(q), with h : S 3 → GL+ (3, R).
Directly from (1785),

                               Af,φ0 (q) = Af,φ (q) diag(I4 , h(q), Is ).                      (1789)

   Taking based classes of this product gives

                                    kτ (f, φ0 ) = kτ (f, φ) + 2[h],                            (1790)

    where [h] ∈ π3 SO(3) = Z uses the actual polar deformation and original generator of (1769).
To check the product statement when h(1) 6= I, put H(q) = diag(I4 , h(q), Is ). The based matrix
for the right side of (1789) is

                                H(1)−1 Bf,φ (q)H(1) H(1)−1 H(q).

    Conjugation by the constant positive matrix H(1) is based homotopic to the identity
conjugation along a path in GL+ . Matrix multiplication adds the homotopy classes, as proved
for (1779). The second class is the original rank-three inclusion, whose coefficient is exactly two
by (1780). This proves (1790), including its plus sign. Every integer [h] is attained: compose
the original conjugation map S 3 → SO(3) with a based degree-[h] map of the original sphere,
constructed by the oriented pinch map and reflection when its degree is negative. In particular
the parity in (1788) is independent of the normal frame.
    A change of metric or of normal splitting also leaves that parity fixed. Any second splitting
of 0 → T S 3 → f ∗ T M → νf → 0 differs from thefirst by a bundle map νf → T S 3 . Its effect
on the ordered sum is the triangular matrix I0 D    I ; replacing D by tD is an explicit homotopy
through invertible matrices. Once the splitting is fixed, the remaining change is an oriented
normal frame and is covered by (1790). A homotopy of τ or of φ gives a homotopy of (1785) and
(1786), so keeps the integer k itself fixed.
    Stabilizing (1782) by an identity line is also exact. With the new variable appended to
u, formula (1785) has the new target variable immediately before its final collar coordinate.
Thus the new A is Q(A ⊕ I1 ), where Q is the constant permutation exchanging that appended
coordinate with the collar coordinate. In (1786) the two copies of Q cancel. The new based
matrix is precisely B ⊕ I1 . Its class and the parity (1788) are therefore preserved by the original
right stabilization.
    Framing-extension criterion. For the given parametrized embedding f , there exists an
oriented normal frame for which its surgery trace carries a stable framing extending (1782) if
and only if ετ (f ) = 0.
    Here is the extension proof. A tubular neighbourhood gives the actual attaching map
S 3 × D3 → M . The pullback of the cylinder framing over that entire attaching part is a matrix-
valued function whose restriction to w = 0 is (1785). Contracting the original normal disc by
w 7→ tw makes it homotopic to that restriction. The pair (D4 × D3 , S 3 × D3 ) retracts as a pair


                                                 817
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                     Paper III


to (D4 , S 3 ). Consequently a framing on the attaching part extends to the handle exactly when
(1785) is nullhomotopic in its component of GL(7 + s, R), equivalently when (1786) represents
zero. More explicitly, a nullhomotopy of the central matrix gives an extension over the core D4 ;
the homotopy on the attaching part and the collar homotopy-extension property then restore its
full prescribed matrix on S 3 × D3 . A continuous extension can be made smooth relative to this
collar by matrix approximation; on the compact handle, sufficiently close approximation stays
inside the open set of invertible matrices. This yields a genuine smooth framing of the trace.
Conversely an extending handle framing restricts over its core to a nullhomotopy of (1786), so
forces kτ (f, φ) = 0.
    If (1788) is zero, the integer k is even. Choose h in (1790) of class −k/2; then the new actual
normal frame has integer zero and the preceding construction extends it. If an actual framed
trace exists, that same construction in reverse gives k = 0 for its normal frame and hence parity
zero for every frame. This proves both directions of the criterion.
    Finally ετ (f ) is invariant under a parametrized isotopy of embeddings. The normal bundles
of such an isotopy form an oriented rank-three bundle over S 3 × [0, 1]. Parallel transport for a
connection extends the starting normal frame over the interval. Equations (1784)–(1786) then
form a continuous homotopy of based matrices. Its two integers agree; any prescribed different
normal frame at the endpoint changes the integer by (1790) and leaves its parity unchanged.
    This proves a value for each actual parametrized embedded sphere and an exact handle-
extension criterion. Dependence only on its homology class, the effect of a general homotopy
through singular maps, and the quadratic law have not been assumed in this construction.

AF.3     Explicit values with every quaternion factor retained
AF.3.1    The standard local sphere has value zero

Take a positively oriented coordinate ball in a framed six-manifold. Its stable frame is homotopic
on a smaller closed ball to its value at the centre, because the ball contracts. This homotopy
does not change (1788). A constant target change cancels in (1786), so it suffices to compute in
the original ordered R6 = H ⊕ R2 with its identity tangent framing. Embed S 3 as q 7→ (q, 0, 0).
The oriented rank-three normal frame is

                                 φq (w0 , w1 , w2 ) = (−qw0 , w1 , w2 ).                      (1791)

    The minus sign is required: moving the outward radial vector past the three positively
oriented tangent vectors reverses orientation. At q = 1, the ordered list (i, j, k, −1, e5 , e6 ) has
positive determinant.

                   (z, w0 , w1 , w2 ) 7−→ (z − q Re(q̄z) − qw0 , w1 , w2 , − Re(q̄z)).        (1792)

AF.4     The full finite quadratic calculation
We next prove the algebra that will receive the geometric construction. Its objects here are actual
finite quadratic spaces. No quadratic law for the geometric values of section AF.2 is presumed.
    Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F2 , and let λ : V × V → F2 be a nonsingular
alternating bilinear form. Let q : V → F2 be an actual function satisfying



                                                    820
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                                          Paper III




                 q(0) = 0,          q(x + y) = q(x) + q(y) + λ(x, y)                      for every x, y ∈ V.     (1809)
   All additions in (1809) are in the specified field. The alternation condition gives λ(x, x) = 0,
and expanding λ(x + y, x + y) = 0 proves λ(x, y) = λ(y, x) in this field.
   Choose e 6= 0. Nonsingularity supplies f with λ(e, f ) = 1. The actual projection

                                         P (v) = v + λ(v, f )e + λ(v, e)f                                         (1810)
   has image W = {w : λ(w, e) = λ(w, f ) = 0}, since pairing its right side with e or f cancels
the respective two equal terms. It fixes every w ∈ W and kills e, f . Thus the original vector v
has the unique decomposition

                                         v = λ(v, f )e + λ(v, e)f + P (v).                                        (1811)
   The restriction of λ to W is nonsingular: an element in its radical also pairs to zero with e, f ,
hence with every vector by (1811), and therefore is zero. Repeating this construction gives an
even dimension 2g and an actual basis e1 , f1 , . . . , eg , fg with

                                 λ(ei , fj ) = δij ,          λ(ei , ej ) = λ(fi , fj ) = 0.                      (1812)
    The coordinate map and inverse are retained by (1811) at every step. This does not discard
the original V , its original vectors, or its function q.
    Put ai = q(ei ) and bi = q(fi ). Iterating the actual identity (1809), keeping every nonzero
pairing in (1812), yields
                                                          !
                                                                                                                  (1813)
                                  X                               X                          
                             q         (αi ei + βi fi )       =         αi ai + βi bi + αi βi .
                                   i                                i

   For one pair this follows by considering αi , βi ∈ {0, 1}; for different pairs all cross pairings
vanish by (1812). Induction on the number of pairs proves the displayed formula for every original

AF.4.1     Vanishing and an actual zero-valued Lagrangian

A Lagrangian here is a subspace L ⊂ V with λ|L×L = 0 and dim L = g. Nonsingularity then
gives L⊥ = L: the linear map V → L∗ defined by λ is surjective, so its kernel L⊥ has dimension
g and already contains L. The surjectivity follows by extending a functional on L to a basis of
V , then using the isomorphism V → V ∗ given by the nonsingular pairing.
    We prove

                 Arf(q) = 0      ⇐⇒       there is a Lagrangian L ⊂ V with q|L = 0.                 (1819)

   For the forward direction use induction on g. The case g = 0 has L = {0}. If g ≥ 1, (1818)
with Arf zero gives at least three zeros of q, so choose a nonzero e with q(e) = 0. Choose f with
λ(e, f ) = 1 and define the specified new vector

                                              f 0 = f + q(f )e.                                     (1820)

   If q(f ) = 0, it is f . If q(f ) = 1, (1809) gives q(f + e) = 1 + 0 + 1 = 0. Thus in both cases
λ(e, f 0 ) = 1 and q(f 0 ) = 0.
   Use (1810) with f 0 and let W = he, f 0 i⊥ . The exact isomorphism

                          F22 ⊕ W −→ V,           (α, β, w) 7−→ αe + βf 0 + w                       (1821)

    has inverse (λ(v, f 0 ), λ(v, e), P (v)) by (1811). Formula (1809) identifies its quadratic function
exactly with αβ + q(w). The sum over α, β is 2 by (1815), so G(q) = 2G(q|W ). Since G(q) = 2g ,
(1816) for W shows that its Arf invariant is zero. The induction hypothesis constructs a zero-
valued Lagrangian LW ⊂ W . Then L = F2 e ⊕ LW , with its actual inclusion from (1821), has
dimension g, zero pairing, and zero q by (1809). This proves existence with explicit inclusion
and projection maps at every step.
    Conversely suppose such an L is given. For every v ∈ V , the sum over its original coset is

                                                                                                    (1822)
                                X                              X
                                      (−1)q(v+`) = (−1)q(v)     (−1)λ(v,`) .
                                `∈L                            `∈L

    If v ∈
         / L⊥ , choose `0 ∈ L with λ(v, `0 ) = 1. Pairing the term indexed by ` with the term
indexed by ` + `0 cancels that entire sum. If v ∈ L⊥ = L, every term is one because q|L = 0, so
the coset sum is 2g . Only the zero coset contributes to (1814). It follows that G(q) = 2g , hence
Arf(q) = 0 by (1816). This proves the reverse implication of (1819).

AF.4.2     Exact reduction and addition

Let U ⊂ V be any subspace with zero pairing and q|U = 0. Its dimension need not be g. For
v ∈ U ⊥ and u ∈ U , (1809) gives q(v + u) = q(v). Thus the actual quotient map

                                  p : U ⊥ −→ U ⊥ /U,           v 7−→ v + U                          (1823)

   defines a function q̄(v + U ) = q(v) and pairing λ̄(v + U, w + U ) = λ(v, w). Both are
independent of representatives because the original U is orthogonal to U ⊥ . The radical of λ|U ⊥


                                                      822
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                       Paper III


is U : nonsingularity gives (U ⊥ )⊥ = U by the same dimension argument used above. Therefore
the quotient pairing is nonsingular. If dim U = d, its dimension is 2g − 2d.
    Partition the Gauss sum into the original cosets of U . The cancellation in (1822), with U in
place of L, kills precisely the cosets outside U ⊥ . Each remaining coset contributes 2d (−1)q̄(v+U ) .
Hence the full equality, with its factor, is

                               G(q) = 2d G(q̄),         Arf(q) = Arf(q̄).                      (1824)
     The second equation follows by substituting the actual dimensions into (1816); the first is
the exact comparison that proves it.
     For two given spaces V1 , V2 with their functions, the orthogonal direct-sum function is
q1 (v1 ) + q2 (v2 ). Directly summing all ordered pairs gives

                 G(q1 ⊕ q2 ) = G(q1 )G(q2 ),      Arf(q1 ⊕ q2 ) = Arf(q1 ) + Arf(q2 ).         (1825)
   No isometry-class replacement is needed for either identity.
   On the original two-dimensional space with coordinates (α, β), the values q(e) = q(f ) = 1,
λ(e, f ) = 1 uniquely give

                                               (α, β) (0, 0) (1, 0) (0, 1) (1, 1)
                q(α, β) = α + β + αβ,                                                          (1826)
                                               q(α, β)     0      1      1      1
    by (1813). Its Gauss sum is 1 − 1 − 1 − 1 = −2, and its Arf invariant is one. These are the
exact algebraic values that match the three product embeddings calculated in section AF.3. A
proof that the geometric construction supplies (1809) on all of middle homology is required before
(1826) can be called the invariant of the framed product. That proof is given in section AF.5
and section AF.6.
    The algebraic definition (1817) is recorded in Victor P. Snaith, The Arf-Kervaire Invariant
of framed manifolds, arXiv:1001.4751v1, original author TeX lines 1218–1243, citing Cahit Arf,
Untersuchungen über quadratische Formen in Körpern der Charakteristik 2, J. Reine Angew.
Math. 183 (1941), 148–167. The complete arguments (1810)–(1826) above are supplied here.
The source’s geometric construction at lines 1265–1268 and surgery discussion at 1440–1488 are
bounded reading context: the asserted cohomotopy identification and geometric quadratic law in

                                    dfx (Tx S 3 ) + dfy (Ty S 3 ) = Tf (x) M.                             (1827)

    The order of the sheets changes an integral intersection sign in dimension three. The count
in (1828) is deliberately the count of unordered pairs modulo two; it does not assign an invariant
integer sign to such a pair.
    We prove that two homotopic self-transverse immersions have the same Qτ . The proof retains
both defects of a general homotopy, including the failure of its derivative to have rank three.

AF.5.2    A generic homotopy and its rank-two points

Let F : S 3 × [0, 1] → M be a smooth homotopy between the two immersions, constant in the
parameter near its ends. Write Ft (q) = F (q, t), and let Dv F be its derivative only in the three
sphere directions. We may perturb the homotopy relative to those end collars to have the
following properties:

  1. Dv F has rank at least two, and its rank-two points form a finite subset of the interior of
     S 3 × [0, 1].

  2. Its derivative section meets the rank-two matrix stratum transversely.

  3. Away from the diagonal, the simultaneous equation Ft (x) = Ft (y) is transverse; there are
     no triple points for any t.

    Here is the relative perturbation argument in the dimensions at issue. In a coordinate chart,
the space of six-by-three matrices of rank r has codimension (6 − r)(3 − r). For r = 2 this is four,
equal to the dimension of S 3 × [0, 1]; for r ≤ 1 it is at least ten. The first-jet perturbations are
                                                                                
                                                               3
                                                                                              (1833)
                                                               X
                        F (q, t) 7−→ F (q, t) + χ(q, t) a +         bj (qj − qj0 )
                                                               j=1

    in a target chart, with a, bj ∈ R6 . On the smaller chart where χ = 1, their value and vertical
derivative parameters are independent. The parameterized section is therefore a submersion to
the first-jet fibres. Apply Sard to its inverse image of each rank stratum. In pairs of disjoint
domain charts at the same parameter, use independent value parameters a; the difference of the
two target values is then a submersion. The pair domain has dimension seven and the equality
has codimension six, so its transverse locus is one-dimensional. Three distinct domain points
have parameter-domain dimension ten and two target equalities of total codimension twelve,
hence have empty coincidence locus after transverse perturbation. Cutoffs vanish on the end
collars.
    These constructions are relative versions of the finite chart perturbations proved in the
included Whitney and complement companions. For completeness, the noncompact part of
the distinct-point domains causes no new assumption: exhaust it by compact sets on which
all point separations are at least 1/n. Make the successive parameter choices transverse on
the n-th compact set and small enough in each of the first n derivative norms to preserve
every earlier transverse compact set. Choose the bound at step n smaller than 2−n times those
positive tolerances. The resulting smooth limit has all the required transversality properties.
Alternatively a single sufficiently small choice handles the compact complement of the local
diagonal neighbourhoods described below. The rank-two points are isolated in a compact set
away from the end collars and thus finite. The argument below also proves the required control
near the diagonal.

    At a rank-two point choose local coordinates and two independent columns of Dv F . A smooth
invertible target change sends these columns to the first two coordinate vectors. Subtract their
components from the third column. In these coordinates the derivative has the exact block form
                                              

                          Dr : R3x ⊕ Rt −→ R4        is invertible at the zero.                 (1835)

AF.5.3    The exact local framing contribution

Identify the last four coordinates in (1834), in their displayed order, with H, and set a = r/|r|.
The first three derivative columns in (1834) are lifted to a complete positive frame by

                                  diag(I2 , La ) diag(1, 1, |r|, 1, 1, 1).                      (1837)

    The third column is exactly r, since the first column of La is a. The other three quaternion
columns give an actual normal complement. Replacing the positive entry |r| by (1 − u)|r| + u,
0 ≤ u ≤ 1, is a homotopy through positive matrices, so it contributes zero to π3 . The stable class
of (1837) is therefore σ, using the original generator Lq of section AF.1 and the actual degree
(1836).
    Every row or column comparison made in (1834) extends over the four-ball. Its boundary
map consequently has zero π3 class. The coordinate trivialization of T M , its comparison with
the specified τ , the original tangent frame on the parameter sphere, and the appended stable
directions also extend over this ball. They therefore change neither the local class nor its parity.
An arbitrary other positive normal frame changes the stable integer by 2n, with n ∈ Z, exactly
as in (1790). The full local statement is thus

                            [G∂D4 ] = σ + 2n,         [G∂D4 ] ≡ 1     (mod 2).                  (1838)

     This is a calculation of the actual derivative defect. It does not assume a classification of
immersions by a derivative invariant.
     Remove disjoint small open four-balls around all the rank-two points and call the remaining
parameter manifold P . The vertical normal bundle of F on P is an oriented rank-three bundle.
It is trivial. To see this, S 3 × [0, 1] is a four-sphere with two open balls removed; after the further
removals, its interior has the homotopy type of R4 minus finitely many points. Shrinking each
removed coordinate ball to its centre and retracting its collar gives this homotopy equivalence.

                                                   826
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                    Paper III


Joining small spheres around those points by disjoint arcs gives a CW model consisting of a tree
and one three-sphere for each point, hence a wedge of three-spheres. An oriented rank-three
bundle on each three-sphere has a clutching map S 2 → SO(3), which is nullhomotopic by (1769);
over the joining tree its frames can be matched by paths in SO(3). This constructs a frame on P .
    Use such a frame to define G : P → GL+ (6 + s, R) by (1829). The oriented boundary relation

AF.5.4    Compactifying the unordered double points

The double-point locus away from the diagonal is a smooth one-manifold by property 3. We now
compute all its possible ends on the diagonal, rather than discard those ends.
   In a coordinate chart of S 3 , write an ordered nearby pair as

                      x− = x − ρ2 u,       x+ = x + ρ2 u,          |u| = 1,      ρ > 0.     (1842)
    For unordered pairs u and −u are identified, so the boundary direction belongs to RP2 . Use
a local choice of u to describe that quotient. In a common target chart the divided difference is


                                           Ft (x + ρu/2) − Ft (x − ρu/2)
                          Ψ(x, u, ρ, t) =
                                                          ρ
                                           Z 1/2                                            (1843)
                                         =       Dv Ft (x + ρau) u da.
                                             −1/2

   The second line proves smooth extension to ρ = 0, where

                                       Ψ(x, u, 0, t) = Dv Ft (x)u.                          (1844)
    Changing u to −u multiplies (1843) by −1; its zero set therefore descends to the unordered
quotient.
    At a boundary zero, u spans the one-dimensional kernel of a rank-two derivative. The
derivative of (1844) in the two local projective-direction variables maps isomorphically onto the

                                                    827
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                  Paper III


two-dimensional image of that derivative. Modulo this image, its derivative in (x, t) is the map
(1835), up to the nonzero scalar specifying the chosen unit kernel vector. It is an isomorphism
onto the four-dimensional cokernel. Consequently the full derivative

                                 D(x,[u],t) Ψ : R3 ⊕ R2 ⊕ R −→ R6                          (1845)

    is invertible. The implicit function theorem then makes the zero set near this point a single
smooth half-interval parametrized by ρ ≥ 0. Thus each rank-two point supplies exactly one end
of the unordered double-point curve. If Dv F has rank three there is no boundary zero at all.
    The space of unordered pairs can be compactified by precisely these direction charts and
the ordinary charts away from the diagonal. This can also be constructed by taking the real
radial blow-up of the diagonal and then the free exchange involution; the explicit coordinates
(1842)–(1844) specify the construction used here. Since S 3 × S 3 × [0, 1] is compact and the
direction fibres are compact, this compactification is compact. Its closed zero locus is a compact
smooth one-manifold. Its boundary consists of the double points of F0 , the double points of F1 ,
and the one end for each of the c rank-two points. No triple-point end occurs by property 3.
Critical points of the time function on the double-point curve are interior points of that curve
and contribute no boundary.
    A compact one-manifold is a finite disjoint union of circles and intervals: follow a nonzero
tangent field in each coordinate interval and use compactness to obtain either a circle or an
interval ending at boundary; a finite coordinate cover excludes infinitely many components. Each
interval has two boundary points. Counting the entire boundary modulo two therefore gives

                                  µ(F1 ) + µ(F0 ) = c (mod 2).                             (1846)

   This counts both defects in the same homotopy. Equations (1841) and (1846) prove

                                         Qτ (F1 ) = Qτ (F0 ).                              (1847)

AF.5.6    The resulting homotopy-class function

Every smooth map S 3 → M 6 can be perturbed to a self-transverse immersion without triple
points. The single-map rank-two codimension is four, greater than the three-dimensional domain,
so it has no rank-two points; the distinct-pair dimension is six, and the triple-point dimension is
nine against codimension twelve. The same chart perturbations and compact diagonal control
used above prove the assertion. A sufficiently small perturbation is homotopic to the original
map by its short target-chart paths, or by a metric exponential on a finite compact cover.
    It follows from (1847) that

                          Qτ : [S 3 , M ] −→ F2 ,         [f ] 7−→ ετ (fe) + µ(fe)           (1854)

    is well-defined, where fe is any such perturbed representative. The brackets here denote
unbased homotopy classes. For an actual embedding it equals exactly (1788). The constant
homotopy class has value zero: use the embedded small coordinate sphere of section AF.3.1,
which bounds its coordinate four-disc, has no double points and has the calculated k = 0. In
particular every nullhomotopic embedded three-sphere has framing parity zero.
    If M is two-connected, the included first-Hurewicz comparison identifies its π3 with H3 (M ; Z).
Its simple connectedness removes the basepath ambiguity between based and unbased classes.
Thus (1854) already defines a function on the original integral middle homology, and its value
on an embedded representative is independent of that representative and of its parametrization
whenever the oriented homology class is unchanged. The quadratic addition formula and passage
to coefficients in F2 require the next calculation; no such formula was assumed in proving (1854).

AF.6     The geometric quadratic law on the original middle homology
Assume throughout this section that M is closed, oriented, two-connected and six-dimensional,
with the specified stable frame τ . Write its original integral intersection form as


                                                    829

                               λZ : H3 (M ; Z) × H3 (M ; Z) −→ Z.                           (1855)

AF.6.1    Joining two immersed representatives

Choose self-transverse immersions f, g : S 3 → M , mutually transverse and with no triple points
in their union. The chart perturbations in section AF.5 give these simultaneous properties.
Choose one regular image point on each sphere which is neither a self-double point nor a point
on the other sphere. Join them by an embedded arc whose interior avoids both immersed images.
Such an arc exists: start with any path in the connected M , smooth it relative to its end collars,
then perturb it. The avoidance dimension is 1 + 3 < 6, and the pair-coincidence dimension for
the arc is 2 < 6. The relative value perturbations therefore make it embedded and disjoint from
the two images in its interior.
    Remove small embedded three-discs at its two ends and join their two-sphere boundaries by
a thin tube along the arc. An actual choice of this tube is obtained from a three-frame in the
rank-five normal bundle of the arc. Choose the required end frames in the original image charts
and extend along the interval: a rank-five oriented frame bundle over an interval is trivial, and
ordered orthonormal three-frames in R5 form a connected space, since they extend to positive
five-frames and SO(5) is connected. A tubular chart sends the sphere of radius ρ > 0 in those
three normal directions to the tube Sρ2 × [0, 1]. Take the radius small enough that this chart is
injective and its interior misses both compact immersed images outside the specified end discs.
Near the ends use the original disc charts to round the joins. Their radial derivatives have the
required nonzero signs, so the inverse-function and compact separation argument used for the
included handle tubes supplies a uniform smaller radius and no extra intersections.
    This produces an immersion f #g : S 3 → M representing the original sum of the two π3
classes. To verify that class, collapse the joining neck to its core arc and the two attaching
two-spheres to points. The resulting map is the oriented pinch map to the wedge of the two
original spheres, with the joining basepath retained. Simple connectedness makes its basepath
action trivial. Under Hurewicz its class is therefore x + y, where x = f∗ [S 3 ] and y = g∗ [S 3 ].
    No double point is created on the thin tube. Thus the integer counts of unordered self-double
points obey

                               N (f #g) = N (f ) + N (g) + N (f, g),                        (1856)

   where N (f, g) counts the intersection pairs with one preimage on each sphere. The signed
count in the fixed order f, g is exactly

                                                                sgn(dfa , dgb ).            (1857)

AF.6.3    Descent with every integral comparison retained

Let Qτ,Z be the function on H3 (M ; Z) constructed in (1854). Combining (1858) and (1859),
while retaining the actual sum representative, proves

                       Qτ,Z (x + y) = Qτ,Z (x) + Qτ,Z (y) + λZ (x, y) (mod 2).                   (1870)

    This is now a proved geometric quadratic identity.

full universal coefficient sequence give

that H3 (M ; Z) is free and that (1855) is unimodular. Interchanging the two degree-three cycles

AF.7    Embedded representatives and the exact surgery criterion on classes
We prove that every original integral middle-homology class of a simply connected six-manifold
can be represented by an embedded three-sphere whenever it is represented by a map of a
three-sphere. For the two-connected M in section AF.6 every class has such a map by the proved
Hurewicz comparison. This assertion does not require assuming that an arbitrary immersion has
an even double-point count.
    First retain the explicit Whitney immersion

                    W : S 3 ⊂ R ⊕ R3 −→ R3 ⊕ R3 ,          W (x0 , x) = (x, x0 x).          (1880)

   Its derivative on a tangent vector (v0 , v), where x0 v0 + x · v = 0, is

                                   dW (v0 , v) = (v, v0 x + x0 v).                          (1881)

    If this is zero then v = 0. If x 6= 0 the second component forces v0 = 0; if x = 0 then x0 = ±1
and the tangent constraint forces v0 = 0. Thus (1880) is an immersion everywhere. Equal first
components give the same x. The sphere equation then allows only equal x0 , or opposite x0 . In
the latter case, equality of the second components forces x0 x = 0. Distinct points therefore occur
exactly at

                                         (1, 0),    (−1, 0).                                (1882)

   In the two local coordinate charts using x, the two image tangent maps are v 7→ (v, v) and
 7 (v, −v). The full concatenated determinant is
v→
                                        
                                  I3 I3
                             det           = det(−2I3 ) = −8 6= 0.                          (1883)
                                  I3 −I3
    These two x-charts have opposite induced orientations on the boundary sphere. If both source
charts are required positive, reverse the first coordinate in the south chart, and the ordered
intersection determinant becomes +8. Both values and their coordinate conventions are specified
here; the unordered double count is one.
    Translate and positively scale (1880) into any chosen framed coordinate ball. Its homotopy
class there is zero. Equations (1847), (1854), and (1795) consequently give

                          Qτ (W ) = 0,       µ(W ) = 1,        ετ (W ) = 1.                 (1884)

    This proves its framing parity through the already established homotopy comparison,
independently of any classification of regular homotopy classes.
    Now perturb the chosen map representing a given class to a self-transverse immersion f . If it
has an odd number of double points, take its connected sum with a small copy of (1880) in a
coordinate ball disjoint from its image, using a thin joining arc as in section AF.6.1. The ball
exists because a finite union of immersed three-dimensional chart images has empty interior in
a six-manifold. This operation leaves the homotopy class unchanged and changes the integer
double count by exactly one, by (1856), with no intersection between the original image and that


                                                   834
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                      Paper III


local copy. It also changes ε by one by (1859) and (1884), so it preserves the already defined Qτ .
The resulting immersion has an even number of double points.
    Pair those double points. For each pair, label its two local sheets so that the two ordered
intersection signs are opposite. This is possible because interchanging two three-dimensional
sheets multiplies the sign by (−1)9 = −1. Join the corresponding two pairs of domain preimages
by disjoint arcs in S 3 , avoiding every other double-point preimage. Their image interiors are
disjoint embedded arcs: away from the finite preimage set the immersion is one-to-one, and the
two arcs can be chosen disjoint by general position in the three-dimensional domain. These arcs
form a Whitney circle in M .
    The circle is nullhomotopic since M is simply connected. Construct its corner collars in the
two original sheet charts and fill its inner curve by a disc. Relative perturbation makes this disc
embedded and makes its interior disjoint from the entire immersed image and from its fixed
collar. The precise dimension inequalities are


       2 + 3 < 6,      2 + 2 < 6,      codim(rank 1 in six-by-two matrices) = 5 > 2.           (1885)

    To apply the perturbation to the full immersed image, use its finitely many domain charts,
including both charts at each double point; the same value parameters give transversality to each
of these sheet images. Negative inverse-image dimension gives avoidance of every sheet. The
original prescribed collar is untouched.
    The rank-four adapted-frame construction and the supported Whitney move are proved in
section R.2 and section R.3 and section R.4 and section R.5, for the dimension pair (3, 3) in a
six-dimensional level. That proof is local to the two chosen sheets, their arcs and the disjoint
disc interior. It does not require the sheets to lie on different connected components. Apply its
full frame correction, its actual sheet-coordinate comparison and its supported move here. The
move removes exactly the chosen two opposite-sign double points and creates none, since its
support meets the image only in those prescribed sheets. It is a regular homotopy on the domain
patches; its effect on all remaining domain points is fixed.
    Iteration removes all double points, since their finite number drops by two at each step. The
resulting immersion is injective; a smooth injective immersion from compact S 3 into a Hausdorff
manifold is an embedding. It represents the original homotopy class, as every preceding operation
was a homotopy of maps. This proves the claimed embedded-representative theorem with the
odd-count case included.
    For the two-connected framed M , every integral lift x of a ∈ H3 (M ; F2 ) therefore has an
embedded representative. For every such representative the original handle-extension criterion is
exactly


   qτ (a) = 0   ⇐⇒ some actual oriented normal framing of that embedded sphere
                   extends the specified stable frame across its D4 × D3 surgery handle.
                                                                                     (1886)

   The proof is the equality in the second line of (1876) followed by both directions of the extension
construction in section AF.2. No representative-dependent assumption remains. Formula (1886)
does not yet say that several chosen spheres can be made disjoint or that a resulting bordism
has a prescribed homology; those are further geometric calculations.

AF.8     Framed bordism invariance
We first prove the change across an actual stage of index-three handles, then reduce an arbitrary
framed bordism between two-connected six-manifolds to two such stages. The reduction needs

                                                 835
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                             Paper III


vanishing in relative degree two, not an assumption that the whole bordism is a homology
equivalence.

AF.8.1     A complete index-three stage

Let T be the trace obtained from M × [0, 1], with M as in section AF.6, by attaching r handles
Da3j × Db4j of index three. Retain every radius aj , bj > 0, attaching map and original orientation.
Suppose T has its specified stable framing extending that on M . Write its outgoing boundary as
P with its induced frame. The sphere-attaching maps have domain Sa2j . Since M is two-connected
they are nullhomotopic.
    The pair (T, M ) has a relative CW model with precisely r cells of dimension three, and the
reversed pair (T, P ) has precisely r cells of dimension four. These are the original core and
cocore models from the handle-chain companion. The first description gives π1 T = π2 T = 0;
the second shows that P → T induces isomorphisms on π1 , π2 . In the latter claim the relative
groups through degree three vanish because all relative cells have dimension four. Thus P is also
two-connected, and section AF.6 applies to it.
    Put H = H3 (M ; Z), K = H3 (T ; Z), and V = H3 (P ; Z). The complete relevant integral
sequences are

description. All these are the original relative homology groups, with the indicated zero terms
accounted for. Both sequences split as sequences of abelian groups because their right-hand

AF.8.2     Making the interior two-connected with the stable frame retained

Let C 7 be a compact framed bordism from two-connected closed M 6 to two-connected closed N 6 .
We may make its interior connected without changing its boundary. In the eight-dimensional
product trace, attach an index-one handle along two seven-discs in distinct components of the
upper interior face, away from the original boundary. Its new upper face is obtained by removing
those two seven-balls and joining their six-spheres by a tube. The frame on each small attaching
disc is homotopic to its centre value by contraction, with that homotopy implemented in its
collar. The two centre frames join by a path in the appropriate connected component of invertible
matrices; the orientations of the two attaching feet fix that component. Extend over the product



                                                    837
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                       Paper III


one-handle, then restore the full prescribed disc frames using those collar homotopies. This gives
the new upper face its stable frame and leaves both original boundary framings fixed.
    Next make π1 C and π2 C zero by framed surgeries in the interior. Here are the exact existence
and extension arguments. A finite handle CW model gives finitely many generators of π1 C.
Represent them by disjoint embedded loops: the coincidence and avoidance dimensions for finitely
many curves are at most two, less than seven. Their actual oriented normal bundles have rank
six and are trivial because an oriented bundle on S 1 is obtained by identifying its end frames by
an element of the connected SO(6).
    For a surgery on an embedded S k ⊂ C 7 , k = 1, 2, compare the original stable frame on the
attaching region with the parameter frame on Dk+1 × D7−k . The comparison is the same full
radial splitting as (1784)–(1785), with z ∈ Rk+1 , radial component hq, zi, and last coordinate
−hq, zi. Its extension obstruction is in πk SO(8 + s). Changing the actual normal frame changes
it by the inclusion from πk SO(7 − k), by the product calculation of (1789). This is the same
extension-over-the-core argument used in section AF.2, with the original dimensions displayed.
    For k = 1, the map

                                     π1 SO(6) −→ π1 SO(8 + s)                                  (1894)

    is an isomorphism. Each successive sphere bundle SO(j) → SO(j + 1) → S j , j ≥ 6, has
zero adjacent sphere groups in degrees one and two, so its exact sequence proves this statement.
Choose the normal-frame class which cancels the obstruction. The resulting framed surgery
trace attaches an index-two handle in dimension eight; seen from the outgoing seven-manifold
its dual handle has index six. Attaching the original two-handles kills the normal closure of the
chosen loop generators in π1 , and the outgoing inclusion preserves π1 , since its relative cells have
dimension six. Thus the new interior is simply connected.
    Its π2 is finitely generated: Hurewicz identifies it with the finitely generated H2 of the compact
manifold. Represent a finite set of generators by disjoint embedded two-spheres in the interior.
The derivative rank-loss codimension exceeds two, the self-coincidence dimension is four, and
4 < 7; the same relative chart perturbation gives the embeddings and mutual disjointness.
    Their oriented normal bundles have rank five. The stable frame of T C, together with the
actual radial trivialization T S 2 ⊕ R ∼ = R3 , makes each normal bundle stably trivial. Its clutching
class is in π1 SO(5); its stabilization is injective by the sphere-bundle argument just given, starting
at j = 5. Hence the original clutching class is zero and the original rank-five bundle is trivial.
For k = 2, the remaining handle obstruction is zero because

                                          π2 SO(8 + s) = 0.                                    (1895)

    This follows from the covers of SO(3), SO(4), SO(5) in section AF.1 and the successive sphere
bundles; all their relevant degree-two groups vanish.
    Attach the resulting framed index-three traces in dimension eight. Their outgoing dual

AF.8.3    Only indices three and four are needed

Take a finite relative Morse presentation of C 0 , with its actual incoming and outgoing collars.
The included zero/top removal applies because C 0 and both boundaries are connected. The
included index-one removal applies because C 0 and both boundaries are simply connected; its
proof explicitly assumes only those fundamental-group conditions. Apply it also to the reversed
cobordism. This gives precisely the index range 2, 3, 4, 5.
    The long exact sequences of the two original pairs give

                            H2 (C 0 , M ; Z) = 0,         H2 (C 0 , N ; Z) = 0,              (1896)

    since H2 (C 0 ) = 0 and H1 (M ) = H1 (N ) = 0. After index-one removal the relative degree-two
chain group has zero outgoing differential. The first equality in (1896) therefore says that its

basis change. The higher-handle-slide companion realizes this change by the full original framed
slides.
    Use the included Whitney construction with sheet dimensions (2, 4) in the six-dimensional
regular level. The lower level is the original simply connected M . It removes opposite-sign
intersection pairs and turns the displayed incidence coefficients into exactly one or zero geometric
intersections. section U.2 and section U.3 and section U.4 and section U.5 of Actual Morse data
for the modified framed handles realize that presentation by actual Morse data, identify every

    This derivation checks the precise hypotheses of the existing cancellation proofs. It uses no

   for every framed bordism between the stated two-connected six-manifolds.

AF.8.4    The homomorphism on the entire framed bordism group

Every class in Ωfr
                6 has a two-connected representative. Join its finitely many connected components
by framed index-one traces. Kill a finite set of loop generators by interior one-sphere surgery in
dimension six, using rank-five normal bundles and the isomorphism π1 SO(5) → π1 SO(7 + s).
After simple connectedness, kill finitely many π2 generators by two-sphere surgery. These spheres


                                                    839
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                    Paper III


can be made disjoint and embedded since 2 + 2 < 6. Their rank-four normal bundles are trivial:
stable triviality kills their clutching class because π1 SO(4) → π1 SO(7 + s) is an isomorphism,
using the covers and sphere bundles of section AF.1. Their frame-extension obstruction is
π2 SO(7 + s) = 0.
    The traces now have dimension seven. The two-sphere surgery attaches index-three handles,
and its outgoing dual handles have index four; their relative cells preserve π1 , π2 at the outgoing
end. The one-sphere surgery has dual index five and preserves π1 there. These exact cell
comparisons prove the claimed effect on the homotopy groups. Thus the result is two-connected
and framed bordant to the given manifold.
    Define its value to be the Arf invariant of (1875) on any such representative. If two choices
represent the same framed bordism class, a framed bordism between them exists by the definition
of that group, and (1898) proves their values equal. This is a well-defined function

                                           κ : Ωfr
                                                6 −→ F2 .                                    (1899)

    For addition, take two two-connected representatives and connect their disjoint union by
the same framed one-handle trace. The resulting connected sum has middle homology the
direct sum of their original middle groups: apply the Mayer–Vietoris sequence across the joining
five-sphere, whose homology in degrees two and three is zero. The ordered intersection pairing is
the orthogonal sum, since cycles in the two punctured summands are disjoint. Every such class
has a representative in its punctured summand, and (1876) proves that its quadratic value is
its original value. The full quadratic function is therefore the orthogonal sum. Equation (1825)
proves additivity of (1899).
    The zero class has the standard framed S 6 = ∂D7 as a representative and has zero middle
homology. Its value is zero. Reversing an oriented representative reverses its integral pairing and
its orientation data, but the corresponding constant target and normal-coordinate reflections in
(1785) preserve the based parity by the stable conjugation proof following (1831). Modulo two
the reversed pairing equals the original pairing. Thus its value is unchanged, as required for a
homomorphism to F2 . These arguments establish (1899) on the whole original framed bordism
group, not only on a collection of chosen two-connected representatives.

AG.3     Integral Lagrangians and a finite sequence of the actual twists
Let H be a free integral group of rank 2r, with a unimodular alternating pairing λ. A primitive
subgroup L means that H/L is torsion-free. An integral Lagrangian is a primitive rank-r
subgroup on which λ vanishes. We prove that a finite product of the transvections (1937) carries
any such L to any specified integral Lagrangian. All changes below are actual automorphisms of
H; the original group and pairing remain fixed.

AH.1     The actual smooth recognition
The homotopy equivalence of Paper I, Theorem I.1 identifies a smooth homotopy six-sphere. The
smooth statement uses two classical results: the simply connected smooth h-cobordism theorem
and the vanishing of the group Θ6 of oriented smooth homotopy six-spheres. The section AG.7
now constructs the new interior gluing with its full frame defect, cancels every actual handle
and gives the orientation-preserving diffeomorphism to the original six-sphere, homotopic to its
original degree-one map. We first construct the precise cobordism to which the smooth theorem
applies.
    An h-cobordism from a closed manifold M0 to M1 is a compact smooth manifold C with
∂C = M0 q M1 for which both inclusions Mi ,→ C are homotopy equivalences. It comes with its
actual boundary inclusions.
Proposition AH.1. Choose two disjoint orientation-preserving coordinate closed discs D0 , D1 ⊂
X. Then

                                     C = X \ (int D0 ∪ int D1 )                               (2005)
   is a simply connected smooth six-dimensional h-cobordism between its two boundary five-
spheres.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (2006); equation (2007).

Proof. Coordinate discs have collars, so (2005) is a compact smooth manifold with the indicated
boundary. It is connected: any path between points outside the discs can be perturbed to meet
the boundary spheres transversely in finitely many points, and each portion passing through a
disc can be replaced by a path in its connected boundary sphere. Van Kampen, applied when
adding the two discs back along collars of S 5 , identifies π1 (C) with π1 (X). The discs and the
collar spheres are simply connected. Thus π1 (C) = 0.
    Excision gives
                                                                      (
                                                                       Z2 , k = 6,
               Hk (X, C; Z) = Hk (D0 , ∂D0 ; Z) ⊕ Hk (D1 , ∂D1 ; Z) =                         (2006)
                                                                       0,   k 6= 6.
    Here each summand is computed by the relative cell of the disc; its positive generator is its
local orientation class. The fundamental class of X maps to (1, 1), since both chosen coordinate
discs preserve the orientation. The long exact sequence of the pair and Paper I, Corollary E.19
consequently give

            H6 (C) = 0,       H5 (C) = Z2 /Z(1, 1) ≃ Z,      Hk (C) = 0    (1 ≤ k ≤ 4).       (2007)
    The relative boundary homomorphism sends the first and second standard generators in
(2006) to their actual boundary sphere classes in C. In the quotient in (2007) these are opposite
generators. Thus each inclusion ∂Di ,→ C induces an isomorphism on H5 , and also on H0 ; all
other homology groups on both sides vanish.
     Both spaces are simply connected. The included Paper I, Subsection G.2 proves their CW
homotopy type: its formula Paper I, Equation 124 treats the actual punctured cobordism, keeping

AH.2.2     Exercise 11.2. Recovering the normalization groups over the integers

For the constant-sheaf normalization complex, compute the entire cohomology of its degree-zero
global row

                                                                                                (2019)
                         0      D
                       → Z3 −
                      Z−    → Z2 ,            D(a, b, c) = (a − b + c, a − b + c).

   Do the corresponding calculation for the degree-two row displayed in (2020).
   Solution. The first group survives as Z. The kernel of D has basis (1, 1, 0), (−1, 0, 1): the
equation gives a = b − c, and these two coordinates realize every solution uniquely. Thus its
degree-one cohomology is Z2 . The image is the full diagonal subgroup, because D(1, 0, 0) = (1, 1).

                                (s, −s, s),       s = b1 + b2 + b3 − a.                         (2020)

                                     (x, y, z) 7−→ (x + y, z + y).                              (2021)

distinct total degrees gives the ranks 1, 2, 4, 2, 1 of H ∗ (W ; Z). The spectral-sequence filtration
cannot introduce torsion: each successive quotient is free, and a short exact sequence with free
quotient splits by lifting a basis.

AH.2.3     Exercise 11.3. Reversing the base orientation without losing a sign

Retain the original classes θ = 12γ, a = 2q, b = 2γuw, but write the base generator as ω 0 = −ω.
Determine all three differentials in that basis by the product equations.
   Solution. The first differential is d2 θ = −ω 0 . Write d2 a = r0 ω 0 [δ] and d2 b = s0 ω 0 [γδ]. The
unchanged identity θa = 12b, with |θ| = 1, gives

                                12s0 = −24 − 12r0 ,       s0 = −2 − r0 .                        (2022)

   The unchanged identity ab = 0 and the original exterior signs δb = −2 vol, aγδ = 2 vol give

                                              −2r0 + 2s0 = 0.                                   (2023)

   Thus r0 = s0 = −1. All three coefficients change sign together. Their absolute values remain
one, so all three maps remain integral isomorphisms onto their targets. This calculation also shows
why reversing only the first sign while keeping the other two would violate the multiplicative
spectral sequence.

AH.2.4     Exercise 11.4. Why the Euler characteristic does not close the calculation

Produce a closed simply connected oriented six-manifold with Euler characteristic two but with
nonzero second and third integral homology. Compute those groups and compare the precise
missing information with Paper I, Corollary E.19.
   Solution. Take

                                   M = (S 2 × S 4 ) # (S 3 × S 3 ).                            (2024)
   Each product is simply connected. Removing a coordinate disc does not change its fundamental
group: adding it back uses a simply connected S 5 collar, so Van Kampen identifies the two groups.
Gluing the punctured products along that same simply connected collar shows π1 (M ) = 0.
   For 1 ≤ k ≤ 4, removal of a disc preserves Hk by the pair sequence and excision, whose only
nonzero relative group is in degree six. The Mayer–Vietoris sequence for the connected sum
has overlap S 5 , with zero homology in degrees one through four; its degree-zero maps also show
connectedness. It follows that

                         H2 (M ) = Z,      H3 (M ) = Z2 ,       H4 (M ) = Z.                   (2025)
   The product groups here follow from their product cells: S 2 × S 4 has cells in degrees 0, 2, 4, 6,
and S 3 × S 3 has cells in degrees 0, 3, 3, 6, with zero cellular boundaries. Orientation and Poincaré
duality give H6 (M ) = Z, H5 (M ) = H 1 (M ) = 0; the remaining groups are as stated. Therefore

                                  χ(M ) = 1 + 1 − 2 + 1 + 1 = 2.                               (2026)
   Its nonzero H2 and H3 prevent it from being a homology sphere. In the original X, it is
the three primitive integral transgressions, the two parabolic vanishing calculations and the
universal-coefficient argument that remove those groups and their possible torsion. The matching
Euler characteristic alone supplies none of these maps.


AI     Almost complex structures, octonions, and integrability
The following complete arguments are retained as re-derivations of their classical prerequisites.
Source-specific calculations and their hypotheses are stated explicitly.
    The precise algebra convention is compared with Baez, Section 2.2 Baez (2002); the coordinate
factorization is compared with Hill–Taylor, Sections 2–4, in the author version of 8 November
2007 Hill and Taylor (2007). Smooth integrability is the classical theorem of Newlander and
Nirenberg; the statement is cited here in Onishchik’s Russian translation, Theorem 1.1, p. 133
Newlander and Nirenberg (1959). The full analytic argument and its sign correction are supplied
below.
    The construction in this course gives complex coordinate charts on a compact six-dimensional
manifold. The standard octonion construction gives an endomorphism of the tangent bundle of
the round six-sphere. To compare these objects, we need the exact map from coordinate charts
to a tangent-bundle endomorphism and the exact obstruction to reversing that map. We develop
those maps first. We then calculate the obstruction for the octonion field, including its relation
to the associator and all constants in its norm.
    The multiplication formulas below are compared directly with John Baez, The Octonions,
Section 2.2. The sphere background is treated by Panagiotis Konstantis and Maurizio Parton,
Almost complex structures on spheres. The later coordinate construction follows the factorization
of Malgrange as developed in C. Denson Hill and Michael Taylor, Integrability of Rough Almost
Complex Structures, Sections 2–4. We keep their matrix conventions when comparing formulas
and identify the sign correction needed in their equation 3.14.

                                                 869
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                       Paper III


AI.1    From charts to a tensor, and from a tensor to a differential equation
Let M be a smooth real manifold of dimension 2n. An almost complex structure is a smooth
real bundle endomorphism

                               J : T M −→ T M,             J 2 = − idT M .                      (2027)

    It makes each real tangent space a complex vector space by (a + ib)v = av + bJv. The
coefficients a, b are real, and the relation J 2 = −1 verifies multiplication by two complex scalars.
Conversely multiplication by i in a complex vector-bundle structure on T M satisfies (2027).
These two operations are inverse.
    If z : U → Cn is a complex coordinate chart, let I denote multiplication by i on the real
tangent spaces of Cn , and set

                                         J|U = (Dz)−1 I(Dz).                                    (2028)

    For overlapping holomorphic charts z, w, their transition derivative satisfies D(w ◦ z −1 )I =
ID(w ◦ z −1 ), so (2028) agrees on the overlap. A complex atlas therefore defines an almost
complex structure. A structure obtained in this way is called integrable.
    The inverse problem asks for a local map F : U → Cn , with invertible real differential,
satisfying

                                           dF ◦ J = i dF.                                       (2029)

    Such maps are precisely the required complex coordinate charts: the real inverse-function
theorem makes them charts, and the chain rule makes their transition maps satisfy the ordinary
Cauchy–Riemann equations. For completeness, a C 1 map between open subsets of Cn whose
differential is complex-linear is holomorphic. On a closed polydisc in its domain, each component
is holomorphic in one variable with the others fixed, by the one-variable Cauchy–Riemann
theorem. Apply the one-variable Cauchy integral formula in each variable successively. The
resulting product Cauchy integral has a convergent multivariable power series on every smaller
polydisc, and equals the original component. Thus the transitions are holomorphic in the atlas
sense.
    Complexify the real tangent bundle and extend J complex-linearly. Define

                          TJ1,0 M = ker(J − i),           TJ0,1 M = ker(J + i),
                                                                                                (2030)
                             π 1,0 = 12 (1 − iJ),         π 0,1 = 12 (1 + iJ).

   Multiplication of these operators gives (π 1,0 )2 = π 1,0 , (π 0,1 )2 = π 0,1 , π 1,0 π 0,1 = 0, and
π 1,0 + π 0,1 = 1. Complex conjugation interchanges their images. In particular both eigenbundles
have complex rank n.
   The Nijenhuis tensor used throughout this lesson is

                     NJ (X, Y ) = [JX, JY ] − [X, Y ] − J[JX, Y ] − J[X, JY ].                  (2031)

    Its sign is the negative of the convention in Hill–Taylor equation 1.2. Write NHT = −NJ
when comparing those sources. Their zero conditions agree because multiplication by −1 is an
invertible bundle map.
    We verify that (2031) is a tensor rather than an operator depending on the chosen extensions
of tangent vectors. Inserting f X for X, the four extra derivative terms, in their displayed order,
are



                                                    870
Sphere maps and manifold constructions                                                      Paper III




                         −(JY f )JX,     (Y f )X,    −(Y f )X,     (JY f )JX.                  (2032)

    They sum to zero. Thus NJ (f X, Y ) = f NJ (X, Y ). Skewness in X, Y gives linearity in the
second argument as well. Substituting JX or JY in (2031) and using J 2 = −1 also gives

                            NJ (JX, Y ) = NJ (X, JY ) = −JNJ (X, Y ).                          (2033)

     These identities include the exact real-to-complex type information. For sections Z, W of
TJ0,1 M , complex bilinearity and JZ = −iZ give

                       NJ (Z, W ) = −2[Z, W ] + 2iJ[Z, W ] = −4π 1,0 [Z, W ].                  (2034)

   For two sections of TJ1,0 M the corresponding formula is −4π 0,1 [Z, W ]. For one section of each
type all four terms in (2031) cancel. Consequently

                      NJ = 0     ⇐⇒      [Γ(TJ0,1 M ), Γ(TJ0,1 M )] ⊆ Γ(TJ0,1 M ).             (2035)

    The right side is involutivity. In complex coordinates the fields ∂/∂ z̄j span this bundle
and commute; the bracket formula for their smooth linear combinations proves involutivity.
Equations (2034)–(2035) prove that every integrable J has NJ = 0.
    There is a useful scalar version of the same obstruction. Let ∂¯J f be the (0, 1) part of df , and
on forms define ∂¯J to be the (p, q + 1) component of the exterior derivative of a (p, q) form. For
Z, W of type (0, 1), the definition of exterior derivative gives

                       (∂¯J2 f )(Z, W ) = Z(W f ) − W (Zf ) − (∂¯J f )([Z, W ])
                                                                                               (2036)
                                        = df π 1,0 [Z, W ] = − 14 df NJ (Z, W ) .
                                                                              

   Thus the obstruction is both a bundle map and the failure of this first-order operator to
square to zero on functions. All factors in their comparison are explicit.

AI.3      The round six-sphere and its complete Nijenhuis tensor

                    S 6 = {p ∈ Im O : |p| = 1},        T p S 6 = p⊥ ,       Jp U = p × U.      (2054)

    Write D for ambient differentiation and ∇ for tangential projection. Differentiating hV, pi = 0

skewness gives the other identity

AI.5    What changes under a diffeomorphism or a complex atlas

AI.10     The sphere restriction, with a proof of the needed Bott generation
We prove that the positive-dimensional spheres admitting almost complex structures are exactly
S 2 and S 6 . The characteristic-class argument is the one discussed by Konstantis–Parton, Sections
3–6. We supply the needed generation step in complex K-theory by polynomial clutching, so
its required integrality does not rest on an unproved appeal to Bott periodicity. The complete
polynomial clutching and integral generation argument needed here is printed in section AI.10.1
and section AI.10.2 and section AI.10.3.

AI.10.1    Bundles, clutching, and based loops

All bases in section AI.10.1 and section AI.10.2 and section AI.10.3 are compact Hausdorff spaces.
For such a space Y , K 0 (Y ) is the group completion of the direct-sum monoid of finite-rank
complex vector bundles. Thus its elements are differences [E] − [F ], with the relation that adding
the same bundle to both terms does not change the difference. Tensor product makes this a ring.
    We use two elementary bundle facts, with their proofs. Every bundle E over compact Y
embeds in a trivial bundle: choose finitely manyptrivializations and a partition of unity ρi
subordinate to them, and send v ∈ Ey to the list ( ρi (y)vi )i of its local coordinates, with zero
entries off the corresponding supports. At least one ρi (y) is positive, so the map is injective on
each fibre. Its image is a subbundle, and the orthogonal complement gives E ⊕ E ⊥ ≃ 1N . The
orthogonal projection onto the image is continuous, as is seen in a local frame by the formula
T (T ∗ T )−1 T ∗ .
    Second, bundles pulled back by homotopic maps from a compact space are isomorphic. Embed
the bundle over the product with the homotopy interval in a trivial bundle as just described, and
let p(y, t) be its range projection. Uniform continuity gives a finite partition of the interval on
which consecutive projections differ in norm by less than one, uniformly in y. For projections p, q
with kp − qk < 1, the map q : im p → im q is injective, since kqvk ≥ (1 − kp − qk)kvk. Reversing
p, q gives equal ranks, so it is an isomorphism; its inverse is continuous in local finite matrices.
Composing these finite isomorphisms proves the assertion. This proof applies equally with a
compact disk included in the base.
    Apply these facts to a bundle on S 2 × Y . Its restrictions to the closed hemispheres are
pullbacks of bundles on Y , by contraction of the disks. Their restrictions at one equatorial point
identify those two bundles, say with E0 . Adding the pullback of a complement of E0 makes both
hemisphere bundles trivial. The stabilized bundle is then obtained from a clutching map

                                       g : Y × T −→ GLr (C).                                 (2114)

    Changing one hemisphere frame by g(y, 1)−1 makes g(y, 1) = Ir . Homotopies of such based
loops give isomorphic stable bundles: glue throughout the homotopy and apply the preceding
interval result. Block sum of loops gives direct sum of bundles. Pointwise product gives the same
stable sum, by the explicit based homotopy

                                                   cos θI − sin θI
                                                              

AI.10.4    The degree-one map and the factorial

Collapse the union of subspaces of Pn in which at least one factor is its infinity point. The
quotient is the smash product S 2 ∧ · · · ∧ S 2 , the one-point compactification of R2n , hence a
2n-sphere. Identify it with the outward-oriented unit sphere by

                                    (2x, 1 − |x|2 )
                           x 7−→                    ,         ∞ 7−→ (0, . . . , 0, −1).          (2125)
                                       1 + |x|2
    At x = 0, the derivative in the 2n tangent directions is twice the identity, and the outward
normal is the last positive coordinate. Moving that normal to the front has sign (−1)2n = 1; thus
the map has positive local degree. The resulting collapse map f : Pn → S 2n has degree one and

                   f ∗ u = u1 · · · un   for the positive generator u ∈ H 2n (S 2n ; Z).         (2126)

    It is an isomorphism on cohomology in degrees zero and 2n. It is not an isomorphism on the
full cohomology when n > 1: the product has the additional classes uI in intermediate degrees.
This corrects the broader wording in Konstantis–Parton, Section 6 without altering the map
used in their top-degree argument.
